maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is an important day for women in Canada and around the world. On the one hand, it allows us to reflect on the progress we have made towards equality, as we celebrate the tenth anni-verary of the adoption by the United Nations of The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.

At the same time, we are reminded that we have barely scratched the surface of our understanding of the

December 18, 1989
Routine Proceedings
root causes of discrimination against women, and we are profoundly disturbed at the depth of that discrimination and frequently at the horror of its manifestation.
In this battle to eliminate discrimination, the convention is the legal instrument setting out the basic standards necessary to achieve women's equality. It covers areas as wide-ranging as employment equity, equal access to education and health care, participation in public life and equal treatment before the law. Its adoption in 1979 represented the culmination of decades of work by women's organizations and by the UN Commission on the Status of Women.
Canada was proud to ratify this convention in 1981, recommitting itself nationally and internationally to the goal of eradicating discrimination against women in all its forms. As of today, 98 other nations have also pledged to embody and enforce its principles.
In Canada as a society we see the necessity for economic self-sufficiency for women as fundamental to the elimination of discrimination. The ability to economically sustain oneself and one's family is as important to women as it is to men, not simply for survival but for pride, dignity, self-confidence and optimism for the future of one's children.
We also know that violence toward women and sexual harassment are linked at least in part to women's lack of economic self-sufficiency. Unhappily, our struggles to achieve equality and self-sufficiency have failed to eliminate the humiliating and tragic consequences of these most ancient and obscene forms of discrimination.
There is no clearly marked map which delineates the boundary where natural and healthy sexual tension between men and women begins to break down into offensive and demeaning behaviour. Men, as well as women, are struggling to redefine their relationships with each other so that the end result is sexual expression with dignity and mutual respect.
However, for too many still in our society as in other societies there is no boundary. There are still some men who view harassment and violence as their right and as their legitimate means of expressing superiority. It is, in other words, their right to discriminate against women. In recent days, we have been made more acutely aware than ever of where the aberrant form of that manifestation of this so-called right may lead.
The stark tragedy which we have been faced with in Canada can lead us to oversimplify the causes of the barriers we, as women, have still to overcome. It can reinforce our view of ourselves as constantly vulnerable, as perpetual victims.
Let us remember today, as we celebrate this tenth anniversary, that much has been done, that in every avenue of Canadian life, there is activity that is building a better life for all of us. Let us take pride in the fact that women have been the leaders in defining the means to eliminate discrimination and in promoting a broad social agenda that has been embraced by political parties of all stripes and that is changing the way we deal with each other. Let us remember as well that men as well as women must consciously, in their every day behaviour, seek to end the discrimination that diminishes all of us.
In February 1990, Canada will present its second progress report to the United Nations on the measures we have taken to implement the convention. Although much is still to be done, Canada can be proud of its record on women's rights. On the legislative front, the principles of the UN Convention have been embodied in Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Our employment equity legislation reflects the fundamental principle that business and employers, as well as governments, must become responsible for solutions to discrimination in the workplace. Proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act will enhance maternity and parental benefits. We have put in place measures to enforce court-ordered support and maintenance payments and programs to encourage women entrepreneurs, to name a few, among a broad range of initiatives.
In addition, we are urging the provinces to examine women's training needs and health concerns with us and together we are working on the availability and affordability of child care.
There are urgent objectives still to be met. For example, obstacles remain much more acute among certain groups such as aboriginal women, immigrant women, visible minority women, disabled women, elderly women, and, as a government, we are paying particular attention to their needs and concerns.
As a signatory to the convention, Canada has also made a commitment to implement measures that enable parents to combine work and family obligations in new ways that deal with our new social forms, and here governments at all levels are developing strategies to prompt changes in attitudes, programs, services and
December 18, 1989

legislation. But let us not forget that while governments can lead, there must be leadership through a broad range of activities in our community.
Discrimination against women violates the basic principles of equality of rights and respect for human dignity that are the due of all citizens of our planet.
[Translation\
I am confident that, despite difficulties and setbacks, Canada will continue to set an example towards the elimination of obstacles that inhibit the ability of women to achieve their full potential as participants in, and contributors to, society.

Women have much to take pride in, and those of us here today honour them in their ability to contribute and participate as we have in the past. We must all of us remember together that women who perform so much in our society out of their talents and their natural ability to contribute to our well being will continue to do so in the future and will continue to take pride in their ability to do so.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to mark the tenth anniversary of the adoption of the United Nations Convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women. The day is important because it marks the acceptance, at least on paper, of a new global direction, a direction that will eventually tear down the walls of inequality and allow each one of us to live and work without the unfair burden of gender discrimination.
But let us make no mistake. The minister's statement has highlighted an important point, namely, that we still have a long way, a very long way to go in addressing major issues in our society here in Canada which affect women.
The force of the United Nations Convention is only as strong as each independent signatory wishes it to be. As in the case of the United Nations Charter of Rights and Freedoms, some signatories continue to be the greatest violators of human rights.
Can we stand and proclaim that we here in Canada are seriously addressing the problem of inequality and that we can be proud of our record on women's rights? I do not think so. The minister cited the work of this
Routine Proceedings
government listing the first embodiment of the principles of the UN Convention in Section 15 of our own Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
But while the non obstante clause exists and Section 15 is in jeopardy, I do not think that we can congratulate ourselves. What message is this government sending to the women of Canada when we have professed to entrench equality in a document where equality is essentially not entrenched?
The minister further pointed to the employment equity legislation that exists. This is remarkable considering that the government is still embroiled in a dispute with hospital service workers, predominantly women, who are being paid substantially less than their male colleagues. Even with a ruling against the government from the Human Rights Commission, this government has refused to move toward pay equity.
A recently released study has shown that women employed in Canadian banks make only 56 cents for every dollar paid to male employees and, further, although women outnumber male bank workers 70 to one, there are virtually no women in banks' upper management in Canada.
This government recently introduced legislation on abortion which criminalizes women for exercising control over their own reproduction. This government professes to be committed to the cause of women but with a sweep of its mighty arm, it slashed funding by 15 per cent from vital national women's programs. It is one thing to say that we are leaders in the realm of equality and it is another thing altogether to actually lead.
Where is real pay equity and where, oh where, is a national child care program that is acknowledged by all to be the only true bridge to true employment equity?
The road to eliminating discrimination is a long one. I applaud the intentions of the United Nations and of Canadian governments past and present, but indeed let us not forget that there is much work still be done.
The examples that I have listed illustrate that we are a long way from achieving a truly equal society. More distressing, the events two weeks ago at the University of Montreal reinforce the notion that women are still

December 18, 1989
Routine Proceedings
perceived by far too many to be a group infringing on the natural domain of men.
Is there hope? Of course there is. But the hope lies in progress, courage and government action. The hope lies in such government action that is honest, consistent and progressive. The hope lies in government that shows its true commitment to gender equality and acts rather than congratulates itself for work which is still unfinished. The hope lies in the recognition, some day in the future, by this government and by all governments that women truly do hold up half the sky.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women has requested that this day be a day of national mourning for the 14 young engineering students who were massacred in Montreal. I would like to support the call for that day of mourning and also the request that Canadians make donations to their local rape relief centres, to organizations that are working toward ending violence against women, and I would urge members of Parliament and all Canadians to take that day of mourning seriously and to perhaps make donations if they are able.
The minister focused her remarks on the progress that women have made toward equality, and I congratulate the women of Canada for that progress. But on this tenth anniversary of the United Nations Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination against Women, I would like to look closely at the Convention and point out here what still needs to be done in our country.
The minister has said that Canada can be proud of its record on women's rights. I wonder if the government is proud of spending $17 million on 38 strip clubs in Canada while still withholding the bulk of $22 million that is earmarked for Project Haven, a capital grants program for shelters for battered women, because of regulatory red tape.
It is ironic that Article 13(b) of the convention asks signatories to observe equality in credit lending. Women are still discriminated against in terms of bank loans and credit, while this government invests in strip clubs.
Also ironic is this government's recent and rather flagrant violation of Articles 2(c) and (d) and Article
11(d) which deal with equal pay for work of equal value. Pay equity is what the federal hospital workers, mainly women, have been demanding since the early 1980s. They had to take this government to court and they won. The government still refuses to entrench fair wages in the collective agreement. Instead, within the past couple of weeks, we have witnessed the sorry sight of these unfairly treated workers being legislated back to work.
The government's abortion law, introduced this year, contradicts Articles 2 and 16(l)(e) of the convention. This proposed abortion law will discriminate against women because it controls women's reproduction and not men's. It limits women's choices. It targets women's fertility by imposing arbitrary regulations on women's decisions whether or not to bear children.
In Canada it is illegal to discriminate against women because they are women. Yet Employment and Immigration's language training programs for immigrants contain an inherent bias against women that has not yet been addressed by this government. In fact, the government is being taken to court again over its human rights violations.
One in 10 Canadian women is not covered by the Canadian Human Rights Act. In Canada's second report to the convention, on its progress toward equality it mentioned the 1985 Equality for All report. The recommendation to include sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for discrimination is still being ignored by this government some five years later.
Article 7 of the convention guarantees women's rights to participate in the formulation of government policy and to participate in non-governmental organizations and associations concerned with the public and political life of the country. The Conservative government responded to this by slashing the Secretary of State's program for women by 15 per cent and funding to the National Action Committee on the Status of Women by 50 per cent.
I am glad that our party, the New Democratic Party, has contributed to the government's next report on the participation of women by being the first national political party in North America to elect a woman as its leader.
December 18, 1989

Routine Proceedings
Article 11(e) establishes a right to social security, contrary to the government's clawback policy on pensions and on family allowances. Article ll(2)(c) speaks of a development of a network of child care facilities. Where is Canada's much needed child care program? Will this government once again introduce a program two months before an election, only to have it die once again on the Order Paper?
Articles 3 and 5 can be applied to bring in pornography legislation, legislation that attacks violence and pornography and not sexuality.
There are three other points made in Canada's second report on its implementation of the Convention that need examining. One is its glorification of the Court Challenges Program. I hope that this means that the program will be extended. The second is the repeal of discrimination in the Indian Act. However, there still does remain discrimination in the Act since reinstated women can only pass status down to the first generation while men can pass status down to subsequent generations.
The report also discusses the prison for women. I visited the Kingston prison for women and I found the conditions there just absolutely shocking. I would hope that in Canada's next report, there will be real, rather than imagined, progress to comment on as far as the prison for women in Kingston goes.
The preamble of the convention says that signatories are "concerned that in situations of poverty, women have the least access to food, health care, education, training and opportunities for employment and other needs, convinced that the establishment of the new international economic order, based on equity and justice, will contribute significantly towards the promotion of equality between men and women-".
In Canada, the devastating reality is that one in three female single parents in the paid workforce cannot keep her family out of poverty and 53.4 per cent of femaleheaded, single parent families are poor. Three-quarters of all poor seniors are women.
What we need to fulfil our convention obligations is really a new economic order, one that puts people first, one for which full employment is a priority, one that redistributes wealth, an economic order that is based on equality and justice for all.

The petitioners are distraught at the news that the government is going to proceed with the goods and services tax and make the announcement tomorrow that it will be reduced to 7 per cent. I personally feel depressed to read all of the things they have drawn to our attention which cause them to be so discouraged and disillusioned with the government.
In summary, they are asking the government to please have some sensitivity as to what is going on in the country and back off from this cruel, brutal tax.

They state it is an unprecedented tax grab from the pockets of Canadians. It will hit them not only with higher taxes, but with higher inflation, higher interest rates and higher unemployment. They humbly

pray and call upon Parliament to reject the proposed goods and services tax.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege today to present a petition to the House of Commons pursuant to Standing Order 36. There are actually eight petitions signed by 417 people in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt, from the communities of Carmi, Salal, Princeton, Hedly, Merritt and the Lower Nicola.
These people are concerned, as are so many others across this country, with the imposition of a goods and services tax of any nature whatsoever. They have asked the government to ensure, if and when there is a broad public consensus on a sales tax measure to replace the manufacturers' sales tax, that it not be an opportunity for the government to impose a massive tax grab.
They are asking this government to ensure that the tax burden is not shifted to ordinary Canadians but is fairly shifted throughout the whole of Canada.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition signed by quite a number of British Columbia residents opposing the goods and services tax. The petitioners state that this is an unfair form of taxation which permits wealthy individuals and corporations to pay little or no tax while forcing lower and middle-income taxpayers to bear the burden of national taxes. The petition also states that the government is now trying to tax reading, haircuts, diapers, coffins and home heating fuels.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to reject the current proposal, to reform the tax system and to cease with a proposal which will shift the tax burden on to ordinary Canadians through a regressive consumption tax instead of through real tax reform.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I also have a second petition which opposes cuts to VIA Rail. The petitioners ask Parliament to guarantee VIA sufficient support to carry out its mandate to provide passenger services in Canada.

number of people in the Big River community of Saskatchewan in the Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency. It is a petition circulated by One Voice, the senior's network, that calls upon Parliament to abandon the proposed measures that will clawback the old age security and family allowance benefits undermining the principle of universality in social programs. They state that it is a tax that would discriminate against recipients of old age security and family allowance benefits. They call upon Parliament to abandon this and maintain an old age security and family allowance benefit program that is tied to the level of income.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN

The petitioners are indicating that the goods and services tax is a regressive tax. They call upon Parliament to reject the proposal for the goods and services tax, to reform the taxation system so there is an effective minimum tax tax on wealthy individuals and corporations, to ensure that if and when there is a broad public consensus on sales tax measures to replace the manufacturers' sales tax that this reform not be an opportunity for the federal government impose a massive tax grab and, finally, for the government to cease with the proposal which will shift the tax burden on to ordinary Canadians through a regressive consumption tax instead of a thorough real tax reform.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present to this house four petitions certified correct by the clerk of petitions. They contain the signatures of Canadians who reside in the communities of Hamilton, Burlington, Stoney Creek, Ancaster, Dundas and Caledonia.
The petitioners state that the Conservative federal government wants to impose on Canadians a new general tax of 9 per cent on all goods and services which will be hidden from Canadians and applied to virtually everything they buy. They say that the imposition of this new general goods and services tax will cause serious and unfair hardship to low and middle income Canadians and that the imposition of this tax will create an onerous burden on small business. They call on Parliament to
December 18, 1989

reject the proposed goods and services tax, be it at 9 per cent today or 7 per cent tomorrow.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 36 to present a petition from my constituents on the Bonavista Peninsula; Newman's Cove, Amherst Cove, Birchy Cove, Bonavista, Elliston. These communities are looking at the crisis in the fisheries that we will be talking about later on today. They are looking at Bill C-21 under which 26,000 people will have reduced UI benefits and under which 9,000 in Newfoundland will probably lose all their UI. They are looking at the goods and services tax on top of this and on top of the provincial sales tax of 12 per cent, which itself may even rise.
If there is any such thing as a humble prayer and resolution, my constituents are asking for this to get rid of this goods and services tax. As was said by one of my colleagues, the member for Kamloops, let us reduce it from 7 per cent to 0 per cent. Let us get rid of the whole thing.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also rise under Standing Order 36 to present petitions from a number of small businesses in my riding.
This is a petition about the goods and services tax and these small business people, 441 of them, say that the goods and services tax is an unfair form of taxation because it forces small businesses to carry a disproportionate share of the tax burden. They state that it will be an implementation nightmare for small businesses in Canada and that the $600 motion offered to small business to offset the cost of administering this tax is completely inadequate.
The petitioners call upon this government to reject the goods and services tax at any percentage rate and to consult with business, labour and consumer groups to reach a broad consensus on reform of our tax system and to ensure that there is a real reform of the tax system to provide a healthy climate for small business in Canada.

maintopic: TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE ADOPTION BY THE UNITED NATIONS OF THE CONVENTION ON THE ELIMINATION OF ALL FORMS OF DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN

Nanaimo and Vancouver who are opposed to the implementation of the goods and services tax.

Valley): Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition to this House under Standing Order 36 regarding the grief and suffering tax. food for human consumption, most clothing and footwear, and certain drugs and devices for the handicapped are exempt.
Excise taxes of various rates are also imposed under the Excise Tax Act on selected commodities such as jewellery, playing cards, wine, tobacco products, lighters, heavy vans and automobiles, and gasoline.
Excise duties are imposed at various rates by the Excise Act on domestically produced beer, alcoholic spirits and tobacco products.
In addition to the above taxes on commodities, the Excise Tax Act imposes a tax on certain insurance contracts effected outside Canada and a tax on air travel.
The Excise Tax Act also imposes an 11-per-cent telecommunication programming services tax and an 11-per-cent telecommunication services tax.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to have the opportunity to reply so immediately to some of those comments.
On the matter of the cutbacks I feel that I have some obligation to respond to the minister's remarks. I think that the people of the national capital region are indeed aware of the fiscal mess into which the government has got the country. I think they are willing to do their part to try to alleviate the incredible burden that has been thrust upon the nation by five years of fiscal incompetence which has more than doubled the national debt in that time.
I think the government needs to be aware at this time of the importance of national symbols, the importance of realizing, on the part of all Canadians, the fact that we have institutions as well as programs in this country that tie us together.
December 18, 1989

The national capital plays a major part in the development of a system of national values and an awareness of the fact that being Canadian has a symbolic importance beyond where we were bom or where we happen to live. I think we should all be concerned, whatever side we are on, when the government and its ministers try to excuse the inability of the government to manage its finances by somehow criticizing or dumping on one region of the country, especially when that region, more than others, in a way embodies the identity of the nation. I think it is very important that those institutions that are centred on the national capital continue to play that role.
Even as the President of the Treasury Board was standing in the House of Commons on Friday talking about what he was going to cut, the Prime Minister of Canada was in Chambly, Quebec, where there is a by-election by some coincidence going on, talking about how he was spending, about what he was doing to buy votes in that area. I suggest that the government start to look at its own iniquitous practice of trying to buy votes before it starts to talk about the national capital region being some kind of privileged area.
On the matter of time allocation on this bill, I think the minister has also said some things that bear examination. He has talked about the effort on this side of the House to protect the wealthy. I hardly think that asking the House of Commons to take the time to consider the most important social policy change in a generation in this country should be interpreted merely as trying to protect the wealthy.
We have built, for better or for worse, a series of programs in this country based on the assumption that universality should be the guiding principle. We have done that not just with respect to our family allowances and old age pensions, although those are important. We have also done it with our educational system. We have done it as well with our medical aid system. We have accepted the idea that Canadians, whatever their economic situation, should share a common basis of wellbeing based on being Canadian, whether they are rich or poor, whether they live in Ottawa, Orillia, Peace River or Halifax. Wherever they live, whatever their income, Canadians are entitled to a common basis of social programs in this country.
Time Allocation
The government is tearing down national institutions. It is going across the country encouraging criticism of the national capital. It is underfunding the National Arts Centre and its ministers say we should not even call these institutions national because it offends some separatists in Quebec, that we should call them Canadian rather then national. While the government is tearing these things down it is tearing down the basic social concept, the contract whereby we live together in this country, and it is saying, "You can only have a few hours to debate it".
The clawback should not even be in an income tax amendment bill. If the clawback is going to be introduced it should be done as part of social policy change. There should have been a discussion paper following up the one that was issued by the minister of health in 1985 in which the minister of Health at the time, now the minister of energy, said that to tax back old age pensions would be unfair and unacceptable. He said at the same time that it might not be unfair with family allowances. We could argue about that, but he specifically mentioned that the old age pension should be protected.
What happened to the discussion paper? It went to a parliamentary committee, it was studied, it died. There was no further discussion, no more policy papers, no more indication that the government was considering introducing the most significant social policy change in a generation. None of that was done.
Instead the government, and the Prime Minister in particular, went around during the election campaign and said, "Social programs, especially for the elderly, will not be diminished. They will be improved". And with the very first budget after the election we had the clawback introduced. Did he tell his mother, I wonder.
I am sure all Canadians are disgusted at the memory of the Prime Minister of Canada parading his own mother on to an election platform as an example of his good faith to the seniors of Canada. Four months later the Minister of Finance gets up and says he is going to tax back Mrs. Mulroney's old age pension. Why was that not put before the people during the election campaign? Why is it that now, four days before we are to adjourn for Christmas, in an Income Tax Act amendment bill, which has all kinds of things in it from the budget, which the Department of Finance itself tried to amend in committee and all of its amendments were out of order, we have

December 18, 1989
Time Allocation
to be constrained in the time we have to debate such an essential issue?
Instead of having time to study it, instead of having time to hear the groups of Canadians across the country who are concerned about whether the erosion of universality is going to lead to the erosion of universality in so many other areas, we have to abandon that debate, we have to turn it over to the editorial writers and hope that they will take time to raise with Canadians this essential issue of public policy.
This is scandalous, Madam Speaker. It is scandalous not just because it is closure but because it is closure on such an important measure. It should not be done. I suggest to the government, in view of the failure of the Department of Finance to get its amendments introduced at committee stage, in view of the implicit recognition that comes with that failure that the bill itself is fundamentally flawed, that it needs to be amended, that the government should withdraw the bill, forget about tiying to push it through this week, introduce a proper income tax amendment bill in the new year and put the clawback aside until it has been considered and debated by Canadians across Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the young people of Canada are studying the history of Canada years from now they will look back on 1989 as the year that the Government of Canada decided to abandon one of the crucial principles of what being a Canadian is all about. Being a Canadian means that if you get sick, it does not matter who you are, rich or poor, whether you live in Newfoundland or Saskatchewan, you will have adequate medical attention. It means that your children will go to school. You do not have to pay extra. You do not have to send them to private schools or special schools which are going to cost you money. Your contribution through the general tax system will take care of that education. It means that if you are raising children you get a family allowance cheque every month until the children are age 18. And it means that if you are an elderly person, no matter who you are, rich or poor, no matter what your ethnic origins, your religion, or where you live, yob get a pension. That is what it means to be a Canadian.
This year the government decided it was going to change all of that, that it was going to tear universality up and throw it out of the window. The government says that it has had enough. It does not want a fair system for
everybody in this country, it wants charity. If you can prove to the government that you are poor enough to receive a pension, then you will get a pension. If you are poor enough to prove to the government you require family allowance, then you will get family allowance cheques.
This means that we are going back to the old days of the means test, a degrading experience. That is Tory times. This is what being a Conservative in this country is all about. I suspect that those people who are watching the House of Commons on their television sets today, trying to understand what is going on, Canadian is all about. If they look through all the veils and so on of what the various ministers have said, lo and behold, way out there is the free trade deal staring them in the face. Because the free trade deal says that we have agreed, as a country, to harmonize our social programs with those in the United States of America.
We know how abysmal the health care system is in the United States. We know how families are the last sort of caring aspect of the American administration, the American way of life, in terms of support and care,. That is what is happening here today. To make it worse, not only is this government dismantling something that is fundamental to being a Canadian, it is now saying: "We don't want the opposition members of the House of Commons to speak about this because if they speak about it the people who are watching their television sets at home today will be aware of what is going on". It decided: "We are going to muzzle the debate. We are going to curtail the debate. We are going to shut down the debate. We are going to introduce dictatorial, totalitarian methods that say we no longer want the Parliament of Canada to explain to the people of Canada what this government is doing".
That has to be a very dark day for freedom of speech. It is a dark day for those who believe in the fundamentals of a parliamentary democracy. It is a dark day for those Canadians who actually believe that democracy is something we are struggling to keep. As we see other countries, particularly in the east bloc, begin to slowly introduce the principles that we have held high for generations, this Conservative government has decided to dismantle this and make this House of Commons and Parliament of Canada into an ineffectual place. As soon as it hears criticisms coming from members of the
December 18, 1989

opposition parties it says: "We don't want to hear this any more. We are going to curtail debate".
That is what the government has done this morning. I do not know if members on the government side realize what is going on today. The Minister of Justice-of justice of all people-stood up and said: "Listen, I know that we introduced this legislation, that it is dastardly legislation, mean-spirited and cruel." What it means to be a Conservative government is to introduce that kind of legislation. He went on to say: "We are going to drive this through". The government closed off debate at second reading and sent it to committee.
Committee is where experts are asked to come from across Canada and examine legislation. We know what happened. It went to committee and members of the New Democratic Party stood up and said: "Listen, if we are going to change the social policy of this country so drastically as a result of this Conservative government and this legislation, let us bring in experts, let us bring in those who understand the implications to explain to the members of the government what this is actually going to do to people and how mean and cruel this whole legislation is".
Did the government do that? Absolutely not. Once again it did not want to hear what people had to say. It did not want to hear the experts. It did not want to hear what it was actually going to do to families living in Atlantic Canada, western Canada and northern Ontario and Quebec. It did not want to hear what this actually means to those people who struggled and built this country. Now the government says: "Well, we changed our mind. You no longer will get an old age pension cheque. Because you have saved and worked hard to provide for yourself we feel you do not need a cheque any more and so we are going to take away this critical right of what being a Canadian is all about". That is the essence of this legislation.
What did the government members do in committee? They said: "We do not want to hear all of this information because if people understand what we are doing they are going to get very, very concerned." They cut off the witnesses.
Time Allocation
We thought that here we are back in the of the House of Commons, we will have a chance now to explain to the people of Canada what this all means. Then the government introduced today time allocation, the muzzling of Parliament, closure of Parliament. "Do not let them talk on the terms of the legislation". That is what has happened. Two days from now we will not be able to speak on this legislation. This legislation will be passed, all gone, done. This government will have changed the direction of the country forever and ever until the new government, the New Democratic government decides to put it right back where it should be and introduce the principle of universality once again.
Not only is it bad that the Conservatives want to take away people's pensions-which is what they are going to do essentially-not only is it bad that they are going to muzzle Parliament, curtail debate and use their jack-booted tactics to close this debate down, which is bad enough in itself, but the bill itself is a disaster. The government came into committee-something which has never happened in the history of Canada before-and said: "Listen, we have made such a disastrous mistake in drafting this legislation, we are going to require 125 amendments just to make it workable". It is incredible that the government is so sloppy, so loose in its thinking, so uncaring, so callous, so stupid when it comes to drafting legislation that it has to have 125 amendments to it just to make it tolerable to its own members.
As you know, the Speaker said: "This is all nonsense" and threw them all out. He said: "These are not even procedurally acceptable". If the government was just to do the honourable parliamentary thing it would say: "Let's go back and at least draft a bill that you can pass through the House of Commons and do what we want even though it is mean and cruel and against senior citizens and families. If that is what we want to do, then at least let us make it properly acceptable in the House of Commons".
Members of the government did not even do that. The government has shown nothing less than utter contempt for this place. It just said: "Well, if we just draft up anything that is sloppy, you know, we will get it through the House of Commons, the Speaker will let it through". Thank goodness, Madam Speaker, you did not let it through. You said: "Listen, there are some standards in

Time Allocation
here. They can use closure and muzzling of debate and all sorts of procedural tricks to jam inappropriate legislation through". But at least the Chair said: "That is far enough and we are not going to tolerate this nonsense".
If this were the only time the government decided to bring in its heavy hand of the majority and just ignore the minority-if you like the tyranny of the majority-then I suppose we could say: "Well, they did not know any better. They do not understand parliamentary democracy. They do not understand what it means to govern within a democratic framework". This is now a trend. This happens time and time again. It is the only way of course that it can get bad legislation through. From time to time the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party try to improve legislation and make it the best we can. We are not always happy with it but we tiy to do our best.
The government has brought in legislation that essentially, as I said, takes universality and eliminates it, something that as Canadians we have struggled to achieve, something which we hold up high on the world stage and say: "This is what it means to be a Canadian. It does not matter who you are and what you are, you will be able to get the old age security cheque when you are aged 65". Yet this government says: "Well we have changed our mind. We are going to change all that now". This is not the Canada we want to see.
This has happened time and time again. There has been closure, muzzling of Parliament, shutting Parliament down, making it impossible for members to speak. That is not what a parliamentary democracy is all about. That is why we say this government shows contempt for Parliament, the principles of Parliament, the traditions of Parliament and the practices of Parliament day after day.
I want to send to the Prime Minister a very clear message this morning. It is that as far as the New Democratic Party is concerned we are not going to take this any more. To make this place work properly you need to have the support of all of the parties and you need to have the will to make this place work.
In closing, I am simply putting the government on notice this morning that in the future if it plans to use the heavy hand of closure, the jack-booted approach to the parliamentary system, we in this party will not stand
for that. We will pull out all the countless ways and means that we use to make this place effective and efficient. If the government is not going to recognize the practices and traditions of the parliamentary democracy in this country, then I am putting it on notice that we will not co-operate any further in the future and it will not be able to pass, without an incredible struggle, this kind of mean, cruel-spirited legislation that we are seeing here before us today.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot say that I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate. As you know, there are Canadians who would like to hear Members of the House of Commons discuss this bill. They realize it has some extremely negative implications. However, instead of discussing those implications today, we ought to consider the fact that the government will not let us have the kind of open and full debate that we should have here in the House.

One of the problems facing Canadians is to try to figure out why the government is so stubborn about dealing with this particular proposal. It has tried to suggest that people who are suggesting the clawback is not an acceptable proposal are defending the indefensible, defending people with high incomes. Canadians understand the need for a debate on this matter, particularly senior citizens. They understood from the very outset that this was an attack on what was called a sacred trust. They understood from the very beginning that clawing back any amount, no matter what the threshold, was the beginning of the end.
What I find very unsettling is the fact that we have seniors across this country who are among the best organized groups of citizens in Canada telling the government, telling MPs who are not members of the government that we have to debate this issue, that we have to clarify all of the implications that will arise now that the crack is in the facade of universality. We have to go back and tell them that the government has decided unilaterally, because it has more members sitting to your right, Madam Speaker, than to your left, that it is going to impose closure.
December 18, 1989

The government has told us that some seniors support the proposition. I want to quote from Hansard of November 20 when I was involved in a debate on this very issue. I want senior citizens in Canada to understand exactly why closure is being imposed, why time allocation is being imposed. That debate was fairly lengthy and rather heated. I have had people come up to me to suggest that during that debate I should have repeated what hecklers to your right, Madam Speaker, were saying. Out of courtesy I was allowing them to make their interventions, realizing that they were not being picked up and that people who watch these proceedings were not able to understand what was being said. It was suggested to me that that was not a veiy effective means of proceeding because the fact that I might respond could not always be understood because the intervention had not been heard. What I want to do is simply refer to the debate that took place on the clawback proposal on November 20, 1989.
In that debate I was asking members to indicate whether or not when they went back to their constituencies and talked with senior citizens they were being told that this was the kind of legislation that should be introduced, whether it was appropriate, whether it was acceptable, whether it was fair. I was listening to people saying things like: "What about the deficit? What about the debt? Everybody has to pay their share".
It was my argument at that time that many senior citizens in this country have paid enormously to benefit from our system. They have paid in times of war. They have paid in times of depression. They have paid taxes. Most significantly they have paid into retirement plans, the Canada Pension Plan and old age pensions with the thought that the Parliament of Canada would respect what they had done and that the rules of the game would not be changed at a time when they were less able to defend themselves against legislation such as this.
The reason I bring this up is that I want to remind people that the reason the government wants to impose time allocation is that it does not want any more statements like the one I am going to quote. In that debate I was asking the questions: "Do you want senior citizens to pay down the debt? Do you want senior citizens to reduce the debt? Ask them, tell them. Do not
Time Allocation
say it is because you have too much and we want to take some away from you."
In response to my comments the hon. member for Winnipeg South said: "No, that is not what we are saying". Out of courtesy and recognizing what she said I indicated: "What are you saying then?" I asked that in order to provide the hon. member with an opportunity to explain her concern. I want to quote from the debate on November 20, 1989. The hon. member for Winnipeg South said this about the clawback:
What is being said is that what has been given to you is only
deserved if you have an income that is less than what it takes to live on.
Imagine that, Madam Speaker. That is why we are faced with time allocation today. Imagine a Conservative member of this House saying, and I am quoting from Hansard:
What is being said is that what has been given to you-
The senior citizens of Canada:
- is only deserved if you have an income that is less than what it
takes to live on.
That is why we are getting time allocation. When you ask members of the government party to speak out and to explain what is the philosophy behind this, what is the purpose of going after senior citizens in this country, what is the purpose of trying to embarrass them they say: "If you are getting over $50,000 a year there should be a clawback. Never mind whether it is indexed or not. Never mind whether the threshold can be lowered or not". That is why the government cannot afford to have us talk about this too long. People will say, as the member from Winnipeg South said: "What has been given to you is only deserved if you have an income that is less than what it takes to live on".
I cannot believe that all members to your right, Madam Speaker, share that kind of an attitude. Certainly it is shared to some extent. Again in that debate not that long ago-on November 20-the following was said in this House on this very same matter. I was saying that I had been to Alberta and Manitoba and that my experience had not been to have senior citizens say: "My goodness, I am glad that you have begun the process of eroding our security". I have not even heard people 50 and 55 years of age saying that.

December 18, 1989
Time Allocation
I was explaining that what we are hearing from senior citizens around the country is that they are very, very concerned. They are anxious. They see the beginning of the end for any kind of long-term security. Day after day we read reports indicating that people in Canada are living longer and longer. Life expectancy even in the last 10 years has increased dramatically. I am sure that as life expectancy has increased and people are aware that they are going to be around longer the level of anxiety has increased. We have a government that does not seem to understand the need to maintain security in the minds and in the hearts of Canadians-not only senior citizens but, as I indicated in that quote from Hansard, people who are not receiving pensions now but who are very much aware that those days are rapidly coming. They are not very secure.
The point I am making is as to why the government feels the need to clamp down on Parliament, to shut off debate, and we can quote again from that debate in response to the comments I made. I said that I had not heard senior citizens, not even people 50 and 55 years of age, say that they wanted this process of eroding security to begin. The hon. Minister of State for Privatization in response said: "They have said: 'We do not need it, so tax it back.'"
I do not think the government can take much more of that. I believe that it would need to recognize that its members are having a hard time articulating the problem that it is addressing with the clawback. You have one person on the government side saying: "What is given to you is only deserved if you have an income that is less than what it takes to live on". Another member, a member of the Cabinet, is saying that senior citizens are telling him: "We do not need it, so tax it back".
I think Canadians are extremely concerned. As my friend the Elouse Leader for the New Democratic Party said, every time a sensitive issue comes up we are being told: "You cannot discuss it any more. We are going to put it through". I hope that Canadians understand that we are going to continue to fight for the rights, not only of senior citizens in this country, but for everyone who believes that Canada has developed a system second to none in this world. We are going to fight to protect it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to express my great displeasure at this government's attempt once again to gag Parliament. I can certainly understand why the government would introduce such a closure motion today. It is because hon. members opposite have been checking with their constituents. They have been finding out that the longer this debates continues on this and other regressive measures that this government has introduced in this place the lower and lower the popularity of the Conservative Party falls.
This is an abuse of the rights of parliamentarians to a full debate on social policy changes that are taking place around us. This government is intent and hell-bent on making sure that that type of debate does not see the light of day.
I listened earlier when the Minister of Justice spoke. It is no wonder he had such a hard time keeping a straight face. He said that he was getting calls from our constituents. I do not think that he has received calls from any of my constituents telling him that they want this bill passed as quickly as possible. He says that the opposition parties have spent too much time, way too much time, holding it up at report stage. Either he has gone into a deep sleep or he has lost all sense of timing.
This particular measure, Bill C-28, has been debated at report stage for only one hour. It is one of the most major changes that we have seen in any bill before this place. Perhaps the only more significant change was with the free trade debate, and the government did the same as it has done today. When it has a piece of legislation that it does not want Canadians to listen to debate on, it invokes closure or time allocation. It did it then and it is trying to do it now.
On this particular piece of legislation it is important for Canadians to know that what members of this government are doing is ending universality of social programs through the back door. It is doing it in a bill called C-28. It is doing it with the clawback, the scratch back, the gouge and screw back. That is exactly what it is doing.
The Minister of Justice said earlier that the Liberals do not want the rich to be taxed. I hate to tell him this but since 1984 with the inflation rate the purchasing power of $50,000 is equal to about $33,000 in 1984. Not even that member opposite would have had the gall to get up in this House in 1984 and say that somebody who makes $33,000 a year is rich. I do not think he even has the gall to get up today to say that someone who makes $50,000 a year is rich. Let us look at how regressive this
December 18, 1989

particular bill is. Then we will understand why they wanted to invoke time allocation again to kill the debate.
Let us take an example of two individuals who worked the same number of years in the workforce. Those two individuals made about the same amount of money. Both are heading for retirement. One of them made sure that they lived on as little as they possibly could. They did not take their trips to Florida. They did not move into a five-bedroom house when a three bedroom house would do. They did not spend money on Bingo or go to the horse races to bet at the track. They had a pretty tough life. What they did was put their money into investments so that when they retired they would reap the benefits of good fiscal planning.
Buddy next door said: "This is crazy. I could be dead tomorrow. So what I am going to do is have a heck of a time. I am going to Florida. I am going to spend every penny that I can possibly spend. I am going to go out boozing every night. I am going to go to the racetrack. I am going to drive the biggest car on the block. I am going to have one hell of a time". That is what he says.
Ele spends his disposable income. He does not invest. Then he turns 65. Under this legislation because he did not plan and because he had such a great life he is going to be allowed to keep his old age pension. The poor bugger next door who planned all his life and had a pretty meagre life will now find himself because of good planning getting his old age pension taxed back.
Surely to goodness there are no members opposite who are going to look at that particular scenario-and it is not a far-fetched scenario-and say that this is fairness, that this government policy wreaks of fairness. It wreaks of something, and it is not fairness.
The other thing that most Canadians and I have a lot of problem with in this legislation is the fact that this government has misled the Canadian public on its intentions on universality and its intentions to tax back old age security. Let us not forget-and I know members opposite would love to have this forgotten, which is why they are trying to put closure on this debate-that in 1984 the Prime Minister told everybody that the Conser-
Time Allocation
vative Party would never touch social programs, that they were a sacred trust. Then they came in and tried to deindex the old age security pensions. That is what they did. If it was not for a lady from Ottawa-Vanier who pointed her finger at him and said: "Good-bye Charlie Brown", we would have had the deindexing of the old age pension. You know: "Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me".
In 1988 during the election campaign we had the Prime Minister-and this shows you, in my opinion anyway, the complete lack of faith in the Canadian electorate, and I guess perhaps the single-mindedness and the almost arrogance of this government-knowing full well that he had misled the seniors of Canada in 1984 during the election campaign using his mother as a prop. He took his mother out during the campaign and said:, "My mother is on old age security. Would I ever do anything that would harm my mother? I certainly would not do anything to harm her." He used his own mother as a prop. How low can you get? That is pretty low, Madam Speaker. I cannot think of anything lower, except the use of closure on the debate of this bill.

speechtext:
My hon. friend over here says: "They are digging a well-" If the Canadian public had their way they would dump them in the well and they would fill the well in.
This particular debate that is not going to take place is a debate on our social programs. It is a debate on fairness. Let us not forget that up until 1971 the people of Canada who were working and paying income tax paid in to the old age security system. I think 1971 was the last year that it was still on the income tax forms. It was a special surtax of about 4 per cent. This was not a bit of welfare. It was the Canadian people saying through their government that they believed that those individuals who built this country and made it strong had the right, when they were looking at retirement planning, to expect something back from the government. They paid taxes all their lives. They built this country and made it strong. They paid into the fund and the least that they

Time Allocation
should expect is a few dollars a month coming back from the federal government when they go into retirement.
What this government has done with this bill is to ensure that those seniors who are making over $50,000 start to get their old age pensions taxed back. If that were not bad enough, what it has also done is to ensure, because there is not full indexing on that particular provision, that the older Canadians get the poorer they get. That is absolutely despicable.
I think the Leader of the Opposition back on May 9 in a question in the House put it very well. He talked about what effect the Consumer Price Index minus 3 per cent would have when the threshold would be reached in the future. What it means is that somebody who is going on retirement right now and perhaps making $35,000-and that is not a lot of money-as a result of good planning, by the time they are 75, just 10 years down the road, they are going to have some of their Old Age Security taxed back. It is not just that this bill is so unpalatable right today, it is the effect in the long term of making older Canadians poorer that this government will have to pay for.
I see that my time is nearly up. I wish to join with other members from my side at least who find this motion on time allocation to be absolutely inappropriate. It is nothing short of an attempt by members opposite to hide their latest dirty deed.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is not a timed speech so you may invoke closure at any time. We are all vety used to that on this side of the House.
As to the definition of universality, we have had a difficult time in getting the government to define it for us. I have taken the opportunity to check in the dictionary. It means "of or belonging to or done by all persons or things in the world or in the class concerned applicable to all cases". The thesaurus goes on to say that universality means cosmic. It means global. It means infinite. It means pervasive. It means total. It means usual.
However, this government has rewritten not only the rules in the House of Commons-closure is a rule rather than an exception- it has begun to rewrite the dictionary and thesaurus.
It does not say that they will give it to you only to take it back. It does not say that if we take back 4 per cent it is still universality, or we recognize that in 10 years it will be 25 per cent. I am sure eventually it will be 100 per cent. That is universality in reverse.
I think that is what the government has planned for us. It is rewriting not only the rules of the House, not only the dictionary and the thesaurus, but it is rewriting social policy for the whole country.
Every once in a while we forget-and we get tired of mentioning it-the free trade agreement, but I think this is what it is all about. Universality is a watershed of social policy that this government is eroding, in fact decimating.
May I talk about the sad chronology of events of Bill C-28. I was to be the lead speaker for our party on Bill C-28. When I heard the speech of the Minister of State for Finance I was sitting here in great trepidation because I thought I was going to speak to the wrong bill. Not once did he mention the words "universality" or "clawback" in any of his very abbreviated speech. That gave me some trepidation that I was going to speak to the wrong bill. Lo and behold, that was a plan. No one in the government speaks about universality or clawback, and now we know why.
This bill has received very little fanfare. It is suggested that it is not a significant bill; let's push it through very quickly and keep its contents quiet. Member opposite are saying that the New Democrats are speaking for the rich. Nothing could be further from the truth.
The people for whom we are speaking are the entire population of the country. That is what they want to keep quiet. They just want to talk about the $50,000 for the seniors. Those are the only people. No one out there wants to suggest that we should not take it back. That is what they are saying but that is a lie. The whole thing has been a fallacy. The whole thing has been a scam.
We have spoken to universality. At least we have tried to, but this bill touches on many other things. It is an omnibus tax bill. It talks about transfers to provinces, regional development, and post-secondary education. However, because of the way the government has handled it, ramming it down everyone's throats, we have not been able to address most of the issues. We have zeroed in on universality. At least we have tried. The

government's suggestion is: "Let's keep them in the dark. What they don't know won't upset them.''
We presented to the committee a list of 20 possible witnesses. The government members said: "Let's take five or six. We will pick them. You don't. They will all come and say the same thing over and over again." I suggested at that time that government members did not want to hear what they have to say. They were mute and did not ask any questions of any of the witnesses who did appear. It is a story they did not want to hear. That is a sad evaluation of some of those people. The five or six who did come suggested 35 minutes for presentation and questions.
For the committee members on the government side it was a revolving door of individuals. Once in a while I do not mind being laughed at, but throughout the hearings there was a great deal of laughing: "Why are you concerned? Let's wrap this up for Christmas. Let's give the seniors and families of this country a Christmas present."
Some 120 government amendments were thrown out. They were heavier than the bill itself. It was suggested that they would come back with another bill in the new year and clean it all up. I suggest that that is not acceptable. Why this week? Why are we hurrying this up? Tomorrow is GST day, another bit of sad news from members of the government. They know that this clawback will get lost in the GST, another cover-up of the whole thing. They have worked out a very sad stratagem. It is indeed a sad evaluation of the government.
The opposition is growing, but we know it is growing too late. Everybody is tied up with the Christmas shopping rush and they are preoccupied with Christmas spirit, but it is not in the spirit of Christmas that this government operates.
Bill C-28 is personified by Scrooge. They say: "Seniors, humbug. Families, humbug". We are not surprised by the government action. It is expected. We do not accept it, but we are powerless to do anything. Powerless now, but time is on our side. The seniors' time will come; the families' time will come; the Canadian people's time will come. The Canadian people will turf this government.
Time Allocation
We shall not forget their callous attitudes and actions. They are changing the direction of this country. We are headed southward. History will recognize this bill for what it is. Unfortunately history will not unfold for quite a long period of time, but this government and its members will be judged very harshly.
Fie on this government for this bill, fie. If one does not understand what fie is, it is a euphemism for a curse or a plague upon this government for introducing this legislation. The Canadian people shall not forget.

Madam Speaker, I must say that I rise today with great difficulty to discuss Bill C-28 or, more important, the closure that comes with it. As a new member of Parliament I have a lot of difficulty, as do a lot of members, trying to figure out the procedures of the House. When we first came to the House we were told that this was one of the procedures that would not be used very often. I recall the discussion we had with the Whip who told us not to be too worried about closure, that it only happened once in a while.
All of a sudden I notice that closure takes place almost every day in the House. I am getting to know the rules quite well and understand the procedures, but I want to talk a bit about closure and about what this House is supposed to be for. I think it would be important in this debate for members opposite to pay a little attention so they could understand my reasons for thinking why they are here and why they were elected by their constituents.
I was elected to voice my opinion on behalf of the people of Kenora-Rainy River. When I return to the riding on weekends and when the House is not sitting, on a regular basis the people of Kenora-Rainy River give me their input on what is important to the country and what direction they want us to go.
One thing that really bothers me is the fact that on all bills that we have debated closure, in particular, nobody on the other side gets up to represent their constituents. I find that deplorable. It is one thing to vote with the government side because you are a member of the government; "Hold your nose", as they say, and "go ahead and do it".
It is difficult in our party system to vote against your own party. That is understandable. I think people can understand that, but they do not understand when people come to the House, sit here all day long-or in this case for an hour-and not rise once to defend the reason closure is in place, to defend the reason this particular amendment of Bill C-28 is taking place. If

Time Allocation
they agree with closure, then let us change the procedures of the House so that we only debate for an hour and, if that is acceptable to Canadians, then so be it. However if it is not, then we should stop using this particular procedure which was put on the books for purposes of emergencies.
This is not a great emergency. I do not see any seniors outside saying: "Hurry up and put this in place. I can hardly wait to have my hard earned funds taxed back and clawed back as quickly as I can, so get on with it!" I think that is something that the members opposite should pay close attention to.
The people back home are starting to pay closer attention to what the Conservative members are doing. One thing they must be asking themselves over and over again is: "Who is speaking for me? Who is speaking out? Why are they not saying what they think?" If they really believe that this is the way to go for the future, then by all means they should be standing up in their place and doing that.
Another thing that we should touch on is: What does closure really mean? You close the door, the window, or perhaps the lid on something that is open. Whether it be in the fridge or in the cupboard closure means basically that. You put a stop to something. The environmental aspects of closing a door is that you do not want the cold air to come in or, for that matter, they might not want the fresh air to come in.
What we are seeing here with members opposite is that they are putting closure in place because they do not want us as opposition members to use our abilities to speak in the House and to tell the people of Canada what is taking place. That is a very dangerous precedent. To continue doing that on a regular basis really undermines democracy and the ability to speak our minds whether or not they agree with it. Really, it does not make any difference whether they completely agree with my point of view. In this country I have the ability to speak for the people I represent.
Another thing I have noticed is that the government opposite does not like the members of the opposition, members of the Liberal Party in particular, to speak
about the clawback. In essence, they believe that we do not know what we are talking about.
Today I have prepared some quotes we have heard over and over again to make members opposite more aware that aside from the seniors we are not the only ones who are saying it is not good. There are other people who have a common voice, a lot of exposure, and are well respected members of Canadian society speaking on this issue. I think the government should pay closer attention to that.
One Voice, the Canadian seniors network states: "History will remember the clawback as the end of universality, not for its drop in the deficit bucket".
Then there is Don McGillivray, our good friend from The Ottawa Citizen who states: "The policy pretends to continue universality, but in fact cancels it".
Then there is Hugh Winsor of The Globe and Mail of all places who states: "If, as Mr. Mulroney subsequently admitted, tampering in the indexation was wrong in 1985, attempting the same thing with the threshold levels is wrong in 1989".
Leonard Shifrin, in an article published in The Ottawa Citizen states that the finance minister "proceeded to undermine the universality of family allowances and old age pensions".
A report from the National Council of Welfare states: "A social program that delivers benefits to everyone and then collects them all back from some recipients is not universal".
We are not the only ones in Canada who are disappointed that what this government is doing through the back door in a sneaky way is moving away from universality. What it is doing is changing the way we look at ourselves. That is something that should be heavily debated, not something that should be just fed in there very quickly.
A perfect example is the discussion we have had in the House for the last months about VIA. There was no heavy debate on VIA. Therefore we still do not know what we are going to do with VIA Rail.
Do not make the same mistake as other governments have made by not discussing that particular issue. If they want to change the way that Canadians look at themselves, then change the way we as governments are either to give benefits to Canadians or take back benefits

through the tax system. Let us stand up in our place and debate it. If Canadians accept that, then so be it.
One thing of utmost importance is how we as Canadians look after other Canadians. Is this to become a dog eat dog or an "I'm okay, Jack" type of country where if you are lucky enough, you get a good education, good employment and are able to save the amount of dollars required in this day and age to have a long retirement.
Senior citizens are having longer and longer retirements because there are early retirements and people are living longer now than they used to. We are really talking about our future seniors, not necessarily the seniors of today, because the level and the threshold will reduce themselves over time. It will not happen over night. People 20 years from now will be more adversely affected than those of today.
Members opposite keep using the argument: "Why are you protecting the rich, those who make $50,000 a year and over?" I say to them that we are not. We are talking about a fundamental change in direction in how we are looking after the people of Canada. If we are going to do that, we should do it a constructive way.
We should not have closure and one measly hour to debate something so fundamentally unacceptable to Canadians and something that we as opposition members will have to explain in our ridings time and time again in the future. That is very difficult when nobody on the government side wants to stand up and argue the point.
How do I go back and tell the people in my riding why the government is clawing back old age pensions if government members have not stood up and told me why. Therefore, I have to go back and say: "The Conservatives do not know anything. They have not got a clue where they are going, no agenda whatsoever". I suggest that there is no agenda because if they had an agenda they would not be afraid to stand up in their place and tell us why they are doing what they are doing.
