Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to stand up in the House to participate in different debates. However, the one we are participating in today is one where this
Time Allocation
particular government has gone back on its promise. Let us look at the record.
In 1984 the Prime Minister was running to become the Prime Minister of this country. I guess this was probably the biggest mistake the country ever made. At that time he stated: "We will not deindex seniors' pensions. We will not even touch them, the sacred trust". What did his buddy sitting next to him, the Minister of Finance do? In 1985 he turned right around and said: "Seniors, we are going to stick it to you". They attempted deindexing, and the Prime Minister had to face some seniors in front of this House and say: "I would not do it to my mother". Then they tried to deindex seniors' pensions.
What they were not able to accomplish then, they seem to want to accomplish now. The government is preaching one thing and on the other hand tries to do another. It speaks of universality. However I do not think it knows what the word "universality" means. The government continuously preaches one thing and does another: "We are all going to be equal, yet if you make over a certain amount and you happen to be a friend, as we have seen, you will end up being better for it".
There are many examples where the government of the day has let its rich friends eat from the public trough. We could go through them, but the one I really want to touch on is the deal whereby CN Express was sold to Route Canada. It is a great example of how the friends of this government ate from the public trough. They sold CN Express for $29 million and then Route Canada turned around and went to the bank and borrowed $50 million. They walked away with $21 million clear. They will not open the papers yet so many jobs were lost at CN Express. Where does one go?
In 1988 the Prime Minister gave to this country what we should be calling a "Scrooge proposal". After the election, he again put forth closure. We were limited on the amount of time that we were able to debate the free trade legislation.
After one year, at Christmas 1989, what do we see? In Toronto only, 7,000 jobs were lost and the Prime Minister stands up and says: "We have created 1.4 million jobs." I wonder what kind of jobs, hamburger helpers at McDonald's?

Time Allocation
In my riding alone, just south of my riding, the van plant of General Motors closed costing many of my constituents their jobs when 1,700 jobs were lost.
Now the government is proposing a goods and services tax. Small business is going to get hit over the head. The average Canadian is going to get hit over the head. Seniors will have to pay an extra 9 per cent for everything they buy. We are going to have the clawback taking it away from them because all their lives they were frugal. They spent all their lives earning and because they have something extra now we are going to take it away from them. That is not enough. We are going to turn around and we are going to hit them over the head with a 9 per cent sales tax.
The Prime Minister is practising one thing and saying another. I think that the meaning of Ebenezer Scrooge is going to have a new sense in the 1990s. Ebenezer Scrooge at least saw the light. I wonder how many ghosts our Prime Minister would need in order to see the light.
This government I believe is discriminating. Yes, it is discriminating against the seniors who worked so hard all of their lives. I was visited just last weekend in my constituency office by a delegation of seniors. They said to me: "We voted Conservative last time around. However, this time we are not going to vote Conservative. We do not even want to think Conservative; we do not even want to say the name of the Prime Minister". They strongly voiced their opinions to me.
I wonder what the Prime Minister's mother would be thinking today. Would she be proud or would she be sad? I think she should be sad.
We are going to give our seniors a Christmas present they will remember the rest of their lives. We are not only going to say to them: "I as your member of Parliament cannot voice your opinion. The democracy that we fought so hard for over the years is going down the tubes. If you make more than $50,000 we are going to claw back your pension". The government of the day states that it is going to stay at that level, but I reassure you, Madam Speaker, that in two years time it will go down to $45,000. A couple of years down the line it will go down to $40,000, and then to $30,000 and $25,000. Where is it going to stop? I wonder.
We have fundamental changes to what we call universality. We have taken the word "universality" and said: "If you make x amount of dollars we are not going to touch you, but if you make more than that we are going to hit you over the head". It is going to go lower and lower and lower. What we are doing is discriminating against the seniors of this country who worked so hard over their lifetime building what we have today, and as we and our children continue to get older that discrimination is going to continue.
I feel very saddened that this House is not let to debate this particular bill. This government time and time again does not do what it preaches. It brings closure on bills in order to steam roll them along. It seems that every Christmas history repeats itself: 1988 and 1989. I wonder what will happen in 1990. To whom are we going to stick it?
Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley
Valley): Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on this particular motion today regarding Bill C-28, which is referred to as the clawback bill. I rise on this occasion to state a few of my concerns with regard to this bill. One must realize that in terms of the clawback provisions certain areas of the country-and I would like to give special attention to the north-are not quite as well off as the rest of the country, particularly the Northwest Territories.
As far as old age pensioners are concerned, I would think that the government would want to reward old age pensioners who are enterprising enough to make in excess of $50,000 net.
However, the government now wants to tax anybody who makes in excess of that after that senior has accumulated that pension over the years. I cannot understand why anybody would want to tax the hard-earned savings by that person which have already been taxed.
It is difficult enough for anybody to make $50,000 in the north because the cost of living is about twice the average of the cost of living in the south. Why would the federal government want to tax a senior who makes over $50,000 in the north when that person's earnings are about half compared to what it costs to be able to live down here? For anybody making $50,000 up north, it would probably amount to $30,000. I remember my colleague said earlier that in 1984 $50,000 was equivalent to about $33,000. That figure would have been approximately $22,000 to $27,000 in the north.
If the Conservatives think that somebody who was making $25,000 is rich and are willing to tax somebody at $27,000, I would hate to see what they would do to tax somebody who is making $15,000 to $20,000 which is what most people are making in the north. They ought to do away with this bill because it is going to create hardships for those people who have, over the years, earned the right to their pension.
I would just like to add my voice to those who have already spoken ahead of me that this is not a fair treatment of our seniors who built this country over the last number of years. Thank you for giving me this opportunity to say a few words.

December 18, 1989
Time Allocation

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I feel compelled to take this opportunity to speak to the time allocation motion on Bill C-28, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act.
I feel compelled to speak because I feel that Bill C-28 to amend the Income Tax Act belies the real intent of the bill which has been spoken to by several of my colleagues, the intent to put an end to the theme of universality in social programs in this country.
Through the amendment to this act the government proposes to put an end to the universality of the Old Age Security program through the clawback of that program whereby, when instituted, seniors in higher income tax brackets will be repaying back to the government the total of the benefit that they receive.
The problem with this is that at this point in time it affects seniors at one income level, but because the clawback is not totally indexed in a very few years every senior will be paying back the totality of the Old Age Security income and, in fact, there will be no benefit to anybody in this country through this program.
The government proposes to do this in view of the serious national debt and the increasingly high deficits that we have on an annual basis in this country. The government uses a totally unacceptable moral ethic in the way it brings about changes to programs which are supposedly going to address our mounting and ever increasing deficits. It uses the lifeboat ethic, where it is seen that the most important problem is our debt and if we cannot afford to keep everybody on the Canadian life raft, we dump those at the bottom level.
In this instance, it disguises that fact by clawing back the Old Age Security from those seniors in the highest income bracket. It is a principle, and the clawback not only applies to Old Age Security but to family allowances as well, and will have in the future, and even today, a very sad impact on those in need in our country.
This government not only has an economic financial problem in terms of the national debt, but in my opinion, it has a more serious bankruptcy problem. It is bankrupt in terms of ideas and leadership in this country.
I do not think there is one member in this House who is not concerned about our national debt and would not be willing to sit and discuss ways and means of addressing it. I am very concerned. I have the sense that I am an elected member of Parliament here to warm a seat in
this House and in various committees. We in this House and in committees have the opportunity and the privilege to listen to people who have very broad experiences and expertise. But this government proceeds with very drastic and dramatic changes, in this case to social policy, without any consultation with any of the elected members of this House.
For example, we have a tremendous change in passenger rail services in this country through Order in Council. Again, it is the lifeboat ethic. The government says it cannot afford to maintain the service so it will just throw off certain people. There is total neglect to the strategic need and the ultimate importance to certain people in this country of having services such as rail service. For some people in my riding it is a matter of life and death. They depend on that service for their health needs.
We are seeing here the erosion of the notion of universality. It is an erosion which will lead to its total elimination and yet there is a total bankruptcy in terms of this government's ideas for addressing the needs of those people who are dependent upon our social programs. Instead of providing for those most in need, as is the proposition from this government through effective programs, it simply eliminates all programs in the name of trying to address a national debt problem.
This government, I believe, has only two masters. One is the United States and the other is big business, overlooking totally the most important contribution of the middle and low-income people in this country, who, because of the national debt and through paying taxes, are paying interest to the high-income people in this country who can afford to invest in bonds. The masses of people in this country at the lower spectrum of income are those who are most hard-hit by this government, a government that does not have a conscience or a modicum of concern for them seen through consulting with the members of Parliament in this House who have been elected by the Canadian people.
I object totally to the time allocation motion made concerning this bill. I think that when you are bringing in a bill that has such a serious impact, which totally changes the nature of our social policy in this country, we must have a full debate and consultation among all members of this House. If it is this government's opinion that it is necessary to erode or do away with the idea of universality, we must replace it simultaneously with

something that is going to address the needs of those most in need in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this debate will not last more than two hours because of the government's motion for time allocation, which will limit debate to one day per stage, the debate on this very important bill, Bill C-28, which contains measures whose purpose is to claw back sums of money from Canadians Old Age Security Pensions, from people who were often counting on those amounts and who depended on the money to be able to plan for a well deserved retirement.
Madam Speaker, the government is once again using a measure to limit debate because it wants to tell Canadians as little as possible. The government wants to keep bills that are difficult to explain to itself. It wants to keep them from away as the public opinion as possible, and to do so, it uses measures like closure, which limits debate to one or two days on a very important subject, or time allocation, which is also in our Standing Orders, a measure that the government has used as well.
I asked the clerks in the House for some statistics. During the 33rd Parliament which ended with the 1988 election, the government used time allocation 20 times. Madam Speaker, this government decided to limit debate 20 times, and one wonders why Canadians have trouble understanding what this government wants to do! Because it doesn't want to explain. It doesn't want to. It limits the time for debate. It hides important details from Canadians, and Madam Speaker, if today Canadians are confused and cynical about this government's policies and objectives, it is the government's own fault.
As far as this session is concerned, since November 1988, the government has used closure ten times on ten different bills. Don't get me wrong. These are not your run of the mill bills. These are very important pieces of legislation. In this case, we have Bill C-28, a bill that, as you know, is a concerted attack on the elderly, aimed at recovering certain sums of money paid to Canadians for their old age security pensions. This bill proposes to attack these pensions, one more instance that belies the
Time Allocation
fact that the Prime Minister said that Old Age Security Pensions were a sacred trust.

I want to remind members of a statement made by the Prime Minister in Sydney, Nova Scotia during the last election campaign. He said:
As long as I am Prime Minister, social programs, especially those
for the elderly, will be improved not diminished.
This is the same Prime Minister whose government today is proposing a bill that attacks senior citizens, that attacks old age pensions and that attacks the rights of children because it will clawback some family allowances.
It, therefore, is an attack directly on Canadian families. It is an attack, no doubt, on the universality principle which has been with us for some years. As the members have been told before in this debate, the Prime Minister and his government said these were "sacred trusts". Well, they sure as heck did away with that commitment. There is nothing sacred any more as far as this government is concerned, social contract or no social contract.
I view this as a betrayal of the Prime Minister's promises. It is a betrayal of the Prime Minister's so-called "sacred trust". We take exception that these important pieces of legislation are being bullied through the House through time allocation or closure. The government will say to Canadians: "In the interest of balancing our books, in the interest of dealing with the deficit, we are indeed in a hurry to get the legislation dealing with old age pensions through, so we are going to use time allocation or closure".
This bill got first reading on June 20, 1989. It was called by the government, which brings forward whatever bills it pleases, on October 11, 17, 18 and November 20, 1989. Closure was put on second reading and the bill was sent to a committee. As of November 20, the House had spent 15 hours and 37 minutes in debate, discussing a bill which contains 48 amendments to social programs and which ends universality and penalizes Canadians.
I do not know how the Prime Minister and his Cabinet can continue to say they know what is right for Canadians, when Canadians across this country have been

telling them: "We don't want you to meddle with pensions especially with the universality principle which to us is a very important principle".
I want to read something that was said by an important group of Canadians concerning the proposed measure to claw back some of the pension benefits. I quote an editorial from the Vancouver Sun: "As a political issue, the clawback is a sleeper because initially it will not affect many Canadians, and even those will not be seriously inconvenienced at first because the plan is to phase it in over a three-year period".
It goes on to explain that the government has sold the plan as a "high income taxpayers measure". I will not read the whole article, but it goes on to say that the real problem is the inflation which becomes, in the editorial's own words, "a two-edged sword against Old Age Security Pensions, cutting their value through the clawback as well as through increased consumer prices".
We would have loved on this side of the House to debate the importance of preserving the value of our senior Canadians' pensions that inflation reduces every year. This measurement will claw at their pensions. Today, $50,000 may sound like a big number but eventually with inflation this figure will soon affect a million Canadians whose entitlement to pensions will be reduced.
We would also love to discuss the impact on married seniors. There is a good article written by Leonard Shifrin in the Ottawa Citizen of December 14.
Mr. Shifrin makes the point that indeed women, particularly senior women, are getting a raw deal from this legislation.
When I was on the government side, I remember the Trudeau government facing the problem of seniors, especially female seniors who were found to be in need. They were not entitled to the CPP because the way in which the CPP was structured did not allow those people to receive a justifiable amount of money since they were not contributing to the plan. Therefore they depended upon Old Age Security. What did we do? We increased the Guaranteed Income Supplement to allow these people to at least get a reasonable income so that they could cope with day-to-day requirements.
I find it totally abhorrent that this government has more or less abandoned women, especially seniors. I happen to have many seniors in my riding, who deplore the fact that this government in the last five years has not increased the GIS. We would like to have a debate on that. Why is the government clawing back the old age pension upon which these people depend for their livelihood in the years to come?

At 1.21 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, to show Canadians that support for Canadian culture would be business as usual under free trade, this government promised prior to the last election that postal subsidies for Canadian magazines, newspapers and books would remain close to current levels for five years.
How times have changed. With the election over and free trade a fait accompli, the government has now caved in to American pressure and broken its promise not once, but twice. First, the Conservative budget slashed $45 million from postal subsidies and last week they cut another $64.5 million.
Do the Ministers of Finance and Communications not realize that publishers earn pre-tax profits of only 2 per cent and that is why for more than 100 years all governments, regardless of political stripe, have supported this subsidy? It gives all Canadians equal access to magazines, books and newspapers with a Canadian perspective, no matter where they live.
This Conservative government's slashing of a vital link between publishers and readers will affect 95 per cent of Canadians who read our magazines. Does this govern-
December 18, 1989

ment not realize that Canadians like to read Maclean's, Equinox and Chatelaine? Where is the government's sense of Canadian cultural priorities? Is it in Newsweek?

Mr. Speaker, in Gre-vet, in my riding, a new mining camp is about to open. According to Mr. Christian Derosier of Exploration VSM, the one deposit is worth $700 million and exploration was financed by means of flow-through shares. A pre-feasibility study is now under way to assess various options for opening the mine between Miquelon and Chapais.
However, one of the concerns of people at VSM and SEREM is railway transportation. Representatives of both companies have attended public hearings and also emphasized the need for maintaining the Franquet-Cha-pais subdivision of Abitibi, which CN closed down without prior authorization or consultation.
Mr. Speaker, this is another underhanded manoeuvre by CN management. The people of Senneterre and Chapais and the people of Quebec are waiting for the National Transportation Agency's decision on CN's unwarranted application.

Mr. Speaker, this government's goods and services tax will impact veiy heavily on the Canadian housing industry. The Canadian Home Builders Association estimates that the goods and services tax will increase the price of an average home, average being around $150,000 now, by at least $3,000. Most Canadians realize when we mortgage our homes, by the time we pay off that mortgage, the $3,000, that goods and services tax will be well above the $6,000 or $7,000 level.
The implications for the home building industry are evident. Not only will this tax put the Canadian dream of owning a home well beyond the reach of many Canadians, it will affect the very heart of the lumber industry in our country.
The lumber industry in British Columbia, Alberta, northern Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada will be hard hit. Not only are we an export-based industry, but we rely very heavily on domestic consumption and the domestic market. In light of the 15 per cent export tax on the softwood lumber industry and the continuing appreciation of the Canadian dollar, the lumber industry in Canada cannot afford another set-back.
This government must realize that our single largest industry is in some difficulty. This industry should be helped and not hindered.

Mr. Speaker, today is a national day of mourning instituted by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women to commemorate the death of the 14 young women in Montreal. All Canadians are encouraged to reflect on violence against women and, if possible, to make donations to rape crisis centres and to shelters for battered women.
On Saturday, a vigil was held in Vancouver for a foreign domestic worker who was continually raped by her employer. Foreign domestics are often the victims of violence and economic exploitation.
The National Organization of Immigrant and Visible Minority Women has recommended that the federal government work with its provincial counterparts to establish employment standards and to ensure that these standards are being implemented and enforced with sufficient resources.
It is imperative that domestic workers be given more protection. I hope the Minister of Employment and Immigration will attend to this serious issue, and not make it more difficult for domestic workers to receive landed status in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, 1990 will be a very busy year for Dow Chemical, located in my riding of Sarnia-Lambton, in the environmental area.
Last Friday Dow announced its Sarnia division vision. This policy statement affirms the company's commitment to work in a safe, healthy and environmentally

December 18, 1989
responsive manner. Indeed, it complements a 10-year, $55 million spending history on ecology related projects at Dow's Sarnia division.
Financially, Dow announced a commitment of an additional $10 million toward some further 25 separate ecology projects in Sarnia. The key goal is to separate Dow's plants from direct contact with the St. Clair River, virtually eliminating the potential for spills and harmful discharges into the river.
I applaud those on-going efforts by Dow Chemical to achieve environmental excellence and fulfil a commitment to not adversely impact the environment. I strongly encourage other private sector interests as well as public sector organizations to demonstrate a similar commitment to our most valuable infinite resource, our environment.

Mr. Speaker, there is a crisis on Indian reserves in Manitoba. In the past year, four young children have perished in house fires, two on reserves located in my constituency. These tragedies are further compounded by the fact that in every one of these cases, a fire truck was available at the reserve but was not functioning due to one cause or another.
Steps must be taken to make sure that no more lives are lost. Bands should be encouraging their residents to inspect their homes at least once a year. It seems the Department of Indian Affairs cannot handle the problem. I call upon the Minister of Indian Affairs to enlist the help of outside independent professionals to do the job that it seems this department is unable to do.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Minister of Fisheries was quoted as saying on the weekend with regard to the east coast fishing industry: "Some of these guys are making over $100,000 a year. You sure wouldn't know it the way they sing the blues."
Did the minister really say this? Does the minister believe that? Is he not concerned with the 1,500 people who lost their jobs at National Sea last week? Is he not concerned about the potential lay-offs at Fishery Products International? Is he not concerned about the severe
cuts in the total allowable catch in Atlantic Canada? Is he not concerned about the American lobster restrictions? Is he not concerned about the European quotas in our waters which are three times what Canada requested?
If the minister is not concerned about all of this, he is in the wrong job.

Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago I informed this House about a Canada Post decision to close the McKeman postal outlet located in my riding before Christmas.
The corporation insisted that the outlet, located in Maurice Pharmacy, would be closed unless the pharmacy's new owner, Eugene Barabash, purchased a franchise at a cost of roughly $40,000, an impossible amount considering Mr. Barabash had just bought his new business.
Since then, Canada Post has proven that, like the Grinch, it too has a heart. After meeting extensively with Mr. Barabash, officials from the corporation have determined that the outlet which has served the community for 20 years will not close after all.
I would like to commend Canada Post for its response to the concern of area residents and for demonstrating sensitivity to the needs of its customers. I would also like to commend the residents of McKeman for uniting together to save the Maurice Pharmacy outlet. Their determination should be admired by us all. Merry Christmas, McKeman!

Mr. Speaker, last Friday there was an announcement by the President of the Treasury Board to introduce an administrative fee of 3 per cent on any student loan application that will be processed next year.
Students in the 20th century continue to suffer with the additional costs this government so frequently finds necessary to pile on to the minimal budget with which students have to work. The combination of Treasury Board's student loan administration fees, the Finance Department's proposed GST and Consumer and Corporate Affairs copyright fees will leave some students in
December 18, 1989

the position of not being privileged enough to attend post-secondary education institutions.
I believe our youth need to foster growth and maturation through higher education. If this government's extra fees preclude individuals from becoming involved in higher education, then yes, all these fees that are being tacked on by this government do hit the lower income groups, contrary to what the people of our country have been told.
This is going against the Canadian tradition if it affects Canadians in this way. I continue to question how it can be interpreted otherwise if only the rich can still afford a higher education.

Mr. Speaker, Richard Bilodeau, a Canadian resident of Coaticook, was released by the American authorities last Saturday on $100,000 bail.
Mr. Bilodeau has come home to his family and will be able to spend Christmas with his wife and children. This was made possible thanks to a tremendous movement of solidarity on the part of all Quebecers, the involvement of all levels of government-federal, provincial and municipal-and especially, thanks to the much appreciated help of the media which made their contribution towards dealing with this terrible injustice.
Mr. Speaker, this spirit of solidarity went beyond the province of Quebec and was felt across Canada and even in New Hampshire and other states in New England.
This proves that when we stand together, there are no obstacles we cannot overcome, and what was accomplished by this general support for Richard Bilodeau, Mr. Speaker, is reassuring when we think of our future safety on trips in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite concerned about the content of the 1991 census. Officials representing the Canadian disabled community fear that the people they represent will be excluded from this census.
It is of paramount importance to the livelihood of the disabled community that they be included in this census. For the first time in 1986, four questions on the disabled were included. The information obtained by Statistics Canada from this census allowed for more complete and accurate data regarding employment equity. If questions about the disabled are excluded from the 1991 census, Statistics Canada will be unable to gather current information regarding the disabled community in Canada.
I want to inform the Minister of Employment and Immigration that we are indeed aware that the questions regarding the disabled may be left off the 1991 census. Inclusion, not exclusion, is what Canada's disabled community would like.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to pay tribute to a very successful project in my riding of Delta. Taking advantage of the balmiest climate in Canada and using waste wood as an energy source, Houwelling Nurseries are a true success story.
Starting in 1985 with six acres under glass, they now cover 15 acres and are currently shipping the last of their poinsettias, 62 per cent of which are shipped to the United States. They are currently planting English cucumbers, tomatoes and peppers which they will start harvesting at the end of January to be shipped as far east as Montreal and Pittsburgh and as far south as Los Angeles.
There is a vast market in Japan for their produce but the Japanese have not allowed the regular import of these choice Canadian products. I call on the Canadian government to assist this excellent company to open the doors to the Japanese market to bring greater prosperity to Canadians.

December 18, 1989

Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa. He is sitting right over there in the Minister of Finance's seat but he is known as Santa Clawsback.
This Santa claws back your old age pension. This Santa claws back family allowances for young families. This Santa claws back door-to-door postal delivery in rural post offices. This Santa claws back the national dream of Canadians of passenger rail service from coast to coast.
This Santa claws back decent, affordable child care. The Santa claws back programs to promote women's equality. This Santa claws back support for our regions, for those of us who live a distance from the money barons of Toronto and Montreal.
This Santa claws back support for students at universities. This Santa claws back support for health care in hospitals and medical research. This Santa claws back our social safety net. This Santa claws back protection from unemployment. Finally, this Santa claws back 9 per cent or 7 per cent or whatever he feels like from virtually every dollar spent by every Canadian.
^ ^

Mr. Speaker, a columnist in The Globe and Mail has recently pointedly summed up five years of Conservative government. "The Conservative government," says Michael Valpy, "is a statement such as we have not heard in this century. It is a statement of evaporating social compassion, of a government who favours the bottom line over people".
The Minister of Finance says that if he lowers the proposed GST rate, he will have to tighten the government's belt. What he really means is that while he and his colleagues continue to travel in luxury, more and more Canadians will be forced to brown-bag it. He says that there has to be a little give and take. Yes, taxpayers give, give and give and he takes.
The Prime Minister says that he needs the GST to reduce the debt. What he really means is that he needs a convenient excuse to severely reduce social programs like the clawback of the OAS, and in the process,
closure, closure and more closure, because this government is not interested in hearing from Canadians.
The reality of five years of Conservative government is that today in metro Toronto, there are more food bank programs than there are the combined total of outlets of the three major burger chains. The reality is that the Prime Minister is demanding even more cuts in spending at the expense of his government's social programs.

Mr. Speaker, in April of 1986, the federal government initiated the review of demography and its implications for economic and social policy. The study was mandated to report on the changes in size, structure and distribution of the population of Canada between now and the year 2025.
On Thursday, December 14, the Minister of National Health and Welfare released the results of the study and presented the report to the standing committee. A total of 167 studies, prepared by over 200 Canadian scholars from across the country, culminated in this report. The projections for the future show what will happen if fertility, mortality and immigration levels remain at the current level. The Canadian population will peak at 31 million in the year 2026.
Contrary to popular belief, the baby boom did not cause the aging population. In fact, it delayed it. By the year 2026, between 20 per cent and 25 per cent of the population will be over 65 and approximately 10 per cent of the population will be over 75. Women in this latter age group will outnumber men two to one.
The research indicates that Canada is not facing an imminent population crisis, but that current demographic trends will produce such fundamental changes that the Canada of the 21st century will be significantly different from the Canada that shaped today's attitudes and policies. The implications for Canada in areas such as immigration, social policy, tax structure, health care and housing will all be impacted by these changes. I would urge all members of Parliament and Canadians to avail themselves of the information contained in Charting Canada's Future.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last election, I said that the Conservatives would tiy to attack senior citizens' pensions and the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance called me a liar. I said that the east coast fishery would suffer as a result of the trade deal and again I was called a liar.
I said the dollar would go up and hurt our exports, and they called me a liar. I said interest rates would rise, and they called me a liar. I said the GST would cost billions of dollars more, and the Minister of Finance called me a liar and said it would not cost one single penny more to the taxpayers of Canada.
A year ago, the Minister of Finance said to us in this chamber: "Conservatives have spending commitments and we have sufficient money to handle those announcements". The Prime Minister said: "Every nickel has been accounted for".
Will the Prime Minister explain to the students of this country, the senior citizens, the public servants, and to Canadians generally, what he was talking about last year when he said he had enough money to handle our spending commitments? I ask the Prime Minister exactly who was lying during the last election?

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member knows explicitly what I said in the speech when I was referring to the veracity of the things that he was saying, and they were not what he referred to in his remarks. So again, he is misleading people by what he is saying.
Clearly the fiscal position of the Government of Canada has been greatly affected by the change in interest rates, what was anticipated at the time of the election and also at the time of the last budget. To be precise, we were looking at interest costs of, I think, $33 billion. Instead, they have gone up to $39.5 billion. That has meant a significant change in the fiscal position of the government and it did require a number of the actions that we have taken.
Oral Questions
The point that must be made here is that if you apply the increase in the debt of the country from 1984 to the present time and relate that to the interest costs on the debt that was in place at the time that we took over, you will find that it is almost exactly the same.

The fact is that this Minister of Finance, advising his Prime Minister, told the people of Canada during the last election that all the spending commitments were commitments for which there was money and that the sales tax that he contemplated would not cost one single cent more to Canadian taxpayers. That is what he said.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's statements are very revealing. Last week, when he was campaigning for the Tory candidate in the Chambly by-election, the Prime Minister of Canada repeatedly told voters how much money the government had spent in their riding. He was practicality saying: Vote for the Conservatives and money will come pouring into the riding. However, as soon as he left, he started talking about the need to cut spending. Why is the Prime Minister prepared to spend taxpayers' money on winning a by-election, when he reduces appropriations for students, the elderly, food assistance organizations and regional development?
Does he think he can buy a by-election in Chambly like he bought the Environment Minister's seat in Lac-Saint-Jean?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition will leave this House with very little ceremony if he maintains the tenor of his questions. He ought to know that, contrary to what he said, in Chambly I never made single reference of the kind the Leader of the Opposition is putting into my mouth. I did refer to economic expansion in the Montreal area, which is occurring thanks to this government's intervention in industries such as the automobile industry, petrochemicals, aerospace and pharmaceuticals, while the Liberals in the Senate and here in the House were effectively smothering Bill C-22. I mentioned, quite appropriately, what the federal government, together with the Quebec government, has done to stimulate the economy in the greater Montreal area including, of course, the town of Beloeil.

December 18, 1989
Oral Questions
Now if the Leader of the Opposition is against economic recovery in Montreal, if he is against intervention by the federal government in high-tech industries in the Montreal area, including the riding of Chambly, let him come out and say so, instead of applauding this in Beloeil and speaking out against it in the House.

I dare him to say
anywhere else what he says in Chambly, Mr. Speaker!

Interest rates in Canada are too high. The spread between Canadian and American interest rates is at an almost historic high. The government's tax policy is in a mess. Instead of scrapping the GST, it is now trying to perpetrate some phoney changes on us.
The fiscal policy is a mess. They make all kinds of special promises during the election and then they break every one of those promises. The trade deal is a mess and we are now moving into a trade deficit.
What is the Prime Minister going to do to avoid a recession in this country? Does he think that the deceitful promises he used during the last election are going to work this time to salvage the Canadian economy?

Mr. Speaker, I will tell you what we will not do. We will not follow policies like those followed by the Liberals when the Leader of the Opposition was the Minister of Linance and gave rise to the deficit and the recession that this country began to go through. He is responsible for it.
Program spending in Ottawa increased by 20 per cent a year when the right hon. gentleman was the Minister of Finance. Program spending has been held to 3.5 per cent by this government as opposed to the 20 per cent under the Leader of the Opposition.
Last week, a leading columnist in The Globe and Mail said that the period from 1975 to 1984, led by the former Prime Minister and his ministers was the period that devastated the economy of Canada. He was right. The policies of this government are making the economy stronger and more competitive and we will pursue them because they do not involve printing money and bringing on inflation and dragging up unemployment. They involve getting Canada ready for the next century in a very confident and modern economy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Everybody agrees that the goods and services tax is more bad news for the Canadian economy. Small businesses are already struggling under the burden of interest rates that are too high, while at the present time, consumer spending is going down.
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Finance whether he agrees that his proposed goods and services tax will bring Canada into a recession. Will he now listen to people across this country who are asking, who are begging him to withdraw his proposal for a goods and services tax?

Mr. Speaker, we have listened very carefully to the consultations that we have had as a government and that the finance committee has had in the course of its hearings across the country. We have listened carefully to what Canadians have had to say. I will be reporting to the House on that tomorrow, as I indicated last week.
I say again to the hon. member that he would have more credibility as a spokesman for his party if he would come up with some alternatives rather than saying scrap this, scrap that. That is no way to deal with the problems that we are facing today.
The members of the Liberal Party are walking away from the problems of taxation, the problems of high inflation and saying you can't do this, you can't do that, but they have not got a brain in their heads to propose another alternative policy.

Mr. Speaker, two quick proposals would be to reduce the interest rates and try to reduce the value of the Canadian dollar. That would do more than anything else to help exports and business in this country.
Oh, oh!

That would be a nice start, Mr. Prime Minister, to reduce interest rates.
The Minister of Finance has said consistently that he would not change his position on the goods and services tax. The Prime Minister defended the Minister of
December 18, 1989

Finance saying that the proposal would stand as it was presented.
Since it was to be revenue neutral, visible, and have provincial co-operation, the proposal that the Minister of Finance has presented to this point and undoubtedly will continue to put forward tomorrow has none of those components in it, will he not understand that the only appropriate thing to do at this time is to withdraw his proposal, reduce interest rates in this country, make sure that exports are protected and try to get it right?

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member. He says: "Get interest rates down". This is not Santa Claus. This is not Christmas Eve and this is not just a question of saying: "Let's have lower interest rates".
I ask the hon. member to consider how he is going to get lower interest rates. We have seen bank loans growing at 11.5 per cent. To get interest rates down the hon. member would start printing money, which means that bank credit would be increasing at 12, 13, 14, or 15 per cent with an economy that is growing at around 7 per cent.
How is that going to address the problem of inflation? It is going to feed inflation, it is going to feed higher interest rates, it is going to feed the very problems that he is concerned about today. All he is saying is deal with the symptoms of the problem and ignore the cause.
We on this side of the House understand the causes and we are dealing with the causes of that problem, not just fluttering about saying: "Do this, do that" about the symptoms, which he knows will do absolutely nothing to solve the problems we are facing today.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance as well. The minister said in this House on Friday that he fully supports the high interest rate policy of the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Also on Friday the chief economist from the Bank of Montreal said that Governor Crow wants to deliberately weaken the economy to prepare for the introduction of the GST.

Oh come on.
Oral Questions

Those are the words of the chief economist of the Bank of Montreal.
Is it government policy to deliberately create slack in the economy in order to create unemployment so that workers will be scared to push for wages to compensate for the rise in the cost of living when the GST comes in? Is that the policy of the government? Was the chief economist of the Bank of Montreal right when he said this is happening?

Mr. Speaker, let me say right off the top that I completely reject that machiavellian interpretation of the policy of the government.
The hon. member knows exactly why we are following the policies that we are, and that is because we have some very real concerns about the level of inflation. I ask the hon. member to reflect on the impact of inflation on senior citizens, on people who are on fixed incomes, on people who are in low income brackets. These are the people whom we are concerned about when we follow the policies that we are following today.
If the hon. member wants to ignore those policies, again I ask him to think back to 1981-82 when there was that sense of despair in the country, when people were saying: "We are going to have a 12 or 13 per cent inflation rate for a long time to come". With that came the high interest rates. Think back to that time and reflect on whether or not the policies that we are following are the right ones because we are doing everything we can through the policies that we are following to avoid that happening again.

Mr. Speaker, thinking back to 1982, the Prime Minister at the time, Mr. Trudeau, said: "It is still possible to scare the hell out of people by creating more unemployment". What I really want to know from this Minister of Finance is whether or not he is following a similar policy.
We now have about the highest interest rate in the industrialized world, a rate that is about 400 basis points higher than in the United States. We have rising unemployment and we have the first monthly merchandise trade deficit in some thirteen and a half years.
How much more of a decline in the economy is the Minister of Finance going to accept before he has a

December 18, 1989
Oral Questions
heart-to-heart talk with John Crow and demands he bring down the interest rates? Has he, for example, ever thought of firing John Crow, giving him a pink slip?

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly never going to defend the policies of Pierre Elliott Trudeau, so don't ask me to do that.
Here we have a question comparable to the last one asked by the Liberals, possibly with a little more attention to what might come up on the evening clip on television tonight. The answer is the same. The NDP are saying: "Please Santa, give me some lower interest rates". You cannot just wish these. You cannot just wish lower interest rates, you have to follow some policy direction to get them.
The policy direction that I have heard from the NDP and from the Liberals is print money and that will raise interest rates a few months down the road, although there may be a short-term drop. That is not the right way to cure inflation.
That is exactly what happened in the 1970s under the policies initiated by my friend across the way. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace was there at the time as well. They started printing money. They took the inflation rate from 5.5 per cent up to 13 per cent. They took the unemployment rate from about 7 per cent up to 13 per cent and they took interest rates from about 10 per cent up to 24 per cent.
Shame, shame.

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance wants to know how to bring down the bank rate, all he has to do is ask the chairman of the finance committee. He will tell him how to do it, and so did the finance committee last June.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance about the unemployment rate. We now have an unemployment rate of some 7 per cent in this country. About 1 million people are unemployed. What unemployment rate is the Minister of Finance going to tolerate before he changes monetary policy in this country? Is it 8 per cent or is it 9 per cent, because at 9 per cent another 250,000 people will be unemployed.
What is the bottom line? What unemployment rate will he tolerate before he instructs the Governor to roll back that bank rate? People in this country really want to know.

Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member is very well aware of the performance in this country on employment. We have seen 1.5 million jobs created. We have seen unemployment come down in every province, except for one, Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Oh, come on.

speechtext: Go ahead, I'm listening. Just don't mislead.

In the last eight years he has managed to produce the first month-overmonth trade deficit. There are some economists who are suggesting that over the next year our trade deficit could go as high as $20 billion.

I would appreciate if the hon. member would stand up and tell me what he thinks we should be doing about inflation, how we should be getting the inflation problem under greater

control, because it is the inflation problem that is causing the things to which he has referred.
At the heart of this is the difficult fiscal problem that we inherited in 1984, which he very conveniently avoided mentioning, and that is a deficit that was close to $38.3 billion which we have brought down year by year with a very great deal of difficulty, and we are committed to getting it down further. That is one of the difficult causes of the inflation problem that we have today.

My supplementary question is for the same minister, Mr. Speaker. It really frustrates me that he cannot take responsibility for his own actions. The fact of the matter is that in the last four months our inflation rate was around 2.7 per cent on average. I would just like to know at what point in time he would react to inflation.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada is not responsible for managing the economy of this country; the Minister of Finance is responsible. At what time will the Minister of Finance assume his responsibilities? At what point in time will he ask the Governor of the Bank of Canada to act? Will it be when there is 100,000 jobs lost, 200,000? At what level of human misery will the minister act?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has said that I am not prepared to accept my responsibilities. I am quite prepared to accept, and I accept those responsibilities day by day, every day that I am in this job.
The hon. member again is playing kind of loose with those numbers. If he takes notice he will see that the inflation rate increased last month, not decreased. It's you.

How is the government going to deal with the problem of inflation today? That government, for years and years, dealt with just the

symptoms of the problem and did not get down to dealing with the causes.

Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CONTENT OF BROCHURES-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I should advise the House that I have two questions of privilege to deal with.
On November 20, 1989 the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands raised a question of privilege related to certain pamphlets on the goods and services tax which a constituent of his had informed him were being distributed in a local grocery chain outlet.
In view of the Chair's ruling on October 10, 1989, the hon. member questioned the propriety of the distribution of the pamphlets. He suggested that this constituted a contempt of the House, pointing out that in the text of the pamphlets the presumption that the GST will be law by January 1991 is everywhere asserted with none of the appropriate references to the legislative process through which the GST must pass.

Later that day, the Minister of Finance rose on a point of order to explain that the pamphlete in question were part of the initial information package prepared by the Department last summer and distributed last August. The Minister assured the House that the distribution contracts for the dissemination of that material had been completed by October and that, subsequent to the Chair's ruling on the advertisements for the GST, steps had been taken to have all offending materials returned to the department.

The hon. member for Windsor West intervened to question whether the disputed material was still being distributed.

The Chair undertook to look further into the matter. I have now carefully considered the issue raised by the Honourable Member for Kingston and the Islands and the remarks made by the Honourable Minister of Finance. It appears that the point at issue is the timing of the removal of the pamphlets from public distribution.

The Chair is satisfied that the material in question was part of the summer advertising campaign and that given the intricacies of the nation-wide distribution of such material some time delays may have occurred in recovering material from that campaign. The minister has assured the House that the department had taken appropriate steps to have the material returned to it and has asked, in light of the complaint raised by the hon.
December 18, 1989

member for Kingston and the Islands, if members would bring such aberrant cases to his attention so that corrective action may be taken where required.
In light of this information the Chair is satisfied that the hon. member's complaint has been fairly and expeditiously dealt with and considers the matter settled. If hon. members have further information to bring to the Chair, the Chair of course will hear further applications.

subtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS-SPEAKER'S RULING

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STANDING COMMITTEE ON CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I am now ready to rule on the question of privilege raised on Friday, October 20 by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell regarding proceedings in the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations the previous day. The hon. member had made the case that he had been convened to a meeting of the committee to discuss the specific subject matter, that during the course of the meeting a motion was moved relating to an entirely different subject, and that this constituted a breach of his privileges as a member.
He further argued that the committee notice of meeting is equivalent to the Order Paper of the House and that if a single item of business appears on the committee notice of meeting then only that item can be dealt with by the committee.
[Translation)
I have carefully considered the argument of the hon. member and the excellent points made by hon. members on both sides of the question. The Chair finds itself in some difficulty in addressing the specifics of the case made by the hon. member for Glengariy-Prescott- Russell. According to our traditions and practices, the Chair ought not to intervene with the proceedings of a committee unless a problem has been reported by the committee to the House or in extremely unusual circumstances. It is also clear that disputes arising from committee meetings ought to be dealt with in that committee and not raised on the floor of the House.I will therefore not comment on the specific incident in the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The Chair is pleased, however, to comment on the larger questions which arose during the discussion of the hon.
Privilege
member's grievance, which relates to committees dealing with business other than that listed on the green sheet announcing the date, time and place of the meeting.

Although Standing Order 116 states in part that "in a standing, special or legislative committee, the Standing Orders shall apply so far as may be applicable," it is nonetheless a long-standing convention that notice is not required for any motion in committee.
Beauchesne's Fifth Edition in Citation 571 reminds us that flexibility is the watchword in committee deliberations when it states:
Proceedings in the committees are more relaxed in nature than
those in the House as the requirements which must be observed in the
chamber are not so strictly enforced when members sit in committee.
This difference in practices between the House and its committees is nowhere more evident than when dealing with motions in amendment to the clauses of a bill. Motions to amend a bill in committee require no notice whatsoever. In the House, on the other hand, the Standing Orders specifically require that 24-hour written notice be given for motions in amendment at report stage of a bill.

This being the case, and while some members may feel that it causes inconvenience and creates difficulties for the orderly pursuit of a committee's agenda, the Chair must rule that there is no procedural impediment to a committee's dealing with any matter within its mandate at any meeting of that committee regardless of the stated purpose or purposes of a particular meeting.
The Chair must also inform hon. members that it has been unable to find any procedural authority to support the position of the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and other hon. members that the committee notice of meeting constitutes an Order Paper for the committee.
Should the House in its wisdom wish to alter this long-standing practice it can certainly do so, and there are several avenues open to achieve this end.

Mr. Speaker, during Question Period and in response to a question the Minister of Agriculture stated that I had misled the House.
This is very serious. I would like to point out that some of the figures I used came from the minister's own department. I would suspect that likely he was referring to the fact that I said as result of his government's policy farm income would drop by $2.6 billion in the coming year. The minister's own figures show that there will be a drop of $1.7 billion in expenditures of the Department of Agriculture for the coming year.
Therefore I would suggest to you, Sir, that the drop in his own expenditures is in effect as a result of government policy.
I would ask to have that remark withdrawn.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not veiy happy to be speaking this afternoon on a motion to impose closure on a bill that deserves to be heard.
I sat in the House throughout this morning's debate just as you did, Madam Speaker, and I listened to argument after argument by opposition members. These opposition members were stating the obvious, that is this government has imposed closure and time allocation more times than any other government in the history of this country.
It is a sad state of affairs when the government has to impose its will on the people of Canada, rather than do the will of the people of Canada and carry out their wishes and needs. I sat here and listened to the various arguments that were being made. I was quite surprised that I did not hear a single word in response from members on the opposite side of the House.

All morning we debated this bill and the only words we heard from across the way were a very few short statements from the Minister of Justice who said they had to impose closure on the clawback legislation, Bill C-28.
We have no evidence whatsoever that members opposite have listened to a single thing that Canadians have said about this Bill-not in committee, not in debate here in the House of Commons, and certainly not from the people of Canada.
Just prior to that debate this morning I presented a petition from people in Big River, Saskatchewan. It is a smallish community in the northern part of my riding, The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, in north west Saskatchewan. Big River is on the eastern side of my constituency.
The seniors of that community sent me a petition that had been provided to them by One Voice, the seniors network. These people from this small community in the northern part of Saskatchewan were adding their names to those of other Canadians and seniors from right across this country who are telling this government that it cannot claw back the old age security pension, the family allowance program, or take money our of the pockets of seniors and do away with universality.
Did the government listen to those petitions? Did the government listen to the petitions that have been presented by the other members of this House who we have heard day after day after day in here? No, not at all.
I have been listening to the debate in this House. I have not heard much debate from the other side of the house. Obviously they must be listening if they are not speaking. However, if they are listening, why are they not doing what the people of Canada are suggesting to them?
It is like the other things that we have heard about in the last little while on the subject of interest rates. It was demonstrated quite clearly in the House today during Question Period. Is this government listening to the people of Canada, to the small business people of western Canada, to the farmers of Canada on the subject of interest rates? No, it is not listening to the people of Canada.
Has it listened to people on the subject of VIA Rail? Has it listened to the seniors from coast to coast who are
Time Allocation
using VIA Rail? Has it listened to the students who are using VIA Rail? Has it listened to the tourists who have travelled this country all summer long on VIA Rail proclaiming it to be not the best service but a good service for them as tourists coming to this country? Has it listened? No, it is not listening on Bill C-28. It is not listening on clawback or on universality. I think it is a shame and a sham that it is trying to impose this on us. I say that, the people of my constituency say that and certainly, as I indicated this morning with my petition, the people of Big River are saying that to this government.
There is total chaos in this bill. Certainly the process by which we have seen the matter handled through committee, the introduction of amendments, the whole mismanagement of this matter, tells me that rather than imposing closure on this bill and rushing it through the government should be doing everything in its power to withdraw the bill and start over again so that we can have good, unflawed legislation and a government that demonstrates that it can manage not only this piece of legislation but the economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext: And that it cares for Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-28
speechtext:
That is right. My colleague is absolutely right. It has mismanaged the economy and this piece of legislation, and we should have none of it.
I know that I do not have much time, but I just want to indicate something here about the bill. Bill C-28 is essentially a clawback on the old age security pension. This is being done by not fully indexing the program-an attack on universality.
I just want to put a couple of thoughts on record. Talking about universality, obviously the government has accomplished the withdrawal of universality by not fully indexing what it calls a trigger figure of $50,000. If inflation rises by 4.5 per cent next year, the trigger figure will rise by only 1.5 per cent. That means that over time through inflation more and more of us will be caught in this whole process.
Here are some examples concerning the old age security pension. Right now a 25-year old who makes $25,000 a year for the rest of his life will have part of his old age pension clawed back at retirement. Where is the $50,000 there?

Time Allocation
Here is another example. A 30-year old making $30,000 will have part of her OAS pension clawed back when she retires at the age of 65.
The same is true for 35-year olds making $35,000 a year, for 40-year olds making $40,000 a year, and for 45-year olds making $45,000 a year.
This is where the end of the universality program attacks a growing number of seniors in our society as time goes on. All told-and the government knows this, which is why it is not saying a dam word today-the clawback will catch about 128,000 Canadian pensioners in 1990. In 20 years from now that figure will rise to over one million Canadians. Where is this process of universality? Where are the government members standing up and saying: "Universality is a sacred right in this country"? We have on the old age security program more and more seniors coming under attack.
Is it any wonder that at national conferences across this country when seniors get together they talk about how this government is hitting them harder and harder with every single move that it makes? It is happening on this old age security program, on VIA Rail that transports them from one place to another, and on the GST which attacks almost everything that they buy and reduces their buying power.
I am appalled that this government wants to oppose closure and does not want to talk about the legislation here in order to give Canadians the opportunity to hear what we have to say. I am appalled that I have to stand here today and talk to them about this, but I know it is the only way that Canadians across the country will know exactly what those people across the way are thinking and doing, because obviously they are not interested in communicating that message themselves.

They had been in opposition for decades and had all kinds of ideas on how Parliament would be improved. They instituted a series of reforms that Your Honour knows about. We are now faced with a situation where instead of living up to the spirit of those reforms and following through with them they are going back to the old closure rules that they condemned so vigorously when they were in opposition and which they now use willy-nilly on almost every bill that comes along.
I see the hon. member for Macleod is grinning. He should be red-faced with shame at the constant use of closure that this government has embarked on in this House. I want to make some reference to this.
I think the record is a broken record, a dreadful record. This government has used closure in this Parliament already, and we have not yet been sitting for a full year from when we started last December. The government has used closure more than any other government in any other Parliament in Canadian history. Not by one or two times more; it is almost double the number of times. I think it is at 11 on closure, and that this is the second or third time we have had time allocation. That is not counting the fancy suspension of the standing orders we have had: one on the bill last week and one on the free trade bifl a year ago in December.
That is the kind of record that most governments would be terribly embarrassed about. Instead, this government goes on with its dictatorial ways trampling on the rights of Parliament right, left and centre.
I want to go through the history of its dealings on this particular bill. The bill was introduced following the budget and was given first reading on June 20 this year. It was called for second reading on October 11.1 would like to remind you, Madam Speaker, that the House adjourned on June 27 last summer and, at the request of the government, we did not meet again until September 25, a full two weeks later than the rules would normally have provided.
