We certainly believe that those conditions can be met by the Hibernia project, but that they will take continued work, monitoring and action by the government. We intend to ensure that the federal government meets all of its responsibilities to the Hibernia project.
Hibernia is a national project, one which the Liberal Party of Canada has long supported. The commitment of the federal government to Hibernia has been questionable, to say the least. The April 1989 throne speech did not even bother to mention the Hibernia project, the deal that was supposed to be signed, sealed and delivered four days earlier, on March 31.
This bill may be heading toward a master agreement for Hibernia. But there are many obstacles we still must cross before this project is the best deal for all Canadians. Hibernia is seen as the cornerstone of the Canadian offshore industry. Hibernia could be the key to future development, it could be the springboard discovery which provides us with much of the infrastructure, the technology and the impetus for development of our eastern offshore industry.
My colleagues and I will support the second reading of Bill C-44, which serves as implementation legislation. What it really does is allow the federal government to enter into a master agreement with other parties involved in Hibernia. We note that the minister shall present a summary of each of the agreements before the House. Certainly I am looking forward to this bill being sent to the legislative committee. I hope that it will lead to a far swifter management of the Hibernia project than this government has demonstrated to date.

Madam Speaker, I must say at the outset that I intend to take the liberty of addressing both this bill and Bill C-45.
Given what I understand to be the principle both of this bill and of Bill C-45, the bill which sets up the fiscal regime for the government's participation in the OSLO project, and given that the central principle in each bill is
to create the fiscal structure under which the government will participate, and given the sums of money involved, I must say that I am somewhat surprised that these bills are sponsored by the minister of energy and not the Minister of Finance. However, they are sponsored by the minister of energy and must therefore be seen to constitute, at least in part, the government's energy strategy. So, I will be dealing with that aspect of the bills as well.
If I might, I would like briefly to summarize the two bills. Both of them set out the proposal for the expenditure of government money in the two projects.
In the case of Bill C-44 which deals with Hibernia, we are talking about a grant for the defraying of capital costs in the amount of $1.04 billion. We are, as well, talking about loan guarantees on the capital project of up to $1.66 billion, a direct loan in the amount of $300 million, loan guarantees for what is called a temporary financing facility in the amount of $175 million, and interest payable guarantees on the $1.66 billion loan guarantee. In other words, if the loan is going to default what the government has guaranteed, not only will we pay the principle but we will pick up the interest charges as well.
Therefore, we are talking about a direct expenditure, a grant to Hibernia of up to $1.04 billion, a $300 million loan, and various and sundry loan guarantees and interest guarantees in the amount of $1,835 billion for a total possible government investment of $3,139 billion, a tidy little sum in anybody's books.
For OSLO, we are talking about a grant for the capital costs of up to $425 million. We are talking about a price of oil production subsidy of $48 million. This is a sort of project specific guaranteed floor price for oil. If the cost of production of oil exceeds the price the OSLO project is getting, then this $48 million will kick in. You will find a floor price for Canadian oil in no other aspect of the industry even though New Democrats, federally and provincially, have been vigorously calling for such a thing for many years now. However, for OSLO this is a sort of "most favoured" status, I suppose.
OSLO will have this $48 million floor price guarantee. As well, there will be loan guarantees on the capital project of up to $642.5 million. There will be loans-the terms are not set out, of course, in the bill-of up to $250 million. And loan guarantees, again, for this temporary financing facility of $62.5 million. We are looking once again at a direct expenditure in OSLO of up to $425 million, direct loans of up to $250 million, various

December 18, 1989

guarantees of up to $705 million, for a possible total government involvement in OSLO of $1.4 billion.
These bills would allow the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, with the approval of the Governor in Council, to enter into firm agreements on both the Hibernia and OSLO projects, thus involving the potential for government fiscal involvement in the two projects of up to $4.5 billion.
I do not want to consider these complex financial arrangements or get into the details of the bills today. That is a job most properly left to be handled in the committee. I want, instead, to deal with the principle of the bills which is the commitment of this amount of money to these particular projects. I also want to deal in part with what I understand to be the government's energy policy, of which these two projects are definitely centrepieces. In other words, I will make some general remarks about where these bills fit into that over-all policy.
Since the initial plans for these projects were drawn up, there has been a revolution of sorts in the energy sector. Canadians, regardless of what their governments have done, believed or wanted, have themselves added a new criterion to those by which energy policy is to be judged in Canada. Canadians have added the new criterion of the effect of our energy sources on our environment.
After all, in the words of the Brundtland report called Our Common Future, quoting from page 7-1: "-choosing an energy strategy inevitably means choosing an environmental strategy".
I would note that the government has been very quick to adopt the rhetoric of the Brundtland report. But they seemed somewhat more reticent in adopting the counsel of the Brundtland report.
Listen to what the Prime Minister said on June 27, 1988 at the International Conference on the Changing Atmosphere held in Toronto. He said at that time: "The world is coming to recognize what we believe to be self-evident-that development and environmental protection are mutually reinforcing, not mutually exclusive.
Government Orders
Our economic activity must be increasingly compatible with today's environmental facts of life".
Later, in the same speech the Prime Minister added: "In no area is the link between our economic activity and environmental disruption more evident or more troubling than in the area of energy policy".
This is not Audrey McLaughlin speaking, this is not Ed Broadbent speaking. This is the Prime Minister of Canada, the leader of the Conservative Party. He goes on: "Canada is committed to applying the principles of sustainable development to our energy future".
That is commendable, Madam Speaker. One of the most important environmental issues of the day is global warming. In the statement coming from the Toronto conference that I just finished quoting, the International Conference on the Changing Atmosphere, June 17,1988 entitled "The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security" stated: "The earth's atmosphere is being changed at an unprecedented rate by pollutants resulting from human activities, inefficient and wasteful fossil fuel use and the effects of rapid population growth in many regions".
It was stark language that the conference used in speaking of the changing atmosphere, and again I quote: "Humanity is conducting an unintended, uncontrolled, globally pervasive experiment whose ultimate consequences could be second only to a global nuclear war". These are very strong words and in the opinion of many, absolutely warranted words.
The Prime Minister, again a fine sounding environmentalist, on March 11, 1989, signed The Hague Declaration entitled "Our Common Future: It's in our Hands". That declaration emphasized the importance of all countries doing their bit to prevent atmospheric pollution and stated: "Because of the nature of the dangers involved, remedies to be sought involve the duty of the community of nations vis-a-vis present and future generations to do all that can be done to preserve the quality of the atmosphere".
So on the level of official pronouncements, the Mulro-ney government is quick to agree that much needs to be

December 18, 1989
Government Orders
done to protect the environment, but its pronouncements do not mean anything significant, because Canada has to begin to put its own house in order.
We clearly have a valuable role to play. After all, while Canada is directly responsible for only about 2 per cent of the total global CO2 emissions, carbon dioxide being the key greenhouse gas, we are one of the most energy inefficient countries in the world. Canadians consume more energy per person than is the case in the U.S.A., Sweden, Germany, the United Kingdom and Japan, and the situation is getting worse. From the perspective of energy use per $1,000 of GDP, we also use more than the U.S.A., Sweden, the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan.
It is true we live in a cold country. Mainly our population is spread out along a long thin southern line. Our industries have to deal with the effects of cold winters, as do our people. But this is no excuse, because in taking account of all that, nonetheless we are extremely wasteful energy users. We could use substantially less energy, thereby polluting much less, without significant changes to our way of life.
So far the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been running in the wrong direction and has been using as an excuse that he favours a market oriented approach. So what has the government done? In the last budget, the government eliminated completely the 12 conservation and renewable energy offices across the country. These offices were run on a shoestring and provided information to people in the regions on how they could save money and energy at the same time. They were not even a significant intrusion into the market-place. They were funded at too pitiful a level to be that. Nonetheless the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources closed them all down.
As well, the government also dismantled the branch of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources that oversaw research on energy conservation and alternate energy sources. The government cut funding for conservation and renewable energy-using its own department's figures-from $410 million in 1984-85 to $49 million in 1989-90. What is the justification for all this slash and burn of alternatives and conservation? The argument is that conservation efficiency and renewable energy sources just cannot compete. They cannot compete. They are not as marketable, they are not as efficient.
There is not a free market in energy in this country, there is no so-called level playing field between the fossil fuels and the alternatives, between spurred consumption on the one hand and conservation on the other. To all Canadians who may have any doubt that there is not a level playing field in energy resources in this country, I simply say, look at Bills C-44 and C-45: up to $4.5 billion in government commitments to two fossil fuel projects.
This government, in proposing to provide the $4.5 billion to these two energy projects, is simultaneously slashing funding for conservation and energy alternatives to just $49 million per year. That is the government's level playing field. That is the government's demonstration of the hallowed free market in action, an increase of $4.5 billion for just two fossil fuel projects, and a decrease to $49 million for all energy conservation and renewable projects.
Most Canadians believe their tax money should be put to wise use, in part to influence the choices that we will have in the future. That is why most Canadians want their money to help prevent environmental degradation. But these bills will use their money not to fight global warming but to add to it.
Think for a minute of how far $4.5 billion could go in the sectors of energy conservation, efficiency and renewable energy.
We could have perpetual energy savings by encouraging better insulation of the houses of ordinary Canadians. We could have energy savings through the use of energy efficient lighting in commercial buildings. We could have vastly more fuel efficient cars. We could have greatly enhanced support for public transportation systems, especially in the urban areas. We could have the development of an ethanol fuel industry in Canada. We could have viable co-generation production. We could have solar power. We could have small, independent power producers feeding into provincial grids. Think of the harnessing of a good portion of the wind energy streaming off the mountains in southern Alberta or around the Great Lakes and Hudson Bay shorelines of Ontario.
As the August, 1989 DPA study conducted for the minister recently pointed out, many of these investments would not only save energy, they would also save money.
December 18, 1989

Government Orders
Let me offer an analogy. Let us say you want to wash the walls in your living room and for this purpose you have a bucket, but the bucket has a number of holes in it. These holes, when the water runs out of the bucket, gets your beautiful carpet wet. So you have a choice: you can spend your time and money pouring in more water as fast as you can and rushing the washing job before the carpet gets completely soaked, or you can plug the holes in the bucket and get on with the job.
What will OSLO and Hibernia mean for the environment? They will mean more C02 leaking out the holes. The parliamentary secretary made mention of the Environmental Assessment Panel and the study conducted on Hibernia in 1985, and as he correctly noted, they came up with 50 recommendations. But that study did not even consider CO2 emissions. It was never on the agenda. It was not considered and no recommendations were forthcoming. You can bet that people in Atlantic Canada will be very interested in whether the changes in design will affect the project's safety.
OSLO will doubtless mean a greater burden of sulphur dioxide emissions on to the soils in northern Alberta and even more in Saskatchewan. During the recent environmental review for the ALPAC pulpmill, it was pointed out that the vast majority of these soils are very sensitive and prone to acidification.
When it comes to carbon dioxide, environmentalists know and have told us that heavy oil is particularly bad from a global warming perspective. A recent paper by H. G. Hengeveld, on staff at Environment Canada's Atmospheric Environment Service, titled "Climate Change Implications for Energy" points out that on the basis of emissions of carbon dioxide per unit of energy, energy from oil sands is worse in the sense of being a greater producer of CO2 than biomass energy, gas, oil and even coal. I hope that our scientists in the various pertinent departments are studying this aspect in some detail, because CO2 emissions are clearly going to be an important issue when these bills get to committee, especially when there is considerable pressure for Canada to reduce over-all CO2 emissions by 20 per cent by the year 2005.
The best estimate that I have seen is that these projects combined will cause, and contribute to, the emission of between 20 and 30 metric tonnes of CO2 each year. That is one hell of a lot of CO2. It is an increase in total current Canadian CO2 emissions of between 4 and 7 per cent, and that is just between these two projects.
Even the energy minister is worried about CO2 emissions and global warming. I was delighted to read in the transcript of the hearings of the environment committee on December 11 last week that the minister stated, and I quote from the transcript:
Based on every information I have received in the department from the scientists and others who are working on global warming within the department, I am convinced that we have to reduce emissions, that they have negative effects on climate, that they have negative effects as described by those who have studied the project in detail.
Admirable, Mr. Minister. Unfortunately, these projects fly in the face of that statement. However, I consider that to be the minister's problem, not mine.
Let us ask for the moment what will the projects mean for jobs and regional development. There is no question that jobs will be created. Any large capital project creates jobs. When you are talking about $4.5 billion in maximum total contribution to the two projects, you have to be talking about a lot of jobs. The question is how many jobs and at what cost per job?
Canadian experience shows it is quite common for large projects to be very inefficient creators of jobs. Indeed, I would note parenthetically that decentralized energy efficiency programs would probably be much more effective job creators. In Atlantic Canada, people are more deeply concerned about jobs than ever because of the actions of this government. I note, for example, the cuts in unemployment insurance benefits; the ACOA funding being spread over even more years and, of course, for all the reasons that will be made clear during the emergency debate tonight, the threats to all of the jobs in the Atlantic fisheries.
Yet the number of jobs for Newfoundlanders and for Albertans that will be created by these projects will, I think, be few in terms of the capital invested. We know from past experience with energy megaprojects, that the

Government Orders
dollars per job created is incredibly high by any kind of economic average. But I assume that this too will be the subject of extensive study in the committee.
In that committee, we will also be looking at the question of royalties and tax revenues that will accrue to the provinces involved and to the federal government. Many people doubt the glowing estimates that were made just a few years ago, and they have reason to.
If I may, I would like to return to the question of the government funding, especially in light of Section 3(2)(a)(i) in each of the bills. Those are the sections in each of the bills that mandate the gifts of money, the $1.04 billion for the Hibernia project and the $425 million for the OSLO project. These are gifts. This is free money. No strings attached. It is an incredible thing. I have not really encountered anything like it before.
At the Ottawa Airport this afternoon when the plane came in I was talking very briefly to a member of the government benches who expressed surprise to me when I told him that this was not equity for the federal government, these were gifts. We get nothing in return for this $425 million and $1.04 billion. That is absolutely astonishing. Even in Alberta we know from our experience with the Syncrude project that you can get equity in an energy megaproject for the government that is shelling out the money. We did that in Alberta with Syncrude. That, too, is something to which we will be paying very close attention in the committee study of these bills.
I would like to conclude by reviewing the four conditions for these projects that my party set in a news release and background paper on November 7, 1989, the same day the minister introduced Bills C-44 and C-45.
The government is obviously going to press ahead with these bills. Consequently we want to have on record for the government's consideration, as well as the consideration of others, those four very constructive suggestions that, I will note, received the approval of the energy and environment critic for the federal New Democratic Party in this House, and as well, of the energy and environment critics of the New Democratic Party in the Legislative Assembly of Alberta-that all four of these individuals could come to an agreement on anything is little short of miraculous; in this instance, I think it doubly so.
Let me note very clearly that we are not opposed in principle to these two projects. We are opposed to the fiscal arrangements set out in the bills, and we are opposed to the government's energy policy generally because of the lack of cognizance it takes of environmental concerns.
However, with specific regard to the two projects, the following four conditions constitute the minimum acceptable for the projects to enjoy the support of the New Democratic Party.
First, no investment of public money without equivalent equity held by the Crown.
Second, guarantees, in the agreements among the parties, that production costs will not be subsidized, now or in the future, by the public purse, unless, I will note, such floor price subsidization applies to all oil and gas production in the country.
Third, the immediate restoration by the federal government of expenditures on research into, and development and commercialization of, energy alternatives and conservation up to a minimum of the $400 million budget in 1984.
Fourth, concrete steps and guarantees to minimize the environmental impacts of the projects, including: (a) complete, thorough, joint federal-provincial environmental impact assessments, with extensive consequent public hearings featuring full intervenor funding, to be undertaken in each instance prior to any project commencement; (b) in addition to all measures implemented or planned for the purpose of reducing Canada's CO2 emissions by 20 per cent by the year 2005, the further reduction of CO2 emissions, principally through conservation and greatly enhanced use of fuel ethanol and propane, to a degree equal to the total CO2 emissions from the projects, such that the projects result in no net increase in Canadian CO2 emissions; and, (c), the use of best available technologies for pollution abatement and emissions control, especially with regard to CO2 and
so2.
These are not unreasonable conditions. In fact, these are conditions that I think most Canadians, on reflection, would find not only warrantable but indeed necessary.
I would just note that because the government at the moment cannot for whatever reason see its way clear to accepting these conditions, especially with regard to these two projects, we cannot, in conscience, accept the principle of the fiscal arrangements set out in the bills

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: The Chair has granted leave to the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso to move the adjournment of the House pursuant to Standing Order 52 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the situation in the Atlantic fishery.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso) moved:
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: That this House do now adjourn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: I understand that an arrangement has been entered into among all three parties in which it is the disposition of the House to hear the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, but on the understanding that the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso will be heard later. Is that agreed?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by thanking my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso for moving the motion which we are debating before Your Honour tonight.
This young member has shown more compassion and more concern for Atlantic Canada in one year than the federal Conservative government has shown in the last five.
What we are debating here this evening is not just another crisis. It is not just another local problem. What
we are debating here this evening is the collapse of the entire Atlantic fishery. I want the people from other parts of Canada who may be watching this debate this evening or following Parliament to understand the depth of what we are saying here.
For many Canadians, Atlantic Canada seems remote. Put yourself in a situation where the entire steel industry of Sault Ste. Marie or Hamilton were to be closed down, everybody thrown out of work. Imagine what the reaction would be in the province of Ontario, particularly when the Prime Minister of Canada told them they never had it so good. It is as though the financial district, Montreal or Toronto, was closed down and then the prime Minister were to tell the workers, clerks, office people, they have never had it so good. This is what this Prime Minister has said to the people of Atlantic Canada.
It is more than a crisis. It is a calamity. It is a calamity which is driving pepple out of the Atlantic provinces, a calamity which is wiping out whole towns and villages, a calamity which is destroying a way of life. What has this government done? Let's look at the record of the Prime Minister who in 1988 said during the last federal election in Saint John, New Brunswick on October 13, 1988:
I feel something special for Atlantic Canada and its needs.
If that is something special, the people of Canada want something different and they want something different fast. What are we seeing? We have seen the Marine Ecology Laboratory at the Bedford Institute disbanded, repeated cuts in the fisheries staff, mismanagement of the fish stocks, slashed unemployment insurance payments to Atlantic Canadians.
The federal government has withdrawn the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, reduced commitments to post-secondary education and health care. The provinces of the Atlantic are particularly vulnerable. It failed to renew regional development agreements, closed Armed Forces bases in Atlantic Canada and announced a new national sales tax which in most crippling to Atlantic Canada, because the

December 18, 1989
farther a region of the country is from the source of production the more transportation is needed to bring that good to market, and the more that tax will bear.

To this show of serious concern on the part of the Prime Minister shoud be added the pirating of our fish stocks, something the government does not seem to want or be able to stop. It lets Spanish and Portugese fleets pillage our fish stocks, it lets France steal what is left, and it lets the Europeans set incredibly high quotas.
The present government is being made a fool of by others and, instead of defending the interests of our fisheries, yields to the demands of other countries.
France wants more fish? Our government sees no problem! Just reduce the quotas for our own fishermen. If French traulers don't catch enough fish, our government gives them a consideration to compensate for their loss.
Spanish and Portugese fleets sailing under flags of convenience exhaust the fish stocks just outside our territorial boundaries. What could be more normal.

Let us turn to the United States. The Americans do not like our fish processing regulations. They are the regulations which used to ensure that fish caught in Canada would be processed in Canada. It meant that the Canadian fish plant workers on both coasts, on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, had jobs. This government sold out the fish processing industry in the trade deal with the United States because it gave up our right to impose an export tax on fish, thereby allowing us to be competitive in the fish processing markets.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY

What does it mean to the people of that community, or any community of that size? Not only the fishermen and the fish process workers, but take any small business in the town, the general store, a real estate operator, a food supplier, a clothing distributor, take any professional; who is going to pay for the service? Who is going to pay for the food? Where is the money going to come from? What is going to happen to the only equity that most of the people in Canso have, namely their own homes? What is going to happen to home values as people try to get out, finding no market for a lifetime of saving and equity based in that home.
What is a fisherman going to tell his children on Christmas morning? What is he going to give his teenage son or teenage daughter? It will probably be a one-way ticket to Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver because there will be nothing left for them in Canso.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
The only choice they have is to move out. The irony of it is they will not even be able to take the train out any more because the government has cut the VIA Rail service to that part of Nova Scotia.
It is the same story in North Sydney where another 280 workers are losing their jobs, and in St. John's, Newfoundland where 492 workers are being let go without even getting a severance payment. It is going to be a bleak Christmas for Atlantic Canadians. An estimated 6,000 more jobs are expected to be eliminated in the next few months. Fishery Products International is expected to announce major layoffs very soon.
What about National Sea's U.S. operations on the east coast, their operations in the state of Florida and in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. Why is this Canadian company closing Canadian plants when it's U.S. plants are not affected? It's former president was one of the great promoters of the free trade deal. In 1987 he said

the deal would create 400 new jobs. Now, only two years later, his company is closing its Canadian plants.
How did the Prime Minister react when we raised the question here in the House? He had no answer and no plan. He brandished statistics. He said the Atlantic region was doing well. He even quoted double-digit unemployment in Newfoundland as if it were an achievement, and the trained seals behind him applauded enthusiastically.
The answers given by this Prime Minister and this government are invariably the same: it's all the Liberals fault! Mr. Speaker, I think we should recall that the Conservatives have been in power for five years, and it was the Conservatives who formed this government.

The Canso closure is a direct result of this government's mismanagement of the fishery in Atlantic Canada. Chalk up yet another ghost town to the Tories.
Premier Joe Ghiz was in town today, talking to the Prime Minister about Summerside. Summerside, now Canso. That is something this Prime Minister has been well trained for because he closed Schefferville. At least in those days he was only taking orders from Cleveland. Now he gets them direct from Washington.
The Prime Minister also promised that a committee of cabinet would investigate and come up with a plan to deal with the crisis.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: This is your swan song, is it?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
They said that there would be compensation for those thrown out of work. They said that there would be other programs, other initiatives. Where are those other programs? The fish processing workers on both coasts are still waiting. They are going to join that long line of other employees across the country who are being thrown out of work by the trade deal, waiting for the adjustment programs the Prime Minister promised and continues to promise.
Do you remember those programs, Mr. Speaker? Do you remember that commitment? The only people in Canada who no longer remember that commitment are the Tory ministers who made it.
One of the main reasons they have done nothing is that under the trade deal with the United States they have agreed over the next five to seven years to negotiate the definition of an unfair trade practice or a subsidy with the American government. What has happened is that the government's own trade deal has tied its hands. This government is afraid to come to the aid of a threatened fishing industry because the Americans have told them that any financial support for that industry, particularly when it is export-based, will be considered to be an unfair subsidy by the United States. We are being told by the Americans now much we can finance and rescue our perishing industry in Atlantic Canada.
What about the rate of exchange? The high value of our dollar is killing our exports of fish.

What about the U.S. lobster law signed by President Bush?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: What about your dollar?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
We have the hon. minister from St. John's. I tell you he ought to feel red as one of those lobsters because even he couldn't be exported to the United States under those rules. He is as red as a lobster tonight when he listens to the truth here in the House of Commons.
What about that U.S. lobster law? It was signed by the president. Has our Prime Minister told his great friend, the President of the United States, that this is a serious blow to Atlantic lobster fishermen? Did they discuss the issue at all, at his last visit? Or is a Kennebunkport

December 18, 1989
lobster worth more to the Prime Minister of Canada than the lobsters from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and the east coast of Quebec?
Take another little incident. What about the ramming of the Canadian destroyer Saguenay by the U.S. scallop dragger The Concordia. In this and other instances of American overfishing our government has allowed us to be internationally embarrassed by the fact that we cannot arrest American boats which flagrantly fish illegally in our waters. The minister should refer back-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: What would you have done?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: There is a backbencher who is skulking, he is skulking-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: What would you have done?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
I will tell you what I would do. The minister and the back-bencher who has just spoken, behind the curtain, should refer back to the? I'm Alone case of 1929 to understand the international rules of hot pursuit moving from within territorial waters into international waters. In 1929 the U.S. Coast Guard pursued a Canadian vessel, the I'm Alone for two days and nights in international waters and finally sunk it when its captain refused to surrender.
I am not suggesting that we need to blow U.S. fishing boats out of the water. What I am saying is that it is about time that we started to uphold our rights to protect our fish stocks from this kind of piracy from American and French boats by arresting them and bringing them back into Canadian waters.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is here and he is one of the nice guys, one of the international patsies on behalf of Canada. When we have got a problem he cannot stand up. We concede, we make concessions, we yield but never when there is a confrontation do we stand up and protect our rights.
As if our fishing industry were not in enough trouble, the government has slashed the unemployment insurance scheme. The Minister of Employment and Immigration who has defended the cuts to the unemployment insurance program tells us that by cutting benefits and putting money instead into training her department is doing a great and wonderful thing.
We all ask the question, on this side of the House, training for what? Are you going to train a New Brunswick fisherman to be an automobile worker? Training for
what? Where are the opportunities? Where are those other industries? The minister can talk all she wants about her training programs. It is a wonderful theory, a wonderful plan on paper, but what does it mean to the people in those communities where there are no other job opportunities.
In the words of one local co-ordinator: "It is a disguised resettlement program". In other words, if you want a job to use that retraining, move to Halifax or Montreal or Toronto.

And the Prime Minister blames the Senate for delaying legislation on unemployment insurance reform that will raise variable entrance requirements from 14 weeks to 20 weeks.
The Prime Minister failed to tell Canadians that every year since 1977, we agreed here in the House to an exemption for our fishermen which set this requirement at 10 weeks. His government has failed to table a similar bill. In fact, the present government has put everything into one single bill, and is trying to blame the Senate for its own incompetence. The Maritime Provinces and the rest of Canada will not swallow this explanation, Mr. Speaker.

The government has been talking about taking action to meet the crisis in the fishing industry. It has been talking for months about the crisis brought about in large part by the mismanagement of the industry by this government. It is all talk and no action. The government is bankrupt of ideas. It is about time they faced the brutal truth. It is their own mismanagement which has got the Atlantic fishery into this mess.
In October the minister of fisheries, who is here in the House, said the industry was in good health. That is about the dumbest thing that any fisheries ministry in this country has said since Confederation. Here is how Brian Giroux, Executive Director of the Nova Scotia Dragger Fishermen's Association responded to the minister's ridiculous statement. He said:
Maybe he should have his salary tied to our fish quotas. We have
got to take a 30 per cent cut in our quotas. Maybe if he had to take
a 30 per cent cut in his pay he would think different.
Well, I would think different too. A 30 per cent cut. That minister ought to have a 100 per cent cut.
December 18, 1989

This same minister is now telling impoverished east coast fishing towns that lose their fish processing plants that, in the minister's words, and I quote The Globe and Mail of December 12, 1989: "They have a bright future". The people of Canso, the people of the Avalon Peninsula, the people of the Acadia Peninsula, Caraquet and Tracadie, you have been told by the minister of the Crown that you have got a bright future. What a minister.
Here is another example of his great compassion and understanding at a time when thousands of Atlantic fishermen are being laid off and thousands more are facing incredible hardship. The minister said this, and I am quoting The Toronto Star of a conversation he had December 17, 1989: "Some of those guys are making over $100,000 a year. You sure would not know it the way they sing the blues". If that is sensitivity, I want to hear something else.
We have a Prime Minister who has joined the jet set, burning up fuel not to mention taxpayer's dollars with fleets of government jets to take them all over the capitals of Europe, Africa and Asia, not to mention those obligatory stops in Washington. What does he do when he gets there? What does he talk about when he meets all those leaders? Why has he not been able to convince his counterparts in Europe that the quotas they set for the northwest Atlantic are totally unrealistic? Has he ever raised the issue with those governemnts or is he just there for a few photo opportunities and really does not want to deal with the tough questions?
This government has cut Atlantic Canada adrift. This is not nation building. This is not national reconciliation. This is not building a stronger, more prosperous, more independent and sovereign Canada. This is the destruction of an entire region of Canada, the destruction of a way of life, the destruction or the dreams of thousands and thousands of people who trusted their government to defend their interests.
Frankly, I bleed for the people, the fishermen and the fish workers of Atlantic Canada, good hard-working honest Canadians who have been sold out by their government. My cry to the people of the country and to this House of Commons: Let those of us who are
members of this place take notice of the negligence of this government. Let us condemn this government for that negligence, condemn it for the shameful and utter disregard of the people of Atlantic Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister established a special committee of senior ministers to design effective short-term help and constructive long-term measures to assist communities and individuals who would be affected by serious changes in the Atlantic fishery. I chair that committee which has met a dozen times and drawn together ministers with a particular interest and responsibility in Atlantic Canada. It is supported by a task force of senior officials chaired by Ken Stein, a task force which has met extensively with the fishermen, with the industry, and with provincial governments.
The problem, Sir, is the following: In January of this year federal scientists determined that northern cod stocks were not growing as fast as predicted. There were fewer fish to catch. Unless the quotas were reduced we would seriously jeopardize future stocks and thereby put the industry at even greater risk. Quotas for 1989 were reduced from 266,000 tonnes to 235,000 tonnes. Dr. Les Harris has been asked to check those scientists' findings.
If his report confirms the lower growth of the stock an even lower quota will be required for 1990.
Members of the House should understand that the northern cod stock is the largest commercial fish stock in the northwest Atlantic. The fishery is the sole source of employment in hundreds of communities in Atlantic Canada. Many of those communities are isolated from other economic opportunities.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. A week ago, as the House knows, National Sea Products announced the closure of fish plants in St. John's and Canso and the significant downsize to the plant in North Sydney.
That day my colleagues, the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Public Works announced an immediate assistance plan to help the individuals and the communities involved. That plan involves counselling, training, income assistance under unemployment insurance and special help under the program for older workers. These programs are designed to provide immediate help to the individuals and the communities concerned.
Once the full extent of action to be taken by large companies is known, we will be able to give more details about the amount of assistance. What is important at this stage is that each and every affected worker has complete access to the short-term programs that we will have available. The larger challenge for all of us, Sir, is
December 18, 1989

to deal with the long-term impact of these changes in the Atlantic fishery.
We have been reviewing the role that the federal government plays in areas such as scientific assessment, enforcement and regulations. We believe there are ways in which these functions could be better carried out and in some instances we have already taken action. We expect to receive the Harris report before the end of this year.
We are continuing our work with the provinces with a view to identifying the most effective means by which we can encourage the long-term diversification of the New-foundland-Nova Scotia economies. Newfoundland, in particular, is far too dependent on a resource that is cyclical. Obviously, this is due in part to a lack of other viable options. We will do our utmost to identify effective options for viable diversification of these economies and to create a more viable and a more reliable fishery.
While it is important to find alternatives to the fishery it, of course, will continue to play a major role in the economy of these provinces. We must take steps now that will allow these important stocks to grow at a sustainable level. No quick or magic solution is available. What is needed is years of prudent conservation oriented management. The temptation to artificially prop up the industry is strong, obviously. However, it would be in no one's interest to do that. The problem we face today has been faced and avoided too often before. If we put off dealing with these problems now they will only return again as they have consistently returned throughout the past.
What I can promise tonight is the commitment of this government to find viable and effective options for those communities and those individuals who have been affected or will be affected. The work of the Stein task force, the Hache task force, the panel of Dr. Harris, will all be important parts of the process determining what action we can take and should take.
In addition to the work of the cabinet committee, my colleagues and I have been actively pursuing the problem of overfishing outside the 200-mile limit of Canada. The Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, known as NAFO, was established in 1977 to ensure that the fisheries in the areas outside Canada's 200-mile limit are harvested in accordance with sound conservation principles. From 1977 until 1986 when Portugal and Spain
joined the European community NAFO operated effectively and all members benefited from this co-operation.
There are 12 members of NAFO. The European community is one member. NAFO traditionally reaches decisions by consensus and until recent years that consensus was respected and maintained. The NAFO agreement contains an opting out procedure which enables a member to object to its NAFO quota and to set its own quota instead. Clearly such a procedure was intended for exceptional circumstances since to use it frequently would undermine the whole system of conservation management. If NAFO were to collapse chaos would ensue with every fishing fleet battling for as much as could be caught. Harvesting in those circumstances would become strip mining. There would be no winners.
Every year since 1986 the European community has invoked the exceptional objections procedures and has established its own unilateral quotas at levels often many times higher than those approved by NAFO. Those quotas have been so high that they have never actually been caught. Even so, the actual catches, mainly by Spanish and Portuguese vessels, have far exceeded the European community quotas set by NAFO. Thus the European Commission has abandoned in the north west Atlantic the very conservation principles it applies off its own coast. The problem of overfishing has been exported to the other side of the Atlantic, to our side.
All other members of NAFO, including the U.S.S.R., Japan, Norway, Cuba and eastern European countries, have continued to accept their NAFO quotas and abide by the NAFO conservation regime, sometimes at great sacrifice. Only the European community has resisted doing so in spite of two NAFO resolutions appealing for respect of NAFO decisions. The result, Sir, is a very serious threat to important fisheries stocks, an obvious and an unnecessary threat. Much damage has been done and we are seeing the price that must be paid for that damage here in Canada. The situation can still be remedied, but the point of no return is approaching rapidly.
In the past several months, the Prime Minister, the Minister for International Trade, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, and I have put substantial effort into making the European community aware of the serious consequences of overfishing. The right hon. Leader of

December 18, 1989
the Opposition asked the rhetorical question as to whether the Prime Minister has raised the question. Of course he has with the leaders of Spain, with the leaders of Portugal and with the leaders of the European Commission directly. We will continue to do that. We have stressed the importance of consistent conservation rules for the long-term viability of these stocks. This has been done through political pressure and through diplomatic pressure, and it will continue to be done until the problem is resolved.
The Minister for International Trade, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and I have met several of our counterparts in the European member states. In Brussels last week, I took the opportunity to discuss our concerns again with Hans Andriessen, the European Commissioner for External Relations and Trade, and with the Foreign Minister of Portugal, de Deus Pinheiro. We have also done this through a public information campaign in which federal and provincial governments, parliamentarians, industry and labour have all participated. To enhance and co-ordinate those efforts, we designated a special ambassador for marine conservation, Mr. Alan Beesley, who has been leading our campaign since the summer.
We have been able to correct some misconceptions regarding the seriousness of the problem of the fishery in the north west Atlantic and to establish the urgency of addressing these problems. We have made some progress that would not have been made without that kind of pressure.

speechtext: What about the progress?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
I will tell you about the progress.
This year, for the first time since 1985, the European community has recommended unilateral quotas which in some cases accept NAFO quotas and in other cases reduce the European community quotas below the level of actual European communicty catches in recent years.
We were particularly interested to note that the commission was proposing a reduction for two flatfish stocks, American plaice and yellow tail flounder, and for one cod stock, 3NO cod on the southern tail of the bank.
This is a positive step and is consistent with decisions taken by NAFO.
Unfortunately, however, the proposals of the commission include quotas which far exceed those of NAFO for the 2J3KL cod stock. Some 27,000 tonnes of stradding stock cod are proposed as the unilateral European community quota, as opposed to a quota of zero set by NAFO.
Clearly there is still a long way to go on this problem, and it is essential that Canada continue the discussions with the community on all aspects of fisheries managements and fisheries relations.
While this first step taken by the European community is important and welcomed, I urge the community to take a giant step now and work with all other NAFO members along the difficult but rewarding path of sustainable development, because if they do not, as the Prime Minister has made clear in his representations directly to European leaders, it is not simply Canadian fishermen who suffer. When the stock is depleted regularly as is now the case by overfishing by European nations, it affets the livelihoods and the future of fishermen everywhere. It affects them here directly, of course. It affects them in the community as well.
The problems that we face in the Atlantic Canada fishery are complex and they are difficult, but they are problems that affect the lives of thousand of Canadians and we must alleviate that burden as much as possible.
Over the coming weeks and months, my committee and our officials will continue our work in this direction. We will be continuing our discussions with the provinces on a long-term diversification program in which we expect them to play a full part. We will be providing the short-term adjustment programs that are necessary in these difficult times, and we will be looking into decisions that we can take that will help us to better manage this important resource. We recognize that the effect of this problem upon the lives of Atlantic Canadians is considerable and it is difficult.
I can assure this House that we will do our utmost to ensure the long-term economic security of the affected regions and to ensure also adjustment assistance for the affected individuals.
December 18, 1989

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we go into the Christmas season there is a sense of desperation in Canada. It affects many communities. It affects many family homes, many apartments. I would be the first to admit that it does not hit each family in each community, but its grasp is extensive and it affects the lives of many Canadians.
Communities will lose their train service next month, farm families will lose farms that have been in the family for generations, miners in my own community of Lynn Lake will not only lose their severance pay as a result of a mine closing. Towns like Portage la Prairie have not only had the government action of closing down a military base but have also had Campbell's Soup announce that it will be closing its plant as well.
There is desperation for many Canadians who only have short-term jobs and know that they will lose their UI benefits. There is desperation for families who are hard pressed to pay their own bills and who found out on Friday that their children's education is going to have a surcharge put on it, that the government wishes to charge hundreds of dollars to an average student in order to pay for the privatization of the Canada Student Loans Program.
Area of this country that had hope for their own future now see cut-backs in regional development programs, in tourist programs, and in forestry agreements. People are uncertain whether under the free trade agreement this government will ever again help their region or help their industry. People feel that the government is continuing to turn its back on the Canadian people. Nowhere is this more true than in Atlantic Canada and no industry was more directly hit than the fishing industry.
Last week we heard question in the House about the closure of National Sea Products, one of the two largest fishing corporations in Canada. It announced a series of plant closures that will affect 1,500 workers and their families in Atlantic Canada. The plant in St. John's, Newfoundland will be closed and will eliminate 492 jobs. The facility at Canso will close throwing 742 people out of work. This processing facility is the largest single employer in that community. The plant in North Sydney, Nova Scotia, will be converted to a salt-fish operation with a job loss of 280.
Earlier in the year, the National Sea Plant at Locke-port, Nova Scotia, was closed with a job loss of 220 people. Another 150 jobs were lost when the Port Mouton facility of Clearwater Fine Foods closed in March, while another 100 plant workers in New Wave Fisheries found themselves unemployed when their plant closed. That is the action so far and we are now awaiting the Fisheries Products International announcements which are also expected to be very devastating to Atlantic Canada.
One of the most upsetting things about listening to the Secretary of State for External Affairs speak earlier today was the appearance that this was a new problem, the kind of feeling that he was trying to give people in Atlantic Canada and people in the House that they set up a committee six months ago because they discovered there was something new, something which was very damaging to the Atlantic Canadian fishing industry. Nothing could be further from the truth.
We have known for years that the fishing industry was in jeopardy. As far back as 1981, when the government through its own report Resource Prospects for Canada's Atlantic Fisheries, 1981-1987 allowed for a projected increase in the resource, it stated the following:
While 1981 predictions are based largely on formal calculations- projections of stock status in later years are to considerable extent best guesses, based on inadequate knowledge.
No action was taken. In 1982 the Kirby report, while projecting a northern cod stock viable enough to have a total allowable catch for 1987 set at 380,000 tonnes, contained the following statement:
A reliance on growth cannot be sustained indefinitely and in many stocks the biological limits of prudent harvesting have been reached, or nearly so.
Again no action was taken, except that Kirby went to the Senate.
In 1987 the federal government commissioned the Alverson report which examined the trends of the cod stocks off Newfoundland. This report warned, and again I quote:
Estimates of the growth in the total stock may have been overly
optimistic and -has not reach expected levels.
Again no action was taken.

December 18, 1989
Finally in early 1988 there was the Canada-Newfound-land Inshore Fisheries Agreement which contained the following:
With few exception the fishery resources of the Atlantic have
reached their maximum utilization and in some cases there is an
indication that overexploitation is occurring.
Again no action was taken.
There have been years and years of Liberal and Tory governments, years and years of government reports, and years and years of Liberal and Tory inaction on a very important process.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: Years and years of NDP whining.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the Liberals sitting in his little box back there says that we were whining. Yes, we were whining. We were complaining about Liberal inaction just like we are complaining about Conservative inaction now.
It comes to the same issue when it comes to foreign overfishing. It is nice for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to get up and say that we have had a special high ranking commission, with he himself as the head of it and with senior cabinet ministers, that has been meeting for six months. In addition we have officials, all of a very senior level, and they have been meeting for six months. Why were they not doing something when this was a problem four, five and six years ago?
The problems that Atlantic Canada faces now in the fishing industry are not new. They are not something which occurred six months ago. The overfishing is not something that occurred six months ago. The only thing new is that now government is trying to do something to save its own political rump, while Atlantic Canadians are losing their jobs and their homes.
There are things that could have been done and there are things that can be done now. In Iceland, for example, there is a program to make sure that there is no overfishing in the spawning season. We have a spawning season in Atlantic Canada for the cod, which is basically mid-March to mid-May. Why do we not have a similar program in place? Why was this not in place not six months ago but six years ago? Why has that not happened? When is the government finally going to announce that we will have a similar program in this country?
Again, with all the concern that we have as Canadians about our lack of ability to have adequate surveillance off the Atlantic coast, why has the Government of Canada announced this year that the work of the Tracker aircraft will be suspended in that region? Why is it, in the same year that a Canadian destroyer cannot adequately protect our shores, the government is not announcing something to ensure that we can have the necessary surveillance both by ship and by air of our Atlantic fisheries?
Again, this is a government that has prided itself on environmental assessments, saying it is necessary for every major undertaking of the government. Why have we not had a full environmental assessment of the process by which quotas and allocations of our fish resources are set? Why has that not been done? These are not new ideas. These are ideas that the government could have been acting on for years.
Why have we not had Canadian leadership to fight the foreign overfishing off our coasts? Why have we always reacted? Why have we reacted to the lobster decision? Why have we allowed Portugal and Spain continuously to overfish in our areas and off our 200-mile limit?
We listened to the government. We sense that government members really do not have a plan. With each and every decision, whether it is by National Sea or by Fisheries Products International, we get the sense that all of this was a surprise, that they did not know the decision was going to come down, and that they did not know the Americans were going to make the decision on the lobsters. Yet, they have reports in the Deparment of Fisheries and Oceans which indicate that they knew what the American decision was going to be. For that matter, from the department's own report, they actually defend the upcoming American decision with regard to the lobsters:
For conservation reasons, the U.S. government is trying to
increase the size of lobster that can be caught or imported into the
United States.
This government, in its own report, knew what was coming. You would never know it from the reaction of the Minister for International Trade who shouted once the decision was finally made that the full weight and influence of the Canadian government will be brought to bear on the U.S. Congress and the U.S. administration in
December 18, 1989

an attempt to settle this very serious problem in the interests of our fishermen in eastern Canada.
We are waiting to see what reaction is. The people of Atlantic Canada are wondering why there was no protection earlier. Obviously the Department of Fisheries and Oceans knew that this was going to happen.
The same thing is true with regard to the situation with Spanish and Portuguese overfishing. Why do we continue to pretend that this is a new problem? Why do we continue to pretend that the first time ever we have to go to Spain or we have to go to Portugal to deal with this matter?
We have known about it for years. If it is this most recent government or the government that preceded it, it has basically been a program of reaction, a lack of any leadership, a lack of any planning.
I mentioned in my opening remarks there is a sense that the Canadian government has turned its back on many Canadians and that is especially true in Atlantic Canada. When you see your train service going and you see your fisheries going; when you realize tourist programs are not being renewed; when you see that the government cuts back on its own touted Atlantic Canada Development Agency; when you see forestry agreements not being renewed; or agreements when they are renewed, such as the tourist agreement, have only half as much money put into them; when you know that you can no long afford to send your children to university and the government says "go get a student loan and we will charge you a surcharge on that now," costing as I mentioned earlier, hundreds and hundreds of dollars to an average family; when you get that happening time after time, day after day, how can people in Atlantic Canada say that the federal government is going to represent them?
How people in Atlantic Canada say that their members of Parliament from that region really are concerned with the decisions that are made in cabinet? How can any Atlantic Canadian feel that this Parliament and this government is addressing his or her concerns?
I have received more phone calls today on this issue after it became known that I would be speaking for our caucus, than I have on a number of other issues over the
last few months. There is a real desperation out there and without all the political rhetoric there is a real need for real government action to make people in Atlantic Canada feel that we care and that government is going to do something more than hold a committee for a mere six months.
