speechtext:
I wonder if the hon. member for South West Nova would leave it to others who have been designated to assist the Speaker.
I recognize the hon. member for Kamloops.
Mr Riis: Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say that we in the New Democratic Party would be more than willing to co-operate on this most important matter and to indicate that our leader will be speaking later in the debate when she returns from the west coast.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, it is with gravity and emotion that I rise this evening to address a matter of the utmost importance for Atlantic Canada and indeed for the country as a whole, that is the crisis of the Atlantic fishery. That industry employs 10 per cent of Atlantic Canada's workforce, contributes millions to the Gross Provincial Product of the four Atlantic provinces, sustains hundreds of coastal communities and is a way of life for thousands of families throughout our region, a way of life which is now in peril.
I want to begin by expressing my sincere thanks to Your Honour for granting this emergency debate and thereby raising the profile of this issue to the top of the national agenda. My colleagues from Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island will speak to the dimensions of the crisis in their provinces. I will focus my remarks on Nova Scotia and in particular on the town of Canso.

The town of Canso is located at the eastern apex of mainland Nova Scotia and has been the heart of the fishing industry in that area for nearly 400 years. The communities which surround Canso have been dependent upon the fishery, on inshore fishery and on the offshore fishery, for generations. The Canso plant, now known as the National Sea Products plant, has through successive ownerships sustained an industry and an economy stretching from Canso all the way to Antigon-ish. It is the main employer in that area.
A week ago, National Sea Products Limited announced the closure of its fish processing plant and its trawler port thereby directly affecting some 800 to 850 workers. If the decision is not reversed, a $1 million monthly payroll will dry up. Local services which depend on the fishery will be crippled. The town and county, faced with the loss of its tax base, will be unable to cope. The closure of the National Sea Products plan in Canso, if it is not averted, will mean the devastation of not only the town of Canso but of the entire county of Guysbo-rough and much of eastern Nova Scotia.
I was in Canso on the weekend, I spoke with workers at the National Sea Products plant. I spoke with trawler workers, those hardy souls who pursue their livelihoods on the stormy seas of the north Atlantic. Across the street I met with Cansonians doing their pre-Christmas shopping at the co-op store. I met with the mayor, Mr. Ray White, and members of his council on the prospects for the town and surrounding communities in light of the National Sea Products decision. Mayor White and the warden of Guysborough County, Herman Long, have travelled to Ottawa to attend this debate and are in the gallery tonight.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
They and the council of the town of Canso want to underscore the importance of this industry to their future.
The reaction of Cansonians to the National Sea announcement has been one of disbelief. They do not believe that a company which as recently as a month ago praised the workforce at its Canso plant and on its trawlers would suddenly close the entire operation. They cannot believe that a community which has survived on fishing for 400 years, a community where no other conceivable economic alternatives exist, would permanently shut down because of a temporary depletion of fish stocks.
That National Sea Products would choose to pull out of Canso and close its other Atlantic plants after spending millions of its recent profits to acquire a vast international empire, including processing plants in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in the United States, is unbelievable to the people of Canso.
What Cansonians find most difficult to believe or what they cannot accept is a Canadian government, which purports to speak for all Canadians, which is a shareholder in this company, and which has known for months that the situation facing the Atlantic fishery, has so quietly acquiesced to this corporate decision.
The crisis facing the Atlantic fishery was not begun with these recent announcements of plant closures by National Sea Products. The writing has been on the wall for many months. Little has been done to offset this crisis.
When questioned on the matter, the government has always evaded the issue by stating the facts and figures of scientific studies which have been proven to be an inaccurate measure at best. Then they stalled by saying that they are waiting for the reports of Harris and Hache.
It is fine to have independent studies done, but why have they not come up with a strategy for saving this important industry? As usual, the cart is before the horse with this government and the blame falls on poor leadership and mismanagement by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
The government response to the plant closures announced by the Minister for International Trade in St. John's last Monday, and echoed I presume by the Nova Scotia minister in Canso, is a slap in the face to the workers who have invested their lives in this industry.
What is new about telling workers they will be able to qualify for UI? What is new in that? What is new in telling them that they can be retrained for some other industry? What is new in that? What is new in telling them that they can retire early? What is new in telling them that they can leave Canso and find jobs in some other industries elsewhere? That is not a response to an urgent crisis.

The response of the Minister of Fisheries is even more contemptible. He says the fishing industry is fine. His response to the workers is: "Don't worry! Be happy''. They are worried in Canso and they are not happy. They are worried about their future and they are worried about the loss of their livelihood.
Phyllis MacDonald spoke for all fish plant workers in Canso when she told me on Saturday: "I've worked for ten years at this plant. I'm trained to process fish. I'm good at what I do. I don't want to be trained for something else. I don't want UI. I just want to work."
Canso has become a symbol. It is a symbol of the neglect of Atlantic Canada by this government. It is a symbol of the insensitivity of this government to the regions of this country. And it is a symbol of the gross mismanagement by this government of the Atlantic fishery.
How else can one explain the sudden revelation that fish stocks throughout Atlantic Canada are seriously depleted? Who has been managing these stocks for the last four years? Who is responsible for licensing and regulating fishermen and fishing vessels? Who determines where and how much can be fished? Who monitors and collects information on fish landings and on fishing activity? Who polices, or does not police, illegal overfishing by foreign vessels in Canadian waters? Who has been issuing foreign licences to foreign factoiy-freezer trawlers from Russia, Spain, Portugal, Poland, from everywhere? Who has turned a blind eye while the mid-shore dragger fleet off the Scotia shelf suddenly tripled in capacity at the same time as stocks in this area and in Georges Bank were being decimated? If this is not mismanagement, Madam Speaker, then what is it?
This government talks about diversification. It promises a community development fund to wean fishing communities off fishing and onto other activities. But who can believe the government when it slashes regional development spending in Atlantic Canada, when it pulls out of towns like Summerside after promising the moon during the election campaign and when the minister for ACOA announces in Port Hawkesbury, two weeks before the election, that Thyssen of Germany will invest
$58 million and create 500 jobs in the Strait of Canso area, and a year later nothing has happened?
The people of Canada are fed up with empty Tory promises. This government, unable to come up with solutions of its own to the messes that it has created with its policies, is constantly asking the opposition, and in particular the Liberals, for solutions. Well here are some solutions.
Begin by lowering interest rates and the value of the Canadian dollar, a policy which is crippling the export industries of the Atlantic region. Sit down and, in return for a package of assistance, oblige National Sea and Fishery Products International to spread out its quota among Atlantic plants so that towns like Canso, with an historic attachment to the fishery and no alternatives, can continue to survive and stay in the fishery until fish stocks improve. Find innovative markets and uses for under-utilized species, encourage Canadian fleets to catch these species and process them in Canadian, not foreign, plants. Put in place stock-management programs that make sense and that provide benefits to Canadians, not to foreign governments.
I recognize that the Atlantic fishery must continue to be economically viable and that to force companies like National Sea Products and Fishery Products International into bankruptcy would not contribute to its health. However, the Government of Canada can never forget that the fishery belongs to the people of Canada to be managed for the benefit of Canadians, in particular Canadians in Canada's coastal communities who depend with a larger stake in the Atlantic fishery, with a more legitimate claim to this resource, than the town of Canso and the surrounding villages of eastern Nova Scotia. They must not be allowed to die.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to paraphrase my colleague who just spoke, the Government of Canada will not forget the communities of Atlantic Canada and does not overlook the fact that the fish stocks of Atlantic Canada belong to Canadians, but especially to those of Atlantic Canada who have depended on them for their sustenance and livelihoods for centuries.
I understand the intensity that the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso brings to this debate and I compliment him on requesting that this debate be

held this evening. I listened carefully to his comments. Having grown up in a small coal-mining town myself and having seen a succession of mine closings I think I can personally feel the hurt, the anxiety and the frustrations that are being experienced in communities like Canso as we approach the holiday period.
I recognize that Mayor White and an alderman from Canso are in the House tonight. I have had the privilege of visiting communities like Canso, Black Tickle and Meteghan up and down the coast of Atlantic Canada. I know that there is no option that the fishery, particularly the inshore fishery and the fish plants, is really what give people an adequate income in a situation where they can properly raise their children and look forward with confidence and optimism toward the future. So I do not take lightly any of the contributions that have been made this evening to this point and I will listen with great interest to the balance of the speeches this evening.
I think we all feel a special admiration for men and women that go down to sea and we must share their sadness when tragedy strikes, as occurred last week when the Johnny and Sisters II sank in a fierce storm, losing Captain Harry Thorneburn and eight men of the crew, including his son. I think all members of the House would want to send our heartfelt regrets to the families of these lost fishermen.
The problems of the Atlantic fishery are not problems that have just sprung upon us. Were I sitting on the opposition side I would probably be as wont to finding simplistic excuses or criticisms to offer. These problems have been a fact of the fishery for as long as it has been conducted but have become increasingly difficult in these times when we have modem, sophisticated industries and technology allowing us to sell a very valuable product into an international marketplace where we are very vulnerable to the swings of supply and demand and exchange rates.
Even more seriously, we are constantly faced with the increasing advancement of technology and the ability to find fish wherever they are, to put large nets in their path and to harvest them in abundant quantities. Coupled with that, we have to face the real problem that our science is not as highly developed as it ought to be because there are many things that defy the ability of scientists to make accurate predictions about the magnitude of the fish stocks.
I want to point out for the benefit of members that the life cycle of the Atlantic cod being eight years plus makes it very difficult to learn about the first two or three years of that life cycle in order to be able to predict the abundance and set quotas for that stock from five to ten years after it was originally spawned.
We have developed a very elaborate system over the past 15 years, at least since the extension of jurisdiction, to involve all of the interested parties, all of those whose future hinges on the health of the fishery to be a part of the quota-setting process.
So we have an elaborate system of consultation which involves the input of scientific advice produced by our scientists who we believe are among the world's finest. They present, through the Canadian Atlantic Fishery Scientific Advisory Committee, quota proposals based, as I conceded a few moments ago, on an inadequate understanding of how many fish lurk beneath the surface of the sea and how they are managing in terms of food supply, in terms of water temperature and currents and the presence of predators. We take this scientific advice and we then sit down with all of the industry groups each autumn through a structure called the Atlantic Ground-fish Advisory Committee and together with scientists and officials discuss what the quotas should be for the coming year.
That consultation culminates in a meeting each December between myself and the Atlantic provincial fisheries ministers at which the proposed groundfish management plan is further discussed and at which time I try to seek the support of the four maritime ministers, the Newfoundland minister and the Minister of Fisheries for Quebec as we finalize a document which contains the proposed quotas for some 50 groundfish stocks in Atlantic Canada.
This process has evolved, as I mentionned, over some 10 to 15 years and it represents the finest example of consultation in reaching decisions which contribute to the orderly and sustainable management of a finite resource. The policies within which those decisions are taken are modified as a result of suggestions from the Atlantic Regional Council. You yourself, Mr. Speaker, in another incarnation, created this policy advisory group which helps us to decide the forms of policy by which the Atlantic fishery is managed.
December 18, 1989

All of this to say that the question of what went wrong is not simply a matter of accusing or laying the blame at the feet of any particular individual or agency of government. This is a complex process and one which has improved and evolved. I think it was the member for Selkirk who made some helpful suggestions of things we should be doing to better assess the environmental sustainability, I think was how he put it, of these precious stocks of fish. In fact, that is what we have been doing. For some two to three years now we have been working to improve our knowledge of this resource and the means by which we predict the quotas.
I would like to just list a few of the things that I have been privileged to initiate in the more than four years that I have been Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and to state that we would not have taken these initiatives if we were not concerned about the future stability and integrity of the Atlantic groundfish industry.
In January, 1986, at an Atlantic Council of Fisheries Ministers meeting in St. John's we tackled the problem of foreign fishing within and beyond the Canadian 200-mile limit. As a result of that and numerous meetings that I have held with Atlantic provincial ministers, we announced a new policy in June of that year which involved the re-arming of our fisheries patrol vessels, an increase in fines under the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act from a level of $50,000 for a summary offence to over $500,000. We introduced armed boarding parties. We apprehended and pursued vessels half way across the Atlantic and beyond. As a result of the intensification of our enforcement against foreign vessels that would violate our fishing zone, we saw in the subsequent years, 1987 and beyond, a substantial decline in the number of sightings of and alleged offences by these foreign vessels. We introduced full observer coverage on all foreign vessels fishing within our waters.
Another important initiative that we decided was that no longer should the right to fish our precious, non-surplus cod stocks in Canadian waters be tied to some kind of market access consideration. We said the only quotas available within our waters would be of surplus stocks, that is, those which were not of interest to the Canadian fishing industry. We said the countries, in most cases members of the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, which qualify for these quotas would, in turn, have to exhibit good behaviour in terms of meeting our conservation requirements. We introduced increased aerial surveillance, with both fixed-wing aircraft and
5. ft 52
helicopters, in both the Newfoundland and the Scotia- Fundy region.
One of the most important initiatives of all that I recall taking arose from my visits to small inshore communities in Newfoundland in the summer of 1986, and then Newfoundland and the coast of Labrador in the summer of 1987. I listed to fishermen. I visited them at the wharves early in the morning to learn that they were extremely alarmed and troubled by the shrinking size and the disappearance of the inshore cod that they had been traditionally accustomed to catching.
I was troubled by this to the extent that we took major initiatives early in 1987 to end the practice of discarding young fish at sea and to placing observers on our domestic offshore vessels when they were fishing in areas where the cod would be spawning at that time of year. We introduced stiff penalties for the discard and wastage of young northern cod and required that the fishing effort be spread out among the three sub-regions known as 2J, 3K and 3L. This had some initial effect, we believe, in helping the inshore fishery to begin to recover as it appeared to do in 1988.
But when I returned in the summer of 1987 the fishermen were still alarmed. They felt that the quotas which had been set in the mid to late 1980s as a result of the projections of scientific advice in the late 1970s and the advice of the people who advised the Kirby Ihsk Force apparently were too high. The inshore fishermen banded together and created a group called the Newfoundland Inshore Fisheries Association and demanded that we set the quota lower. Contrary to scientific advice, I set the quota lower and at the same time I commissioned a group of eminent international scientists headed up by Dr. Lee Alverton of the University of Washington, Dr. Pope of the University of Lowestoft in Britain and other acknowledged experts to find out whether our scientists were properly predicting the abundance of the northern cod stock.
As we look back now we can see that those were the beginnings of a process which has led to a much more accurate means of predicting the abundance of cod stocks. The age classifications and the survival rate of each age group is much more carefully taken into account. The result was that the scientific advice presented for northern cod last winter suggested that our quotas had been far too high, that the overly optimistic notion that we could extract some 400,000 metric tonnes of cod from the northern cod resource was vastly

exaggerated and that we would have to lower the quota to about half of that and perhaps even less still.
In February of 1989, early this year, I had to take the difficult choice, notwithstanding all of the consultation and all the advice we had received, of reducing that quota temporarily to 235,000 metric tonnes. I commissioned Dr. Les Harris, President of Memorial University; Dr. Alverson, other scientists and other leaders of the Newfoundland fishing industry to re-examine this whole question as to whether we were using the proper scientific methodology to predict the abundance of these stocks.
I am elaborating on this because the member for Selkirk seemed to suggest that we should be doing some kind of a comprehensive environmental study of this resource. In fact, that is the process that has been evolving for three years. We are trying to find the cause of the problem to fix it. I am sorry to say that our findings are not producing popular results. In fact, there are many people who do not want to believe the scientists and do not want to believe these international experts. Those who have made investments predicated on a continuing healthy offshore fishery have now had to re-assess those decisions.
We have all had to re-assess the size of this industry in terms of the capacity that was encouraged by the restructuring of 1982 and 1983, by a royal commission of inquiry at that time, by the pouring of tens of millions of dollars into creating and industry predicated upon certain expectations about the abundance of the resource only to find, as we have suspected for some time, that the resource cannot sustain the levels which had been envisaged for it.
Something has gone wrong in the projections of the resource but all is not disaster in the Atlantic fishery because we have some 50 stocks of Atlantic groundfish producing over 850,000 metric tonnes of abundance. We have the problem of an excessively high price for cod block in 1987 which collapsed in 1988. We have the problem of a declining appetite for fish in the large United States market which is important. Most of all, we have the problem of communities dependent on fish plants which are the very heart and soul of those communities.
We have to find solutions through the package of economic measures which have been described in this House this evening and last week and which we will elaborate upon in the coming days. No amount of economic assistance, no tens of millions of dollars will restore the self-respect, the sense of pride, the sense of fulfilment and happiness that we wish for all Canadians at this time of year.
I hope through the findings that I have described tonight, this new scientific advice, through measures we are taking to tighten up on the overcapacity in the industry, through increased fines under the Fisheries Act for domestic violation, and through the initiatives to end the blatant foreign destruction of our stocks beyond our 200-mile limit, that we can create a greater sense of optimism about the fishery of the future.
It troubles me no end that we have something in the order of 325,000 to 350,000 tonnes of very fine protein in the water of Atlantic Canada which our Canadian industry is not interested in catching; whether this be in the form of redfish, turbot, Greenland halibut, capelin or other species. Under the international law of the sea and Canada's international obligations, if Canadian interests-fishermen and investors-are not willing to harvest that resource, other nations, in this case through the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, have an opportunity to ask our permission to harvest it. It does not belong to Canada but as the coastal state we have first refusal on it.
Last year some 160,000 of those surplus species were allocated to Canadian companies and something less than 50,000 tonnes were harvested. There is a surplus there of about 120,000 tonnes of these species which I believe we can further develop and further exploit for the benefit of communities such as Canso, St. John's and others.
I am not saying that this is the solution to all of these problems but we are putting together a pool of these under-utilized species, and I believe that with the kind of assistance available through the Community Development Program and the economic diversification initiatives that this government will be funding we can help some enterprises in some of these communities to find ways to harvest that significant amount of Canadian resource which, for many years, has been left in the
December 18, 1989

water or given away to the foreigners. In fact, we could claim the full 325,000 or 350,000 tonnes if we could make it work for us.
That is the commitment that I am making together with a commitment for additional measures to bring the capacity growth under control, to create a fishery in which we all show more responsibility toward the resource. In a more personal sense, we need to create a future, to create an industry and to add diversification to that industry in the communities such as Canso and Lockeport and other which have not yet been named to ensure that ther is a continuation of a strong and healthy fishery in their futures.
I ask all members of this House to try to understand the complexity of the issue but yet to share with me the optimism that the problem can be solved for the greater good of all Atlantic Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. LeBlanc) for persevering in his request for this emergency debate. I also wish to thank the Speaker of the House who approved this request. It is a sign that the Chair has fully understood the seriousness of the situation. There are more than enough problems in the fisheries, whether we are talking about the Atlantic, Newfoundland, Nova
Scotia, Prince Edward Island, eastern Quebec and New Brunswick, or about the West Coast, with the salmon and herring fishery. We also have problems with pollution in certain waterways on the coast of British Columbia. We have problems in the Artie fishery. We have problems in the Great Lakes. We have problems across Canada, but we have one major problem, and that is that our fisheries have no one to defend them. We saw an example of that this evening. When it is time to talk about the fisheries and to provide solutions, who rises in the House to talk about the fisheries ? The Minister of External Affairs (Mr. Clark). That is the problem. Because the Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, has been given a free rein to visit foreign countries and conclude all kinds of agreements, we have lost the fisheries. The Minister is simply out to lunch as far as the fisheries are concerned. That is our major problem.
Mr. Speaker, to get back to the Atlantic region, what we are now seeing is a major crisis. For us, in the Atlantic region, it means our economic base is crumbling. Our cod stocks are disappearing. We are faced with overfishing by foreign fleets and a government that refuses to act, a government that lets everything pass. We have been hit by unilateral action taken by the Americans, a decision that restricts exports of lobsters to the United States. The crab season has been a real disaster. There again, stocks are exhausted, which has a particular impact on New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
In New Brunswick and elsewhere, we have been hearing about plant closures, which in some cases, especially in Canso, will cause an entire community to disappear. The community will close down. And what does the government do? What does the government say? Not much! And the worst of it is that the government is siding with the big corporations instead of defending the interests of fishermen and plant workers. What the government fails to understand is that the fish stocks in the sea are there for all Canadians and for the communities that depend on them. So far, this government has refused to protect this resource for those communities. The government has preferred to listen to the corporations which want to do what suits them and transfer fish stocks from one location to the other. In the

December 18, 1989
case of Canso, the whole economic base will disappear. There will be nothing left in that part of the province. We have a government that promises assistance, assistance that has yet to materialize, although the plant closures have already been announced. Those are a few of the reasons why I support the motion by the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso. This perseverance is truly admirable.
Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words about the serious impact of this crisis on the fishery in New Brunswick. I realize that my colleagues from other provinces will consider the specific impact on their respective provinces.
We in New Brunswick sympathize with other Atlantic communities because we know what it means to lose a community's only source of income. I would like to quote what was said by the hon. Denis Losier, New Brunswick Minister of Fisheries and Aquaculture, who stated: "New Brunswick's economy will lose as much as $130 million this year because of declining snow crab stocks and the low prices offered for lobster and herring roe".
The snow crab fishery is in trouble. We had a terrible season last spring, catches were very low and quality was poor. A number of communities have been affected, including Caraquet, Shippegan, Cap-Pele and Shediac. Some examples: Chaleur Bay Packers closed down in Bas-Caraquet; 160,000 people are out of work. Three hundred people lost their jobs when Connors Brothers closed in Shippegan; 250 jobs were lost at L. Gauthier and Sons in Shippegan. The situation has taken on crisis proportions, and this is just in the snow crab industry.
Now a few words about herring roe. Here again, the season was a disaster, not because there wasn't enough fish, but because prices were so low, it wasn't worth the effort.
And now about lobster. Last summer in my riding, fishermen were practically giving the lobster away. They were selling it for $1.50 a pound. Why? Because the packers were stuck with big inventories. Why were they stuck with big inventories? Because our lobster was too expensive for the American market. They were too expensive because the Canadian dollar was too high as result of this government's high interest rate policy. The government refuses to budge. Our lobster is no longer
competitive on American markets. We are losing our export markets.

Madam Speaker, as if we did not have enough problems, the Americans have given us some more. They came up with legislation that will limit the import of lobsters to the United States. This will affect about $30 million worth of lobsters.
This means that we will have to process that lobster. We will not be able to sell it live on the American market. Why? Because the Americans decided to bring in a regulation that limits those exports, after the Prime Minister said that he would do everything to stop that measure from going through. What did he do? Well, we do not know. We know that whatever he tried did not work.
And what do we hear from this government? [Translation]
Madam Speaker, I have come to the end of my speech. We would like to see a far more positive reaction from this government. The government has to act aggressively. It must be prepared to do some serious funding. It must ensure that funding is available to promote the use of under-utilized species. It must help fishermen make the necessary adjustments to be able to catch those species. It must also help the processors and the plants to change their equipment so they can process these fish.
The government must also make and effort on the marketing end, to promote species that will no longer be under-utilized, species that our fishermen will be able to catch.
Finally, Madam Speaker, this government must provide assistance to communities and help them through this crisis, so that as soon as fish stocks have been rebuilt, these communities will still be able to make a living from the fishery.

speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker. As I was saying, I have only 10 minutes to make some points on behalf of no fewer than 16,000 or 17,000 fishermen and plant workers who live in the riding of Burin-St. George's. I understand the reason for the agreement and I respect it because so many people in the Official Opposition want to speak on this very important issue.
First, let me deal with a very important specific that has come up already in this debate. I hear members of the NPD with their fairly limited knowledge of fishery from the perspective of that great ocean-going fishing port of Churchill tell us that it is not a new problem. No, it is not a new problem, and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans says it is not a new problem. But it is a problem that has taken a new twist in the last few years.
When we talk about overfishing I invite members to look at the figures. The overfishing began in 1985 and 1986, after this government took office and after it sent out a very different signal to the foreigners than was being sent out by previous governments. The basic signal being sent out by this government is, "Rape my fish, but love me. As long as you love me, as long as you smile at me, what difference about the livelihoods of fishermen and plant workers?"
My friend from St. John's East, myself and others were in Portugal in November of this year. We had the Director General of Fisheries, Dr. daBreto, look across
the table at us. He said to us in the fall of this year, in November, "If the overfishing problem is as serious as you fellows say it is, why are we only hearing about it now?" Why did it take four years to realize that maybe the minister of fisheries, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Minister for International Trade, should saunter over to Europe and tell the boys and girls over there, we have a problem? Yes, we have a problem, a problem these people created by not sending out a signal that they were going to fight for the fishermen and the plant workers of Atlantic Canada.
Now we have another problem. It is not called the overfishing problem, it is the underfishing problem. The ever-accommodating minister of fisheries took time from his busy schedule to rush into cabinet one day last month to say, "Look, our good friends the French have not caught quite enough fish, I think we owe them a few bucks". He then goes and pays them $456,000 and has the gall in the process to say it is because they have reduced quota. I know he has his usual good academic explanations for this, but it is another example of his not knowing what side he is on or who he is fighting for.
I am glad he spoke because he gave us what must be the best academic discourse we have had in a long time. What was lacking from that minister tonight, as is always lacking, is something in the gut, some feeling for the fishermen and plant workers he is supposed to be fighting for.
If the government is looking for suggestions-and I noticed my good friend from St. John's West is writing very hastily over there-why does he not put down this one as a first step? Step one, get rid of the minister of fisheries. Thke over the job yourself, boy. At least you know what it is all about. You know one end of a fish from the other. At least you will have something in the gut for those people down there. God help us if you do not have any more in the gut than you had for your own people in St. John's last week, though, when you stood by and let the facility down there be shut down.
The minister of fisheries tells us that he believes in the future of the fishery, that it is going to be a stable fishery. He should compare notes with the fellow who spoke before him, the Secretary of State for External Affairs who was talking about diversification. That is a fancy

term for saying we are going to have the fishermen do something else other than fish.
What is it they are going to do in Ramea, an island off the south coast of Newfoundland. Are they going to have a chocolate bar factory there, maybe, for them? How about a car plant on the island where Gaultois is located, on the south coast of Newfoundland? Maybe there could be a bit of agriculture in Habour Breton, if you can find room to get the roots down between the rocks. Maybe we will move the Canadian Mint to Grand Bank. That ought to do the job. And what are you going to move to Fortune, to Burin, to Marystown and to Burgeo? How about St. Lawrence, Rose Blanche, Codroy, and Belleo-ram? You are going to need a lot of diversification.
I have a better idea. Why do you not have these people do what they know how to do well? Why go through the handstands of diversifying, of training, of retraining? These people split fish very well. They catch it very well. And if as the academic the minister of fisheries tell us, it is only a matter of time before the scientists get this thing in hand, and if it is all going to bounce back in four or five years, then does it not make some sense to you, Madam Speaker, that we ought to preserve our facilities, keep the skills in those communities so that when the fish stocks rebound there will be people there to catch the fish, to process the fish, to get a livelihood from the fish, to continue the way of life that they have had for four or five centuries on that particular coast? Why diversify? Why not find something, maybe a share of the paying process? Maybe we cannot have all the plants operate 12 months around. These people have said community by community that they are prepared to have something less than a full loaf during the short term for the next four or five years.
If the government wants a plan of action, I have a plan of action for it. And it is not fancy words like "diversification". It is the suggestion that it draw on the strengths of those people.
What this government needs to do is to go out and take the initiative, with a bit of seed money, and undo that terrible decision of National Sea last week as it affects St. John's, North Sydney and Canso and forestall the decision that we hear FPI is about to let drop on us in some of the communities that I mentioned a few moments ago. Find a bit of seed money.
Do you know why the government cannot do that? Because just as it sold down the river is landing rights on the British Columbia coast and sold down the river its option to do anything for the lobster fishermen in Atlantic Canada, it has also sold down the river to the Americans under the free trade agreement the ability to subsidize a bit, to shore up this industry a bit, at this particular time.
This is what puts the lie to the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that this has nothing to do with free trade. This has everything to do with free trade. The government's response or lack of response, its mealy-mouthedness talking about diversification and so on and so forth is uncoded, an admission that because of the free trade agreement the government is now leaving 16,000, or most of them, fishermen and plant workers in my riding, plus tens of thousands of other fishermen and plant workers throughout Atlantic Canada, dangling. Why? Because our friend the Prime Minister had to choose between Ronald Reagan and George Bush and some fishermen. And guess who he chose, one more time?
It is not fair. It is not good enough. I see the gentleman from St. John's West is getting in gear. When he gets up, after he gets through with the bafflegab and waving his arms, I want him to respond to my suggestion. If the stocks are going to rebound, as his colleagues have been telling us all night, will he in the interim put to cabinet the idea that the limit of stocks ought to be shared among the several plants to help them continue do do what they do well until the stocks do rebound? Will he do that for us.

-from Peter's River, Fermeuse, St. John's from elsewhere in Newfoundland because we do have a serious problem, and not for the first time in the Atlantic fishery.
December 18, 1989

The last time we had a severe problem it was caused by human mistakes. The crisis of 1981 to 1983 was caused by record high interest rates, by double digit inflation, all during the time of the previous Liberal government. That is what induced our last fisheries crisis in eastern Canada. That compares to the fisheries crisis that we have today, which is not caused by anything this government has done or not done. It is caused by a lack of fish, as reported to us with a changed estimate by our scientists earlier this year.
The brilliant analysis is this. Our problem is caused by the fact that we no longer have fish in the water in sufficient quantities to feed the plants that are in trouble now or may be in trouble in the next several months. The fish are no longer there. Why are they no longer there? I do not know why they are no longer there, but I know this. Last year, 1988, the fishery scientists of the Government of Canada said that the total allowable catch for northern cod could properly be 295,000 tonnes. I know that we set the total allowable catch in 1988 at 265,000 tonnes to make sure that we were not taking too much fish.
I know this too, Mr. Speaker. In January and February of this year the same scientists came along and told the Government of Canada that the northern cod fish stock was not as they had thought it was, but that this year, 1989, we could take only 125,000 tonnes fish as our total allowable catch, a reduction from 295,0000 tonnes to
125.000	tonnes, which is a reduction of 170,000 tonnes in just a few months in the estimates by our scientists of what we could take. That is what has caused this present situation.
We set the total allowable catch at 235,000 tonnes this year. Why? Because we were not going to wipe out the whole eastern Canadian fishery on the whims of scientists who one year say that it is safe to take 295,000 tonnes and the next year tell you that you can only take
125.000	tonnes. Whole communities, whole economies cannot be held up to ransom at the whim of scientists. No.
We saw that the total allowable catch for this year was set at 235,000 tonnes. That is a reduction of 31,000 tonnes from the actual amount set last year of 266,000. We appointed Dr. Harris and the eminent people serving with him to review what had gone wrong in the scientific assessment and to tell us what the safe total allowable catch might be for next year and the years to come and
what needs to be done so that this does not happen again.
We are advised in an interim report that the safe TAC for next year of northern cod might be 190,000 tonnes. If it is, that means that the catch has to decline again next year by a further 45,000 tonnes. That is why Canso is having the difficulty that it is having. It is being told by National Sea that the Canso plant must shut. That is why the St. John's plant has been told by National Sea that it must shut. That is why other plants in my province are in danger of having their own fish plants shut as well. It is not by some human error of this government, not by interest rate policies, not by the economic conditions that a government allowed to be created, but by this totally unexpected calamity visited upon us that is no fault of ours but which we are trying to deal with.
I never heard tonight one suggestion as to what other approach we could take, other than the approach we are taking.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: You did. You were not listening.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: I have serious matters I want to discuss with the people in my district and the members opposite are not interested. The people of my province are interested.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: You're the minister for all of Newfoundland, not just for your own district.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
I do not want to have to contend with the braying of the untutored and the uncaring.
I quote now from the Kirby task force report. Mr. Kirby was appointed by the last Liberal government to look at the crisis it created with interest rates and double digit inflation. What did he recommend? He recommended enterprise allocations. Fifty-one of these 57 recommendations were approved. One of them was enterprise allocations or company quotas to the large offshore companies.
He said in his report that the northern cod quota was projected to reach 380,000 tonnes by 1987. What was it in actual fact in 1987? It was considerably less than that. In 1987 the actual total allowable catch was 256,000 tonnes, not 380,000 tonnes. Even the great Kirby was far out in his projections.
Then there was an Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act. What was the purpose given in the legislation? To facilitate the development of viable Atlantic fisheries that are competitive and privately owned through the restructuring of fishery enterprises. That was what the last government did. The last government put over $300

million into these companies-Fishery Products and National Sea they eventually became. It put $300 million into companies.
It was the one who introduced the big company solution of 1983, which members opposite now decry and would they blame us if we give these companies any understanding at all or try to see that they remain viable economic units. There is nothing but scorn from the other side. These are the companies created by the big company solution, the Liberal solution of 1983. It was their restructuring which did nothing for the smaller companies and the inshore sector.
This time that is not the route we are going. We are going the route of helping the communities. We are going the route of helping the people and helping the fishermen of Atlantic Canada.
We are looking at two things-a long-term solution which was never attempted by the last government. That involves the restructuring in Newfoundland and Labrador of our fishery. Just listen to these figures and give some thought to what they reveal.
Fishing contributes 6 per cent only to the Newfoundland Gross Domestic Product but 25 per cent to total employment. Is it any wonder that our people who are in the fishery and in fish processing have only low incomes to look to?
The average Saskatchewan farm family in 1986 had an income of $32,000-34 per cent from farming, 40 per cent from other employment earnings, nothing from UI and 26 per cent from other sources.
The average Atlantic farm family had an income of $33,750.
The average Nova Scotia fishing family had an income of $35,000-53 per cent from fishing, 25 per cent from employment earnings, 16 per cent from UI and 6 per cent from other sources.
In Newfoundland, the place that I am most concerned about, the average fishing family income in 1986 was $19,850 of which only 24 per cent came from fishing, 30 per cent from other employment earnings, 41 per cent from UI and 5 per cent from other sources.
Is this the state that we want to leave our people in who are engaged in the fishery in Newfoundland now or do we want to build a viable fishery? I opt for building a viable fishery, and that is what we are dam well going to do.
Just consider this. In 1975 we had 10,283 plant workers in the fishing plants in Newfoundland. In 1988 we had 28,446 just about triple.
In 1975 we had 15,812 part-time and full-time fishermen. In 1988 we had 29,826 full-time and part-time fishermen.
Is it any wonder that the people involved in the fishery have low average incomes with a large percentage of their income coming from UI. What can we do to change this?
There are two approaches to this problem that we are taking. One is to deal with the immediate results of plants that might have to close because there is no fish there to put through the plants.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: Why is there not fish?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Why? I do not know. I can only tell you what the scientists tell us.
What is the approach? In a community where a plant has to close or is severely affected, all regular programs of course apply-UI, the industrial adjustment service, Community Futures, all of the help that can be given for training or retraining or helping somebody secure other employment. This is an industry where the workers have no rights to pensions. They do not even have a right to separation allowance in Newfoundland. We have the program for older workers which we have introduced and which the Newfoundland government is going to participate in. Those 55 and over who cannot get other employment will receive assistance up to $1,100 a month, 70 per cent if their UI benefit until they become pensionable.
Apart from that program which applies to those 55 and over, we are going further. We are introducing a supplementary plan in this extraordinary situation in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. In this extraordinary situation we are introducing the same kind of benefits to those 50 and over who cannot secure other work or who cannot be retrained for other jobs. We are looking after

the people, not the big companies that were looked after by the Liberals in the early 1980s.
In addition, for the immediate crisis we are establishing a community diversification fund to help the local communities see what other job opportunities can be created, what other industries can be introduced and what other work can be made available. That is an additional program. That is for the immediate problem that affects the communities that are now affected by the plant closings. That is our approach, not the corporate approach, not the pouring of $300 million into two companies as was done by our predecessors.
For the longer term program, we are working in Newfoundland with the government of Newfoundland to see how we can build a viable fishery, to see how we can create diversification in the economy and other job opportunities, because this industry cannot support the number of people now involved in it as the figures show. It cannot support them with a decent income, so other measures had to be taken to try to give those people another income. That is what we are doing. We are not sitting in this House hurling abuse every day at someone else with no constructive alternatives.
What do some people in responsible positions think of that? If we look at what Premier Wells has been saying in Newfoundland, we are not getting a parade of abuse from him. I am reading from a transcript of a December 11 press conference where he states:
The federal government has clearly acknowledged its responsibility and is prepared to take it, and I express appreciation to the federal government for that.
That is a Liberal who is in a responsible position expressing appreciation. He said this at page 10:
1 think we're seeing the beginning of a significant change in the Newfoundland fishery, and we must stop burdening the fishing industry with the responsibility to be the employment opportunity of last resort. We must find the means, and this is what we've been saying for two years in the Liberal Party. We must find the means of providing alternative economic opportunities, and the federal government has a responsibility, along with the provincial government because they can benefit, in fact, even more than the provincial government can by doing so. But we must stop burdening the fishing industry with the responsibility of being the employment opportunity of last resort for our people, and provide other alternatives.
That is from Premier Wells, the Liberal Premier of Newfoundland who approves absolutely of what we are doing. He is not sitting there cackling and abusing the government. He is saying the government is doing the right thing and the Newfoundland government is going to participate with us in doing the right thing, building a viable future for the Newfoundland people in the fishery.
Here is a statement made on the same day by Premier Wells which states at page 4:
We have worked closely with the government of Canada on this problem. Despite some early differences of view on the magnitude of the problem, our discussions have focused largely on appropriate response measures, and I am pleased to state that these discussions have proceeded in a positive atmosphere of common concern and common purpose.
Where is the concern on the other side of the House. Did I hear any concern expressed tonight? Not likely.
On page 5 of the same statement it states:
I wish to commend the federal and provincial task forces for the diligent manner in which they have conducted their work -I also commend the federal government for recognizing its ultimate responsibility for its resource management decisions.
On page 6 it states:
Considerable work and discussion have taken place on this proposed program which could be cost-shared by the federal and provincial governments.
Further down it states:
This would be a long term process and the province is prepared to provide a substantial sum each year for this program over the next 10 years.
That is what is going on. There is no lack of action. You will hear what the program is, Mr. Speaker, when we have finished and completed the details of it with the Government of Newfoundland.
What else are we doing? We are pouring more money into northern cod research with an additional $3 million being spent this year, additional electronic equipment obtained to improve the efficiency of the research, the computer upgraded at St. John's to handle the increased amount of the data, the Gadus Atlantica will be modified during the winter to utilize research acoustic equipment in ice-infested waters and the amount of acoustic surveying in 1990 to be increased significantly, including a doubling of surveys inshore. Additional tagging will be carried out. Other activities being funded include neces-

December 18, 1989
sary electronic equipment to go aboard fishing vessels to collect oceanographic data.
Those are some of the other things that are being done. Much is being done. Much is being done by our Minister of Fisheries whom hon. gentlemen opposite tiy to criticize and denigrate and knock down, but who is doing a great job on behalf of the fishermen and the people of Atlantic Canada.
In 1988 we had a TAC of 266,000 tonnes. I have in my hands a list of Fishery Products' various plants and how much capacity was utilized in the plants. Even when the TAC was 266,000 tonnes they could only utilize the capacity at Marystown 53 per cent; Trepassey, 60 per cent; Harbour Breton, 49 per cent; Ramea, 88 per cent; Gaultois, 43 per cent; Bonavista, an inshore plant, 29 per cent. There is the problem. Even in a year when the TAC was 266,000 tonnes, not 190,000 tonnes, this was the capacity utilization of their plants.
It is suggested that somehow they can keep all plants open and just open them for several months or a few months a year. That way they will go to their economic doom. If they cannot be economically viable entities, who is going to lend them money? Who is going to give them credit? Who is going to invest money with them? No one. Unless they can be economically viable, they are finished. If they are finished, who is going to operate these plants? Not the government. I hope to God it is not the government. That is the kind of problem that we have.
Let us look at the inshore and the offshore catches. In 1982, 113,000 tonnes were caught inshore, 117,000 tonnes caught offshore; 1983, 106,000 inshore, 126,000 offshore; 1984, 97,000 inshore, 135,000 offshore. I will skip up to 1988, 102,000 tonnes inshore, 156,000 tonnes offshore. Now we are faced with a situation where next year the TAC may be 190,000 tonnes. That is the problem. It was not caused by this government. It was not even caused by the last government because they knew nothing about the fact that the cod out in the water was not as the scientists were saying it was, that the mass had not quintupled, that it had only tripled, which we were told last February. It is not even their fault.
To set the record straight with reference to the free trade agreement, the free trade agreement does not prevent us from subsidizing plants. If we want to subsidize plants, it may or may not result in a countervail case in the United States. There was a case in the United States against the fishing industry in 1985. It has nothing to do with the free trade agreement. The free trade agreement does not give them the right to take a countervail action or not take a countervail action. They have that right under their own domestic legislation. They have that right under their own domestic legislation. They had it in 1985, 1986, 1987, 1988, well before 1989 which was the year of the free trade agreement. The Leader of the Opposition knows that but gets up tonight and says something different. Instead of going out taking the larger view, he is going out with this kind of-well, I will not even characterize it. I do not want to waste time.
The free trade agreement has nothing to do with this situation. If we want to subsidize plants, if that was the way to go, if that was the answer to the problem, we could do it and take our chances on countervail. There was countervail in 1985. There is a countervail duty now of 5.82 per cent on fresh. Atlantic groundfish. It is not the free trade agreement.
These are the people I represent, all these people in Newfoundland. I am the cabinet minister in this government who represents them and I have not had a worse six months in representing them since I have been here. I want to tell them tonight that I am making every effort that I can to see that this problem, this crisis, is resolved in the way that is best for them and in the way that is best for their children. If I don't succeed, they can let me know that they think I have failed them and I am quite willing to resign, or they can deal with me at the next election. I can tell you as long as I am here, every possible effort is going to be made to resolve this crisis. The people of Newfoundland, and the fishermen and the fish plant workers will be looked after to the best of my ability, or the best of the ability of any government that can do that.
I am confident that before this is over we are going to have a better fishery in Newfoundland, a more viable fishery, a fishery that contains fishermen and fisherwom-en who are better paid and better recompensed and fish plant workers who are better looked after, who are going to have pension rights, and separation allowance rights. That is what we are going to have in the next 10 years if

December 18, 1989

we are successful in the longer terra approach that has never been taken before.
I want to repeat here tonight something the Prime Minister said on December 13. The leader of this government said this: "We have taken some substantial actions and we propose to take more. Let me summarize for my friend. When the farmers of western Canada were hurting, this government took action, When Atlantic fishermen are hurting, we will take action as well."
That is the pledge of the Prime Minister. That is the pledge that I expect the Prime Minister and the government to fulfil. That is the pledge we are going to fulfil. There are going to be a lot of tough times. It will not be helped by hon. gentlemen opposite with their cheap shots, but by God, with the help of my colleagues in this government, with the assistance of the Newfoundland government, with the support of the Newfoundland people, we are going to overcome this problem, and when we leave we will leave behind a better, viable fishery, better for the people in it, better for the people who participate, better for their families. That is our pledge. We are going to go through some rough times, but they are going to find me by their side. They are going to find the government by their side and together we are going to lick this problem, not caused by us, but caused by events that were outside our control.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to begin by thanking you for allowing this debate to take place this evening. I would like to compliment the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso for bringing this very important matter to the attention of the House and for providing us with an opportunity to discuss these very serious matters.
It is my view that Atlantic Canada has generally fared very well under this government, and indeed the statistical data that we have seen from time to time brought before this House has made that abundantly clear. However, I have to say in all honesty that coastal Atlantic Canada today faces the greatest challenge it has faced sice the post-war depression of the 1920s. Fifty per cent of the economy of coastal Atlantic Canada, in particular Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, is directly dependent upon the fishery and that fishery is in a very difficult situation, especially I might say the groundfi-sheiy which has always been thought of as the backbone of the Atlantic fishery.
It is important to note that there are other sectors of the fishing industry that are doing extremely well. The shrimp fishery is healthy. The tuna fishery, the scallop industry, the sword fishery, the mussels and other mollusc industries are all doing extremely well right now. Indeed, our lobster fishery is healthy although we do have a problem to face with this pernicious piece of legislation that has recently been passed in the United States and which I am sure will be a temporary thing in view of the fact that it will be thrown out because we have access to a free trade panel as a result of the free trade agreement signed a year ago.
Our coastal communities grew up around the ground-fishery. The groundfishery and the plants as well as the fishermen are the key to the social and economic life of the communities along the coast of Atlantic Canada and in particular in Nova Scotia. When you close a plant you close a town. It is not like the prairies where the farmers have an idea of what their harvest is going to be. They are able to know pretty precisely what is going to happen. From time to time, they have to put up with the difficulties of grasshoppers, drought or whatever, but

December 18, 1989
they can see it coming and know it is going to be different the following year.
Fishing communities are in a very different situation because you do not know what the harvest is going to be in any particular year. You can set tax and quotas and so on, but when you go to sea, you go as a hunter and you are never quite sure what you are going to find or what you are going to bring back. As the people of Sandy Cove, Shelboume County, found out last week, and as everybody who lives in a coastal community knows, you are never quite sure even if the men themselves are going to come back. It is a hazardous and difficult life.
When the fishery is in difficulty, it has a domino effect throughout the community because within a fishing community you have not only the fishermen but you have the plant workers. Indeed, if the fishing industry is not healthy, not only do the plants have a problem but the boatbuilders and the people who support the industry, not to mention all the other people in town, the merchants, the grocers, the restaurateurs, everybody suffers if times are tough in the fishery.
When we look at what is taking place in Atlantic Canada right now, we see that it has a profound impact on communities that are frequently very isolated. I am not so sure, quite frankly, that people in the west or in central Canada fully understand the depths of this issue. We are told sometimes that we should consider it just a problem and not, as some of us have said, a crisis in Atlantic Canada. They say: "Let's not escalate this to be a greater problem than it really is."
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that it is a problem and anybody who does not recognize the profoundness of this problem for coastal Atlantic Canada should have been with me in Lockeport on Saturday last when they opened a community support group in that town and asked the question: "Why is it necessary?" "Why do we not have the government solving our problem?" As we heard from the last speaker, it is not as simple as the government being able to create fish. Anybody who suggests that this is not a serious crisis should go to Port Medway. They should go to Port L'Hebert, Woods Harbour, Bear Point or Shag Harbour. These are only communities within my own South Shore riding that have suffered plant closures in the last year.
I see the mayor and a councillor from the town of Canso here tonight. They can tell you about the crisis that exists in the life of their community with the closure of a plant. It is a serious problem, one that we all have to recognize in a national context even though it applies to us in our small coastal communities.
The concept of crisis is a veiy simple concept. Crisis is something that happens to your town, to your community, to your family or to yourself. If you happen to be in a remote community that for 400 years has relied on the fishing industry there does not sometimes appear to be alternatives. Let there be no doubt in coastal Atlantic Canada there is a crisis today and a crisis to which the government must respond.
I would suggest that there are three means by which the government can respond. The first, of course, has to do with dealing with the resource itself. That is the responsibility of the minister and the Department of Fisheries. Their responsibility is to see that this problem is indeed temporary and that those stocks will regenerate themselves. At the same time, part of that process is allow the industry to rationalize itself in such a way that we have those numbers participating in it that the resource itself can sustain.
I must say that measures have been and are being put in place as a result of the capacity committee struck by the minister a couple of years ago, the outcomes that will occur from the various consultations in the Stein task force and the special cabinet committee and indeed the Hache report. It is tough to say no because everybody wants to go fishing. Everybody wants a licence. Everybody wants a quota. If the resource cannot sustain it, it is the responsibility of the minister to be the guy who has the tough job of saying no to people. Thank goodness that we have a minister today who has the responsibility and the integrity to put in place measures that within three or four years will see the regeneration of our groundfish stocks so that once again we will have a healthy groundfishery in Atlantic Canada.
The second responsibility of government, of course, falls within the domain of Employment and Immigration Canada and the special cabinet committee and that is to provide the support that is necessary to families and communities during this transitional three or four year period until such time as we can both have economic
December 18, 1989

diversification as well as the regeneration of a strong fishery in Atlantic Canada.
I look forward to the measures being brought forth. We have had announcements that there will be special measures brought forward. The hon. Minister for International Trade made some reference to it in his remarks tonight, but what I am looking forward to is support for families as well as communities, at least until we have the restoration. We have programs in place such as community futures and we were very pleased to see that program beginning to be put in place in the county of Shelboume. I look forward to it being put in place in Queen's County as well where the Port Mouton plant was closed.
We have excellent work being done by the industrial adjustment service committees in Lockeport and Port Mouton, and of course the changes that are being introduced to the Unemployment Insurance Act will make available more funds to improve the quality of the labour force development strategy programs, programs that are going to enable Canadians and communities to get back to work again.
Would hon. members opposite be kind enough to suggest to their colleagues in the Senate that they let the will of democracy be done and the government's will be done as it should be and stop the interference of that which on January 6 could cause grievous damage to people in Atlantic Canada.
We look forward to more support coming with the announced package. Particularly, I look forward to and urge the government to provide support to the municipal units involved. The town of Lockeport depends 55 per cent on its municipal tax base for the National Sea plant that has now been closed. With a reduction in the value of that plant, the revenues available to that town will make it difficult for the town to function as a municipal unit. There is a growing need to have assistance provided there to make these things work effectively for the town.
These support measures are an interim thing that are very important. We look forward to the government's announcement being made and I urge it to make sure that it is fully comprehensive and includes not only those communities affected by the northern cod difficulties, but the problems with respect to the Scotia-Fundy region as well.
I will be particularly looking to see support for Queen's County and Port Mouton and indeed for the town of Lockeport in particular.
The third arm or the third challenge to the government is in the area of economic diversification and development. Here I look to Industry, Science and Technology and ACOA, as well as the co-operation and participation of the provinces. Clearly the number one challenge we face in Atlantic Canada, and our greatest need, is to reduce our dependency on the fishery as a resource for economic development. We have to look to other potential industries. Tourism is an industry with tremendous potential in Nova Scotia, and indeed in the Maritimes. We have to see this as a potential primary employer and not simply as a secondary industry.
We need more Michelin plants. The government has said that Canada is open for business and we are attracting interest from potential investors all over the world, but we have to see the deals closed. We had an announcement that the Tissan Corporation was going to settle. What a marvellous thing that will be for eastern Nova Scotia when that first plant comes. We look at that company eventually having the impact that Michelin has in Nova Scotia, with its three plants providing 4,300 excellent jobs for people. But the deal is not done. Why is that deal not done? There is an industry anxiously interested in settling in the town of Bridgewater, but the deal and the contract is not signed. When can we expect that?
There is potential for development for Aspotogan. There is another for the north shore of Nova Scotia. I urge the government, and particularly the ministers involved in economic development to get on with getting these deals signed so that we can see the diversification beyond the fishery.
We also have to diversify within the fishing industry itself. The minister spoke about 350,000 tonnes of fish not being utilized by Canadians. We have to utilize those fish and we need to have an economic development diversification fund that will encourage the use of these resources.
Unfortunately my time is up. There are a number of things we have to do and in the last minute I will just mention some of the things we have to do in the fishery. All parties involved in the fishery must not see it as a partisan issue but work co-operatively together with it. We must get rid of the misconception and stick to the facts. Let us solve the problems that exist rather than those that do not. Our fishermen must be prepared to obey the law. We must use science but not be the

December 18, 1989
captives of science. We must preserve people and community as well as stocks. We need to work together and have effective working relationships with the United States as well as to see that they obey the laws that we have set and we must be prepared to enforce them.
My time is up, Mr. Speaker. I thank you for your indulgence. I have to say this: it is a tough time and it is going to be a tough time for a few years for us in southern Nova Scotia, but we have had other tough times and we are going to overcome this one. As the member for South Shore, I am going to continue to work with the government and with members opposite if they wish to work with me to see that better days are ahead.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House and speak to the opposition motion requesting an emergency debate on the present situation in the Atlantic fishery, following the closing of processing plants on the east coast and U.S. legislation restricting imports of Canadian lobster in the United States.
No government can remain indifferent to the difficult economic situation now prevailing in the fisheries industry in the Atlantic region and the Gulf of the St. Lawrence. Today, workers at National Sea Products in Canso and St. John's have been laid off. A few weeks ago, Madam Speaker, the entire Gaspe area was facing the same problem.
The Atlantic fishery is going through a difficult period, due to reduced quotas, overcapacity of fishing boats, a fiercely competitive market and the high value of the Canadian dollar. These are some of the factors that have made fishermen and their communities feel powerless, bitter and desperate.
Madam Speaker, I may remind hon. members that what we are seeing and experiencing today is a very complex phenomenon that would take some time to explain.
We are all aware of some of the factors that have led both National Sea Products and independents in Quebec to close some of their processing plants.
The crisis now facing fishermen and their communities is due to the natural environment, the present state of
our scientific knowledge, to administrative decisions and, of course, to market forces. The interaction of natural and human factors is constantly changing and thus unpredictable, hence the onus on the government to act with prudence and discretion.
Before considering the concrete measures that have been taken to deal with this crisis, Madam Speaker, I would like to recall a number of facts and figures to illustrate this complex situation.
About 65,000 registered commercial fishermen, nearly
30.000	fishing boats, 890 fish processing plants and about
309.000	plant workers, spread over 1,300 communities in five provinces in Eastern Canada, are involved in the Atlantic fisheries.
About 95 per cent of all fishermen are in the coastal fishery, which consists of relatively small fishing boats, not more than 65 feet long, which are owner-operated. These fishermen take about 60 per cent of all catches on the Atlantic coast.
Annual catches in this sector total 1.2 million tons, with a production value of $2.1 billion. Over 80 per cent of these catches are exported.
Groundfish, especially cod, is a very important part of the Atlantic fishery. Groundfish accounts for two-thirds of all fish landings and for over 40 per cent of the total value of those landings.
Catches of northern cod make up 50 per cent of cod catches on the Atlantic coast.
Madam Speaker, I would like to dwell on an increasingly serious problem in the Atlantic region which plays a decisive role in the present crisis, and I am referring to overcapacity of fishing vessels.
Nowadays, fishermen are more efficient than ever before. A recent study conducted in the Scotia-Fundy area reported that the groundfish fleet already had twice the capacity it needed.
Today's vessels are faster. They have electronic equipment capable of locating the fish and they have far more sophisticated fishing gear. Therefore, catches are larger and fishermen can now catch in one to three months the same number of fish they used to take a whole fishing season to catch.
December 18, 1989

In the past, an ordinary trawler could catch 33 tonnes of fish. Today, it can take 164 tonnes in the same fishing season. The cost of the trawler has gone from $200,000 to $750,000, which is a much bigger investment for fishermen.
As you see, Madam Speaker, any improvised solution to the problem of overcapacity could have disastrous consequences not only for the fisheries themselves but also for many fishermen and their families.
Our government reacted. If you look at our government's four initiatives, (1) the Special Committee of Ministers, (2) the Harris Committee, (3) the Scotia-Fundy Task Force and (4) our reaction to overfishing and plundering of fish stocks, you will have to admit that they show the government's determination and are a positive step to help ensure prosperity for the fisheries in the 1990s.
However, I would have liked our government to be more attentive to our fishermen's requests and to control the seal population which is so destructive of living resources.
If additional resources are required to help people, to diversify the industry, to develop new technologies and to discover new markets, our government is ready to consider these options. We will ensure that federal government agencies and departments are prepared to support the people of the Atlantic region as well as possible during this period. Furthermore, we intend to propose amendments to the Fisheries Act in the near future, partly as a result of suggestions from many representatives of fishermen and the industry who are demanding heavier penalties for fisheries infractions.
These amendments will stress stronger deterrents, more efficient enforcement and an updated and improved fisheries management system.
Madam Speaker, if we want our fishermen and plant workers to continue to earn their living from marine resources, we must stop dramatising. We must instead deal attentively with the problems, as we are now doing, find long-term solutions and apply management principles which will ensure the future of our fishing communities and provide them with a relatively stable income.
Only when we have finished analysing the present problems can we give lasting answers.
There are no miracle solutions, Madam Speaker, but if everyone in the fishing industry works together with management, I am sure that we will find innovative management methods to conserve and protect our precious resources for future generations.

It could not withstand the Mulroney government. They are trying to tell us that after 400 years the fish lost their way and did not come into Canso.
