The Leader of the Opposition said that this is a crisis. Make no mistake about that, it is a crisis. I say to people in other parts of Canada who may not think this is a crisis that they had better wake up. Not only is this happening in Atlantic Canada. With this government in power it could happen anywhere in Canada because people do not matter. They do not matter.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is telling us that we brought forward a plan in 1983, that we are responsible for that plan and that we are responsible for the fishery. What unmitigated poppycock. Michael Kirby did not take those shares with him when the Liberal government was defeated and the Mulroney government came into power. December 18, 1989
at the board of directors meeting. It has chosen not to act upon its shares.

going to be reduced from 295,000 tonnes to 125,000 tonnes. That is 170,000 tonnes in a few months.

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to participate in this debate this evening. The crisis in the Atlantic fishery, particularly in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, strikes close to home.
Although the crisis has not struck my riding in the same magnitude as it has in St. John's and Canso, we in Cardigan certainly know the frustration, the hardship and the fears caused by this government's callous and incompetent approach to the industry which is a region's economic life line. In Atlantic Canada we are still reeling from the blows struck by the multinational corporation, National Sea Products, in the closure of its plants in Canso and St. John's.
My constituents and I feel for our Atlantic neighbours. Our thoughts and our prayers are with them as they face the bleakest Christmas they have ever known. I have some trouble reconciling this government's intentions and actions. On December 11, 1989 the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans stood in this House and said:
We are very much in tune with the needs, sentiments and anxieties
of the people living in these communities.
How do we reconcile these words with this government's inaction, its failure to avert this crisis? The people in St. John's and Canso have no where to turn.
Yes, a special cabinet committee is looking into the problems in the Atlantic fisheries. We have the Hache task report and the Harris panel, but what concrete measures has this government taken to save the industry, the mainstay of the Atlantic economy?
We are not talking solely of money, although that is certainly what the government cares about. We are talking about our history and our heritage, a way of life that is precious to us and Atlantic Canadians. This government seems to think it can solve this problem merely by handling out money in the short term while saying it has something up its sleeve in the long term. Who knows?
Maybe it will provide the unemployed fish plant workers with transportation to Toronto or some other thriving metropolis. It will not work. The Atlantic fishery must be saved. Fish plant jobs must be saved. The government must explore other avenues and alternatives. We need a solution that will allow Atlantic Canadians to stay in their homes with their roots and their families, where their children would grow up and continue their culture and heritage.
The problems in the fishery in eastern P.E.I. and Cardigan start at the very foundation. The basic infrastructure of the industry is literally rotting away. Our harbours and wharfs are in desperate need of repair. Maintenance and in many cases reconstruction are necessary.
My fishermen might as well be knocking their heads against a brick wall as asking this government to fix their wharfs and keep them in workable condition. How can lobster fishermen make a decent living when they have no room to moor their boats or set their traps because big sections of the wharfs are unusable? For that matter they may not even be able to get their boats to the wharfs because the harbour is not properly dredged. They run the risk of getting caught on the sand bar and damaging their vessel.
The lobster fishery in P.E.I. is equivalent to the groundfish industry in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland in economic terms. Our lobster industry in 1989 was not as healthy as it has been in the past. Inventories were high, demand was down and prices were soft. These problems were felt in Cardigan in a concrete way. A fish plant in my riding closed its doors, leaving 150 workers unemployed and over 100 fishermen with no place to sell their lobsters, groundfish, herring and scallops.
More bad news came to the P.E.I. lobster fishermen with the passing of the U.S. legislation banning the import of Canadian whole live lobsters that do not meed the American minimum size of three and three-quarter inches.
This measure is based purely on protectionism. It will certainly distort our markets. It will close the doors on fishermen who would like to ship whole lobsters of the intermediary size to those states outside New England. It is estimated that the loss of these potential markets will cost Prince Edward Island lobster fishermen approximately $2 million. That is a large figure in a small economy. So much for open access to the American markets promised under the free trade agreement.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to speak in this debate tonight. I think, like all members of this House, I would rather that this debate did not have to take place.
I, like other members in this House, sympathize greatly with the people of Atlantic Canada, and particularly the people of my province and my city who have felt the despair and hopelessness of this last eight or nine days.
The announced closing of fish plants in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland just before Christmas poses more than economic problems for workers and their families. For many, drawing a living from the sea goes back to ancestors who first settled our coastline many hundreds of years ago. Fishing is literally the soul lifeblood of many communities. I realize that asking whole towns to give up this livelihood is like asking someone to relinquish a precious family heirloom. It is an heartbreaking and emotional issue.
I want to assure the House that this government has already stepped into those communities most affected by the closing. The programs those people need to survive are already in place, but more than that, the assistance this government provides today is not going to last until plants reopen or entire towns disappear. The support that we offer today and tomorrow is propelled by a vision to stabilize the economy of Atlantic Canada and sustain the fishing resource.
It is a fact that the environmental realities of the ocean stocks are dictating the need for management. Scientific studies tell us that the oceans are not as fruitful as even a few years ago. Those who make their living from the fishery have no choice but to withdraw for a while so that the resources can renew themselves.
What does this intentional slowdown signify for those who work in the fishing industry? It means that fishing may be a more viable industry in the future. It also means that communities have to find an alternative means to survive and perhaps eventually to thrive. They need new industry and new skills so their economies can be diversified. We will assist them in those efforts.
National Sea Products announced the lay-off of 1,562 last Monday. Within hours Employment and Immigration personnel moved in with the Industrial Adjustment Services Program. They are setting up a committee of employers and employees to respond to the shutdown by helping workers find new jobs, training and counselling.
Also within a short time of the announced closings, unemployment insurance officials set up shop in plants to help the employees start their claims as quickly as possible. The aid programs that we have provided have had an immediate impact on the lives of workers and their families, but that is not all we are doing.
New skills and businesses can breathe life into communities that previously depended on fishing. Since 1985 Canadian Jobs Strategy programs have been operating in Atlantic communities to retrain people and encourage entrepreneurship. Building on the individual needs of a community and its citizens, innovative programs have been created to revive former fishing communities. In the long haul the initiatives under the CJS aim to equip
December 18, 1989

people and towns to be competitive and prosperous for a long time.
I need not tell members of this House of the success of the Community Futures Program particularly in a community like Port aux Basques in the constituency of the hon. member for Burin-St. George's. Through a number of initiatives from the people and the employers in the area companies were recruited to open plants, including one Norwegian fabricating company that created more than 200 jobs.
As well, more than $1 million in Community Futures funding has been used to train 120 residents as high-tech welders, pipefitters and sheet metal workers. Some 70 are now working full time, another 30 are working part time and the rest are still in school. Further assistance was provided to 24 residents to start their own businesses through the self-employment initiative.
This is just one example of how innovative and flexible programming can serve the needs of communities that must adapt and that must change.
In the last fiscal year the government directly invested $17.4 million in Canadian Jobs Strategy projects in the fishery sector. Of course when the fisheries workers are without work so too are service workers, be they pharmacists or shop keepers, who depend on their business. The strategy helps those too.
Altogether in the last two years $434 million in Employment and Immigration Commission funding has helped 145,000 people in Atlantic Canada attain worthwhile skills that allow them to contribute to their communities. In addition, for several years now the government has responded with additional emergency job development money for fishing industry workers in the region and in Quebec. In 1989 we provided more than $5 million. About 4,000 workers are training and working on employment projects which will allow them to qualify for unemployment insurance while learning new skills.
Let me remind the House also of the recently announced community development fund which will allow for community directed investments to strengthen the local economy and create meaningful job opportunities. Fishing communities can use it to supplement existing adjustment programs. Moneys can be directed at attracting small businesses and establishing a base, for example, for a viable aquaculture.
Furthermore, as the Minister for International Trade announced last week and has said tonight, we are working with the province of Newfoundland and Labrador to develop a program that will take care of the older workers affected by changes in the fishing industry.
Adjustment strategies for fisheries workers have not been developed in a vacuum. The fact is our attempts to create jobs and businesses for the long term have the approval of the provincial governments. Newfoundland and Labrador's Fisheries Minister Walter Carter said recently: "The fishing industry can no longer be the centrepiece of the province's economy. It can and must be an important employer however and, with the help of the federal government, new industry and training can help stabilize the economy".
Bill C-21, having passed through this place, sits in the other place today. The changes brought in by that legislation will free up $800 million which will be used to train UI claimants and encourage the start-up of new business ventures under the Labour Force Development Strategy. Under that strategy funding for industrial adjustment services would be doubled and Community Futures will be boosted by an additional $50 million. Both programs help towns and workers who once depended on fishing for a living.
The government is sensitive to the historical and economic importance of the fishery in Atlantic Canada. We want to help workers in communities affected by those changes. The support we are offering goes beyond helping people buy groceries and pay their rent. In the long run, our programs assist people in communities to build a stronger and stable economic foundation for themselves.
The fishery, under proper management, will survive and will provide good jobs for Atlantic Canadians. We recognize its indispensable economic value and the important contribution that it pays to our economy and our way of life, but we know it will not be worth anything if we keep combing the depleted Atlantic waters. Our programs meet the needs of fishing communities undergoing change. While workers are learning skills and new businesses are established, workers, communities and

December 18, 1989
provinces will be creating with this government's help a viable fishery for the future.
We face realities in the fishery. Decisions must be taken that none of us like. These decisions, with the innovation and the determination of the people in Atlantic Canada, with the support of this government, members on this side from Atlantic Canada and hopefully members on that side from Atlantic Canada, will see a viable, professional fishery that can be depended upon in good times and bad and that can support our communities well in the future because have strong fisheries management and we have a government that responds when the need dictates it.

Madam Speaker, I would like to start my comments this evening by saying that to us in the Gaspe and the Magdalen Islands, in Eastern Quebec, the fishery is vital. And in addition to everything that has been said this evening in the House, I would like to say that technological change has necessarily had an impact on the catches of groundfish in the Gulf. The quantities of fish that are available are caught far more quickly and as a result, the fishing season gets shorter and shorter and plants are swamped at certain times of the year.

In taking into account this statement that has been made, I must say that as a member of Parliament involved in a constituency with a very large fishing industry we should look also at what the government has done. However, I think that we should go beyond the politics.
I would hope-and I speak on behalf of small fishermen and big fisherman and fish plants in my riding-that we would leave politics aside. We know there is a crisis in the east coast fishery and that we can work together.
I state, for the record, a couple of statements that had been made after the federal minister met with provincial ministers. I quote Walter Carter, Newfoundland's fisheries minister: "We welcome these changes to the Fisheries Act".
The second quote is from Donald McGuinnis, Nova Scotia's fisheries minister: "Fishermen are ready for new measures".
The Minister of Fisheries and Aquaculture echoed Mr. Siddon's remarks and added: "These issues are important to all Atlantic provinces and I appreciate the opportunity to contribute to the decisions that affect all of us".

Madam Speaker, this was also said, in French, by the New Brunswick Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. The pressing need to change this legislation was also stressed by Mr. Denis Losier, the New Brunswick Minister of Fisheries and Aquaculture, who said these changes should have been made a long time ago.
Finally, Madam Speaker, Mr. Michel Page, Quebec's Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, sent a message to Mr. Siddon in which he said: "I wish to join my provincial colleagues in co-operating with the federal government, in order to obtain the necessary assistance for fishermen in the Gulf and the Atlantic and for their communities".

We listened to those remarks that were made by people across provincial governments and across different party lines. We must realize when we talk about a crisis in our fisheries that we have one. We have created that.
What we have become in terms of our fisheries is hunters. We are not farmers. With the equipment that we have, with our boats, with our sonar, with our radar, with everything we have, we have become hunters. We have an overcapacity of fish plants, an overcapacity of boats. The big get a little bigger and the little get hurt a lot more.
What we have to do is come from all sides of this House when we talk in an emergency debate. We must say to our inshore fishermen as well as to our offshore fishermen that we are not Liberals, we are not NDP. We do not come from Newfoundland. We do not come from the Gaspe. We want to work together. We have to work
December 18, 1989

5.0.	52
together, because we must have a sustainable resource. If we do not have a sustainable resource, then we are going to be in trouble.
We listened to the people heckling across the House this evening. They are not serious, because they are playing petty politics. I do not play petty politics with my fishermen. I say to my people who are listening this evening, my fishermen and my fish plants, the women and the men who work in the fish plants and the small fishermen, that when they have their quotas, we must stabilize our fishing industry, whether it be in the Gaspe or whether it be in the Magdalen Islands, whether it be in groundfish or whether it be in lobster. Whatever we do, we must work together on this and we must put aside our petty politics.
I would put three recommendations to the House this evening. First, with a reduction in jobs for the surveillance of our fish stocks, priority must be given especially to the inshore fishermen that they will work on the surveillance. I would impress upon the minister of fisheries that he take that into consideration.
Second, for new species that are non utilized presently, we ought to look into the harvesting of these stocks and going into secondary and tertiary transformation of those.
Third, which is a very touchy subject that no one has dared to mention this evening is that of seals on the east coast. People on the other side are talking because they might find me a little boring. We have the question of the Malouf commission, the question of the seal harvesting, the breakage in fishermen's nets, the consumption of fish by seals on our eastern coast stocks and then there is the cod worm. What we should do is look at the three recommendations that I have proposed this evening very seriously and what we do as an outcome of our debate tonight-

Madam Speaker, at the end of our debate this evening, I hope the opposition will be able to say: We are going to work together to help our fishermen. These fishermen are not interested in political factions, Madam Speaker, they are interested in their work, and they want the fish to be there. That is what we want, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I sometimes wonder why the party across the hall fought the last election. The Tories fought to win the government. They are the government, they have got the government, that is where the responsibility lies.
I heard the hon. member talking about non-partisanship and this is everybody's responsibility. The buck stops with the government and they can talk all they like about what affects the stocks. I will tell you one thing that affects the stocks. Sure, there is some Canadian overfishing, but there is a lot of foreign overfishing too. This government has failed to stand up to the foreign interests that are raping and pillaging our stocks, particularly off the nose and tail of the Grand Banks.
If the stocks are in crisis, it is because of overfishing, yes, by some Canadian fishermen but also by foreign countries too. Clearly, the responsibility for that lies with the Government of Canada.
The Europeans are thumbing their noses at the Government of Canada. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister for International Trade travel around Europe offering some comforting words but no action is taken. When foreign vessels invade our waters, Canadian ships are sent out and, again, no action is taken and those ships are not brought to port and no fines are levied.
Off my own coast, 27,000 tonnes is what the European community has set for its own quota this year. NAFO, the toothless tiger of which the Government of Canada is a part, said: "You can catch no fish at all off the Labrador coast this year". The EEC says: "We're going to catch 27,000 tonnes whether you like it or not. It may be affecting your fishermen."
Do you know how many jobs a tonne of fish will create? Roughly 30 jobs, so you can imagine how many jobs are being lost potentially by the action of the European community off the coast of Labrador. The Government of Canada allows that to go on. It takes no sanctions whatsoever. It does not stand up to the foreign fleets and the hon. member has the audacity to say that this is a non-partisan problem and there is nothing the government can do about it.
The government can do something about it. The Tories can stand up to the Europeans. They can say this is our fish and it is affecting our employment and we are going to do something about it.

At the same time as those stocks are being depleted, what does the Government of Canada do? The Government of Canada chooses that particular moment to cut back on the surveillance of our fishing zone. We fought for a 200-mile limit. We got a 200-mile limit. We do the economic analysis in it and we protect those stocks.
What does the Government of Canada do as those stocks are in jeopardy? It cuts back on the surveillance. It is known that no plane, the Aurora included, can do the kind of low-level surveillance that the Tracker aircraft out of Summerside, P.E.I., can do. The people in the Armed Forces will tell you that. The fishermen will tell you that. Everybody in the industry will tell you that. Yet, the government has chosen this time to say, "We are closing down Summerside and we are moving those Tracker aircraft out of there."
The Tracker aircraft has another 10 years of life at a minimum investment, relatively speaking. Yet this is the time that the government chooses to cut back on the best means of support we have.
Apart from that, the whole co-ordination of surveillance off the east coast needs drastic revision. There is a hodge-podge of government agencies and vessels and equipment and personnel trying to do a job. It needs much better co-ordination.
The stocks off our coast are being fished by the Europeans and they are being fished by some large Canadian companies too. Who does not have access to those stocks? Many of the smaller fishermen on the Atlantic coast have been denied access to those stocks.
I am glad the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is listening because he will know that both co-ops on the Labrador coast have applied for a supply of offshore fish and have been denied. The Europeans, the French, have been given 8,000 tonnes off the coast of Labrador this year as an enticement to get them out of the Gulf.
The large companies from Canada and other countries are fishing off the Labrador coast, but the two fishermen's co-ops on the Labrador coast wanted to deep-sea fish and applied to the government and were turned down.
If you want to see the difference between Liberal policy and Conservative policy, here is where you have to
look. Let me take the example of shrimp. In the late 1970s, we discovered a shrimp stock off the coast of Labrador and the northeast coast of Newfoundland. The government of the day and the minister of the day took the decision that those people who were closest to the resource got a priority. It was not all theirs. It was to be shared, but the priority was given to those people who lived closest to the resource and depended on it. That is the way the shrimp stocks were divided up and that is the way the licences were allocated.
But in cod, with this government, it is a different thing altogether. The priority is given to the foreign countries. The priority is given to the large companies and the small inshore fishermen, whether they are individual fishermen or whether they band together in co-ops, come last. That has got to be changed.
At the same time as the stocks are in jeopardy and as the surveillance is being cut back, this is the time the government chooses to gut the only support system that we have which is the unemployment insurance system. Let us look at special response first of all.
The member for St. John's East mentioned that program a moment ago. He knows and I know that that money is not going to support those who need it most. I will tell you what the figures are for the Labrador coast. We have 129 people who qualify, we have 128 people who do not qualify. Those fishermen and plant workers in my area, 50 per cent of them who qualify and have a long-term attachment to the fishery, are getting no help whatsoever. They are being forced to fall back on welfare. Well, you cannot fall back on welfare because you cannot qualify for welfare if your are able-bodied.
So what will people do this year? I will tell you what they will do. On the Labrador coast this year, there will be people bartering, there will be people trading goods and materials and food as they have done in the past. That will be happening in Canada in 1989. So much for the special response feature.
At the same time as that is happening, action is being taken now to completely gut the unemployment insurance system and the government is withdrawing completely from that system and turning it over to the private sector instead of making the kind of changes that would make sense.
December 18, 1989

On the coast of Labrador, for example, the cut-off date for unemployment insurance is May 15. Yet the ice is there in the bays until the end of June. That is the kind of sensible change that should have been made and that could have been made now while that act is opened up, to give some fairness and some justice to the people who live on that coast.
The government saw fit to ignore changes like that, sensible changes that would have given some income support to those who need it. Instead the government is withdrawing completely from that system and, indeed, putting hurdles in the way of people who want to depend on that for a support system.
What about channelling the money into training? What do you train a 40-year old fisherman for? The answer is that this government has instituted what amounts to a resettlement program. The Minister for International Trade, when he was speaking about the response of the government, did not say that the largest amount of money of all in the government's response program is $5,000 for moving to other places. That is what will happen. We have seen it. We have seen them moving from the northern peninsula. We have seen them moving from small communities all over the province to places in central Canada, to places in western Canada.
That, unfortunately, is going to happen because of the lack of imagination and the lack of charity and the lack of concern of this government. Now is the time.
What could they have done? Now is the time to start building infrastructure. Now is the time to start building wharves. We have communities where there are no water and sewer systems. We need road connections. There are all sorts of things that could be done now, action that could be taken by this government to build the infrastructure so that when the fish stocks revive, and they will, then we will be in a position to do the harvesting, to have the onshore facilities that will help us to build in the future. But that kind of imagination was not used. Those dollars were not put into those programs, because this is not a government that wants to invest. This is a government that wants to cut the Atlantic provinces adrift. If you cannot survive in the private sector, well, that is too bad. There is no recourse as far as this government is concerned.
Our people do not want to move away. Their families have lived there for 400 years. Fishing is what they do best. These communities have survived on fishing. These communities are made up of very strong families who want to live there and they can live there. This is the richest resource anywhere in Canada and the richest marine resource possibly in the world. The irony is that with that kind of resource off our shores we, because of the carelessness and the lack of imagination of this government, have no alternative but to move away. But the people will remember, and they will survive. They will outlive this government. Long after this government is gone, these communities are going to be there.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is always difficult to speak following the member for Labrador because the member for Labrador has demonstrated, in the years he has been in this House, a particular passion, a great ability to articulate the views of the people of not only Labrador but all of Newfoundland.
I want to contribute to this debate by referring to a letter I received in the mail today from my riding. I just want to quote a couple of lines. The letter reads:
Dear Mr. Tobin:
It seems it's getting a bit tougher all the time as you know. This has been a very bad year for fishermen-I know for a fact it's going to be a very tough winter-
My Dear God, is there some way to knock some sense in the heads of that crowd we call a government? My God, we will have no one left in Newfoundland; they will have to leave Newfoundland or starve.
It's ridiculous, the Minister of Fisheries is saying there are too many fishermen. Utter nonsense. Oh, yes, drive them out of their fishing boats and let the bloody French have the fish-
I am a senior citizen with nobody but myself and I find it tough. My heart goes out to those who have only one income in the house, and that one very small. I just don't know what is going to happen. I'm very, very concerned -
That free trade deal with the U.S. What a nice thing that is. Crosbie said we could get out of it in six months. It's about time this government started to get us out. Everything is turned bottom up. Food prices have never been higher, and things we sell have never been lower. May God help us.
Trusting you can knock some sense into McDougall and the others who have anything to do with these programs.
Yours truly,
Eli Payne,
Cox's Cove.

Now, that is a letter from just one gentleman, a senior citizen. But it could have been a letter from John Hedderson from Straitsview. It could have been from Cook's Harbour or Boat Harbour or Green Island Brook or Port au Choix or Castors River, Nipper's Harbour, or it could have been from the sea.
What Canadians have to understand and what this government has chosen to ignore, other than dealing with statistics, other than dealing with numbers, other than dealing with limp-wristed explanations for the failure of this government to manage the fishery properly, what this government has to look at is not its own face in the morning when it wakes up. This government has to leave this gilded chamber with these fine wrought-iron chandeliers and these great stained-glass windows and the ministerial cars waiting for cabinet ministers warm outside this Chamber, where the temperature is minus 20.
This government and the ministers have to go down to Atlantic Canada, out of the hotels and the ministerial suites, and into the communities and onto the streets. They have to look the Eli Paynes in the face. What they will see when they look into the faces of the fishermen and the plant workers of Atlantic Canada, contrary to what they are hearing here tonight, is not anger because we are angry, is not great emotion because we are emotional and is not a sense of outrage because we are outraged. What they are going to see when they look into the faces of the fishermen of Atlantic Canada is a profound sense of betrayal, of abandonment on the faces of a people who understand what they are undergoing and are victims of a cultural genocide. It is cultural genocide of a way of life, a rural, labour-intensive way of life that is being brutally destroyed by a government that has been indifferent, not to the statistics because we can quote statistics, but indifferent to the human beings who live in those communities and the sense of community and shared values that they have created over 500 years. That is what is happening in Canada today.
I find it incredible that members opposite say: "Let's be non-partisan. Let's all be together. Let's find the solution". It is just like Clifford Olson saying, when he stands condemned before the dock, that it is all a
mistake, that he misunderstood the values of this society, let us just forget it and from now on he will be good.
This government has managed the fisheries over the last five years and it has taken a deliberate decision that nobody on the other side has talked about, because while the total allowable catch is being reduced from 290,000 tonnes in 1988 to 190,000 tonnes this year-a 100,000 tonne reduction-within our 200-mile zone this year, France took 15,600 tonnes of fish, a quota the French set for themselves. Next year they are going to take 15,100, a quota they set for themselves. The year after they are going to take 14,600, a quota they set for themselves within Canada's 200-mile management zone.
In my riding, an area called the Great Northern Peninsula, an area of a splendid national park, great peaks and the most beautiful scenery on the planet, an area that people are proud to be in and make a living from, this government is ripping the "Great" out of the Great Northern Peninsula because this year the fishery was an utter failure. Those inshore fishermen are being told that next year, they will have no fish. But you know what, somebody is going to have fish there next year.
In the Strait of Belle Isle, there are nine miles of water between Quebec and Newfoundland. Do you know who is going to be sailing through those nine miles next year when the fishermen in my communities are told to stay home? French factory freezer trawlers are going to take
4,000	metric tonnes of cod with the permission of the Government of Canada in the middle of a crisis.

speechtext:
This minister of fisheries, if he had any sense of being the voice of fishermen around the cabinet table, rather than cabinet's apologist to fishermen in the fishing communities, if he had any backbone, if he believed that there was a role for him to play around that table for people who do not have the privilege to speak for themselves around that table, if he had any pride in his responsibilities and the traditions of those who have gone before him, he would resign today in protest at the cruelty inflicted upon the people of Atlantic Canada.

December 18, 1989

spectacle of the member for St. John's West, Newfoundland's member in the cabinet, tonight in this House was pathetic. subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to be in the House tonight speaking on this most important concern to Atlantic Canadians. It is a debate, as many have mentioned this evening, that I guess many of us would be happy not to have to take part in because it clearly indicates there is a crisis in Atlantic Canada, one that we would much rather not have.
Thinking that this is December 18, we are only one week away from Christmas, many individuals are going to have a very difficult Christmas in Atlantic Canada. Many of them, of course, are fishermen who have worked their entire lives on the water and have made their living from the water. This year of all years, they have found it most difficult, very, very distressing and are having a most trying time doing the things they have traditionally done.
I believe that the Government of Canada does understand the problem. We are trying to do something about it and obviously that has to happen in this House. I do agree that the problem has to go beyond partisanship, that we can blame one another, we can blame successive governments, we can blame provincial governments, we can blame the federal government, but I think that if we are going to approach this problem, we have to approach it in a very positive sense. That is what I propose to do.
If I could, I would like to go through some steps that I think we should take as Canadians. Perhaps I could refer to something I would call the fishermen's bill of rights.
Whereas the primary goal of fisheries policy is to maintain successful and sustainable fisheries an whereas the fishermen of Canada are the people most affected by and most knowledgeable about successful and sustainable fisheries, therefore Canadian fisheries policy shall be founded upon and guided by the following principles: (1), that fishermen, as the people with the most immediate knowledge and interest in the fishery stocks of a region, shall be consulted to the maximum extent possible whenever stock assessment procedures, conservation measures or quotas are in issue; (2), that no action detrimental to the interests of the fishermen of any region be implemented until all available appeal mechanisms have been fully exhausted; (3), that in all instances government or departmental decisions relating to stocks, licensing, assessment or quotas be made known to the fishermen of the region affected at least one year before they take effect; (4), that licensing policies be consistent, practical, equitable and predictable, that no such policies be given retroactive effect; (5) that regulatory changes be unambiguous and understandable and be available in both languages at least six months before they are implemented; (6) that public hearings with sufficient notice be part of this stock assessment and quota setting process; (7) that in the development or enforcement of any policies relating to the fisheries the health and safety of fishermen be a paramount consideration; (8) that fish allocations be made with particular regard to communi-caties dependent on the fisheries to maintain a traditional way of life; (9) that fishermen be entitled to compensation for the unfair taking of any licensing or quota privileges and that any changes or reductions not complying with this preamble be deemed an unfair taking.

December 18, 1989
I think we have to be constructive in this House and that is what I am attempting to do. I do not think it does anyone any favour to simply point fingers, holler, shout and wave arms. It is pretty good theatrics but it does not put bread on the table, and I think that is what we are speaking of.
In my riding of Carleton-Charlotte we have gone through some difficulties as well. In the early 1980s we had some difficulties in the herring fishery. I am proud to say that we have the largest herring fishery in Canada. In fact, we have what used to be the largest herring processing in the world and I think is still close to being the largest in the world in Black's Harbour. When that fishery got in trouble a number of years ago, we pulled together as a community and a province and explored other ways to do things and other areas of the fishery that we could make a living in.
What does he do? He is in an area in which options are not readily available to him as they are in other parts of the country. Those are the people whom governments have to help and governments should help. Those are the people who get caught up in this nightmare of fishing in Atlantic Canada in that ground fishery. Those are the people whom I believe this government wants to help.
The Prime Minister has committed resources of this government to help those very people who have been caught in that unfortunate situation. We have been promised the same kind of help that was given to western Canadians, in particular the wheat farmers after the severe droughts and devastation that they have experienced in the last number of years. We owe this to the fishermen as we do to all Canadians. I believe that all Canadians have to enjoy the standard of living that we have all come to expect in this country. When difficult times arrive, we all have to pitch together as we have never done before to help these people over the hurdle.
One of the things we did as a province, with help from the federal government, was look into the aquaculture industry. The aquaculture industry, and the raising of salmon in particular, is one of the largest single industries in my constituency, second to none in Canada or in the world. It is producing a fine product and that came about simply because the people cared and they decided they were going to do something themselves and the government was there to help them out.
It was positive thinking that accomplished this. I refer back to my opening comments about it being one week before Christmas and I think that is the frame of mind that we have to put ourselves in. We look for the good that can come from adversity. That rings true with some of these difficulties and the determination of some people you meet when travelling through a riding like mine. I was speaking to a ground fisherman in my riding who, for some unknown reason, was not able to go out and do the thing that he is good at doing, and that is fish.
I said that this was for some unknown reason but I guess if you dig deep enough, or perhaps not so deep, you will find the reason. Somehow some of these people have been caught up in the system. This gentleman whom I mentioned has a small boat and was taking part in a quota system that was gobbled up by some of the bigger boats. What does he do? He says, "What can I do? I am 60 years old. I cannot go out and look for another job. I have payments to make on my boat. I have payments to make on repairs that I put in."
I would like to conclude by saying that we have a caring government, a government that wants to do something, a government that will do something. I am proud to be part of this government that is not afraid to recognize that there are problems in the industry. This government is prepared to assess these problems honestly and in a comprehensive manner. This government understands that these problems are best addressed by building on the sound practices that we have adopted for the management of this very vital resource.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
This evening, Mr. Speaker, in response to the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. LeBlanc), I intend to direct most of my remarks to the conservation angle. In the next few minutes I will attempt to argue in favour of taking measures aimed at promoting the conservation of fish species landed by Canada's east cost fishermen.
Mr. Speaker, there is one basic principle which cannot be ignored in fishing for and harvesting marine species, to wit: Mankind must not take more of a given fish species than the species is able to reproduce itself. To put it another way, we cannot guarantee the survival of fish species caught along and off the shores of our coasts unless we prevent people from taking more than specific species are able to replenish their own stocks through reproduction.



My immediate concern, Mr. Speaker, is that too many years have gone by without our realizing that fishing and harvesting activities along our coasts ignore that fundamental precept.
There have been major changes in the fishing industry over the past 25 years. During that time fishing boats have been equipped with sophisticated facilities, the fishing and harvesting techniques of fishermen looking for ever more numerous species have improved extremely rapidly, and the year and equipment used by fisherman have been highly refined.
These changes in the three fields I have mentioned have made it possible for fishermen to draw maximum resources from known fishing grounds. They also paved the way to new fishing sites and, finally, they enabled man to reach remode areas which until then had remained untapped.
As conditions evolved, new operators appeared in the commercial fishing industry, not to mention the fact that existing plants were modernized and fitted with the latest and ever more sophisticated processing facilities. Technology revolutionized processing methods and plants became much more efficient. At the same time, new larger and better equipped plants were built in all the eastern Canada provinces.
In only a few years eastern Canada's commercial fishing industiy made the transition from the rudimentary conditions it had been in for three centuries to a modem and effective undertaking.
These radical changes in the fishing and processing industry put added pressure on traditionally harvested species and led to the discovery of new untapped resources in areas which until then had been beyond the reach of fishermen.
As fishing methods improved at an accelerated rate and processing plants became more efficient, the then government under the Liberal Party forgot something which was to have a catastrophic impact on the future of fisheries and the processing industry. Madam Speaker, they failed to evaluate the fish stocks that were being used and neglected to conduct scientific research on stocks of fish species that were not being used.
The government at the time lacked the vision to consider the medium and long-term consequences of additional pressures on fish stocks and increased fishing of new species. It saw the profound changes that were shaking up the fisheries and processing industries, but remained unconcerned about the condition of existing stocks and the negative impact that increased fishing would have on those stocks.
The government at the time should have had the foresight to increase its efforts in pure research on fish stocks and research directly related to the fishery.
Research on fish stocks would, at the time, have made it possible to establish the state of those stocks and determine allowable catch levels. The scientific data would have made it possible to guarantee the continued existence of the species being used and that of new species that were starting to be used by the fishery.
This oversight and lack of vision of the party in power during those years produced the situation that now prevails in the Atlantic fisheiy. This evening, the opposition is trying to make the present government take the blame for the situation. I may remind the Official Opposition that the government of the time must take the blame for the present situation and that the government of the time was formed by the Liberal Party.
I would like to quote the example of our Atlantic salmon. The main parties concerned about the fate of the Atlantic salmon have known for some like that this species cannot tolerate years and years of overfishing. However, it was not until the Atlantic salmon was nearing extinction that radical action was taken to ensure its survival.
People at all levels, the federal government, the provincial governments, sports fishermen, commercial fishermen, native peoples, owners of river property, fishing associations and outfitters realized that to ensure the continued existence if the Atlantic salmon, they had to establish a minimum number of spawners in a given river and let the fish come back to their river of birth to spawn and reproduce. This basic datum has to be known

December 18, 1989
before harvesting levels can be set, and only then can they be allotted among users on the basis of seasonal quotas. This sound management principle has stood the test of time, for the Atlantic salmon stock depletion seems to have stopped. We can therefore hope for a return to safer conditions for Atlantic salmon stocks. People have gone back to orderly and prudent harvesting of or stocks.
Eastern Canada producers and commercial fishermen must now acknowledge and accept this basic truth. I would suggest it is the only way to ensure the health of Atlantic fish species and the survival of the fishing and processing industries on the east coast of Canada.
Our government has already taken bold steps in that direction. Our guarantee of success now depends on supportive action on the part of the provincial governments of the fishermen and processors. Five years of good management by this government cannot undo all the harm done by the overfishing and incompetence which prevailed under the previous administration. We on this side of the House are quite prepared to continue to set up the research mechanisms which will enable us to widen our knowledge of Atlantic fish stocks and species. We need the co-operation of fishermen and producers, we need to combine the resources of the federal government with the ingeniosity and skills of fishermen and producers.
Such concerted efforts will make it easier to achieve a double objective: ensure the survival of fish stocks harvested along the eastern seashores of the country, and ensure the economic survival of communities and families whose bread and butter comes from the fishing industry. Let us look confidently to the future and make a joint effort, for I am convinced we will be able to reach these objectives.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House this evening to participate in this very serious debate about the state of Canada's Atlantic fishery.
We are faced with an emergency in Atlantic Canada. We in Parliament tonight have to turn more of our attention to this very serious issue of the future of this resource in Atlantic Canada, for Atlantic Canada and for the future of all of Canada. We have to turn our attention to the prolonged mismanagement of Canada's
natural resources and our fish stocks, to the failed regional economic development policies and to the elimination of viable small communities and rural life in this country. These are the results of decades of Liberal mismanagement and now five years of Tory incompetence and neglect.
In 1982, the Kirby report to the Liberal government of the day warned and I quote: "A reliance on growth cannot be sustained indefinitely and in many stocks the biological limits of prudent harvesting have been reached". In 1987 and 1988 these warnings were again issued.
The previous Liberal government did not pay any attention to this and other warnings about the fate of the Atlantic fishery. The present Conservative government did not pay any attention either until, in 1989, they began to close down the fisheries and the communities in the Atlantic.
Even a few days ago, in the wake of massive lay-offs in the fishing industry, the Prime Minister's response was to blame everything on the previous administration, despite the fact that the studies were there for the government to see. This government has been in power for about half a decade now and it is time to start accepting a little responsibility. In fact, as I have said, this government has been repeatedly warned about the growing dangers to the Atlantic fisheries.
I said that in 1988 the government had been warned. In fact, the background paper for the Canada-Newfound-land Inshore Fisheries Agreement contained the following warning: "With few exceptions the fisheries resources of the Atlantic have reached their maximum utilization and in some cases there is an indication that over-exploitation is occurring."
Where was the planning when that information came? Where was the planning for more rural development and development in those communities? Why has the government waited until 1989 and caused this devastation in Atlantic Canada?
Let me briefly review, as people have been doing tonight, the emergency that is now gripping the Atlantic fishery. Last Monday, National Sea Products, one of the two largest fishing corporations in Canada, announced its series of plant closures and lay-offs. The St. John's facility will be closed with a loss of 492 direct jobs. The Canso, Nova Scotia, processing plant will close with a
December 18, 1989

cost of 742 direct jobs. In North Sydney 280 jobs will be lost due to plant changes.
These are statistics, but these are people. These are families. These are families who are going into 1990 without knowing what their future is going to be, without knowing whether there is even going to be a future in their community and in their region of the country.
According to the Fishermen, Food and Allied Workers Union, 1,300 more jobs may be lost in the coming weeks if Fishery Products International announces plans to close other operations in Newfoundland. The situation is that in the coming year Newfoundland could lose up to
6,000	fisheries-related jobs. A comparable figure in central Canada would be 115,000 jobs.
This is why we are pleased that this House has seen fit to debate this as an emergency. It is a serious emergency for our country and for that region because these job losses come on top of what is already happening to Atlantic Canada. Cutbacks on VIA Rail have taken jobs away from Atlantic Canada and have reduced options for the people who live there.
In the fisheries industry there are clearly too few fish and not enough jobs for people who fish and for workers in related industries. Today we learned about the number of small plants and small businesses in Nova Scotia which build boats and provide additional services to those in the fishing industry that are closing.
Successive governments have failed to manage the resource. The government must take responsibility for that failure, both in terms of the inability of the government departments to adequately assess the quantities through their own scientific research and in terms of dealing with the impending doom that has been clearly outlined for a number of years.
Past and present governments have set catch quotas, granted foreign fishing rights and allowed the introduction of new technologies without fully comprehending the sustainability of the fishery.
One issue in particular, the foreign overfishing of the Grand Banks, has been a longstanding problem. It is not something new, it is not something that just happened in
December of 1989, two weeks before Christmas, but has been a longstanding problem.
The European community recently announced plans to take more than 50,000 tonnes of fish from the Grand Banks, more than three times the quota suggested by the North Atlantic Fisheries Organization. This announcement comes in the face of the Canadian government's promised commitment in the speech from the throne last April to work toward ending foreign overfishing on the Atlantic coast.
Yet between 1986 and 1989 the nations of the European Community overfished the Grand Banks by 600 per cent; not 2 per cent or 10 per cent or 100 per cent, but 600 per cent. The evidence could not be clearer. Surely it is time for the government to admit the mistakes that have been made and to help these people in the Atlantic to deal with these issues and to keep this industry alive.
Meanwhile, there has been inadequate Canadian funding and resources for the kind of research that might have added to the sustainability of this industry, as well as for planning and coastal patrol. Atlantic Canadians, of course, like everyone in Canada, face the other cuts; the VIA Rail cuts, the unemployment insurance cutbacks, and the possibility of being hit with this goods and services tax which is going to burden even more people already in a very difficult situation. On top of that there is the Conservative erosion of social programs as a consequence of the trade deal. There is no question that there is a serious crisis in Atlantic Canada in the fishery.
Tonight in this House and in the coming days and weeks we have to face the facts and seek real solutions to these problems. Newfoundland New Democrat leader Cle Newhook said today that Atlantic Canadians want to know if this government has the guts to avert the economic and social disaster that is going to take place in his province and in the maritimes. I and my party want to know that too.
We have some suggestions about the kinds of actions that this government should take and take now. Jobs must be saved and jobs must be created. People in the Atlantic do not want a welfare cheque, they want a pay cheque. We have to save the communities of the Atlantic. We in this party do not accept the age-old practice of monopoly corporations and companies that close down plants and whole towns on the basis of short-term

December 18, 1989
profitability. We believe in long-term commitment in Canadians and Canadian resources.
We do not believe in the short term of shutting down, whether it is a Schefferville, an Ocean Falls, a Canso, a Lockeport or the Grand Banks. Canadians, wherever they live, in large communities or small ones, on family farms or in fishing villages, deserve the security of knowing that their communities will survive, prosper and nurture and that their children will have a future. Canadians have a right to expect that our rural communities and our resource based economies can develop and can be protected by a government that does not plan just for the short term but plans for the future of our children. That right and those values must come before plant profits and the quick movement of capital.
We are suggesting that some companies should be encouraged to keep processing plants operating, at least seasonally, in order to continue to provide work in a community economic base. Surely people who are working for at least part of the year are in a better position to keep their communities going than if they have no means of employment.
The federal government should facilitate, help and, if necessary, underwrite the continued operation of presently threatened processing plants to be owned and managed by workers and producers through co-ops if the companies themselves refuse to continue to operate.
The government must undertake a full environment and fisheries resources study on the Atlantic coast to determine the fish stocks and the preservation of spawning grounds and to review how fish quotas and allocations are set.
As we in this party pointed out in our review of Canada's security policy in April of 1988, Canada must improve its own offshore surveillance and coastal patrol capacity, both in the air and on the sea. Canada has to get tough with our European neighbours. For most of this centuiy Canadians have taken up responsibilities for European security and peace. We have every right to demand European recognition of our national resource, our environment and our economic interests in the Atlantic.
The government is obliged to make this clear and definite and to press an immediate European recognition of NAFO quotas for the Grand Banks. Canada, in the end, must make it clear that we are willing to unilaterally extend our economic jurisdiction to all of the Grand Banks if the Europeans fail to co-operate.
The government must take some necessary action at home. It must end its plans to gut the unemployment insurance system, because under these plans 45,000 Atlantic Canadians will lose their qualification to unemployment insurance. The government can help the desperate Atlantic economy and Atlantic fishery by ensuring that there is bread and butter on the tables of the thousands of families already wholly or partially reliant on some unemployment insurance benefits.
Finally, the Atlantic fishery situation is yet another reminder of the total failure of the trade deal. Thousands of jobs continue to be lost across Canada from coast to coast, whether it is in agriculture, in the industrial sector or in the fisheries on the west and the east coasts. Consumers, as we read again today, have gained nothing from the trade deal. So what have we gained from this? As I said the other day, what we gained is that many Canadians are getting the pink slip and it is time that this government gave the pink slip to the United States on this trade deal.
There is a new term, it is "economic restructuring". That is very nice if you do not happen to be one of those people who is affected or one of those communities that is affected by this term. We said a year ago that Canada's social programs are under attack by the government itself in response to demands from the American economy. The trade deal must go. The sooner this government wakes up to that fact the better for all Canadians and for the chances of survival in Atlantic Canada, in western Canada and in all of Canada.
I returned from the Yukon and British Columbia for this debate this evening because it is an important debate about the future of our country and the survival of the Atlantic. It is also a reminder that much of Canada is under a threat at .the moment and, indeed, much of our way of life. Northerners face new environmental and economic threats. West coast fisheries face resource problems, foreign catch and territorial disputes, and serious threats from pollution. As leader of my party I
December 18, 1989

am committed to the survival of rural Canada and of our smaller communities and way of life.
In the north, in the east, and in the west we need policies and new commitments to build a country that is fair and prosperous for all Canadians no matter where they live or how they choose to work. I pledge my efforts and the energies of my colleagues to building that kind of Canada. I urge this government to take action now to save the fisheries in Atlantic Canada so that in the 1990s we can show that we are once again a strong nation that protects and invests in our resources and in Canadians in all parts of this country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also travelled tonight to get here from my riding, not as far as the hon. member for Yukon but certainly deliberately to participate in this debate. While my riding is not directly involved in the fishery, this is an issue with which I can and do identify, an issue with which I am deeply concerned and share the legitimate sense of crisis and perhaps even tragedy at this particular time of year for those families, those people and those communities who are suffering as a result of the closures which we are witnessing at this time.
It is always tempting to engage in political rhetoric, to pontificate and to cast blame at a time like this, but I think that the fisheries situation in Atlantic Canada is really much too serious for that. That is especially so when we contemplate that National Sea has closed or is about to close 1,200 jobs in Canso, close to 500 in St. John's and 300 in North Sydney. When we read today in the newspaper about receivership of a fisheries business in Prince Edward Island; when we read about more than 100 boatbuilders who are in difficulty throughout Nova Scotia, the impact of the Atlantic fisheries and the serious nature of this crisis hits us very strongly and very deeply.
I was disappointed to hear some of my hon. colleagues from the Official Opposition tonight, particularly the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys when he read selectively half of an article that was in The Globe and Mail today about National Sea. He attempted to blame this government for all of the difficulties that are upon the fishery. He was even blaming us for the international diversification of that company.
He left out the first part of that article which pointed out that the Liberal government of his day invested $70 million in the pay-down of a loan, $10 million in preferred shares-$80 million in that company to end up with 20 per cent of the shares, which those who now own 80 per cent of the shares got for $20 million. It was a terrible piece of business. Of course, it has proven to be a terrible example of resource management and fisheries management.
As I have said, I really feel it is not the time for rhetoric. It is really a time for care and compassion, for response, for planning and long-term action. I would like to quote an article of last week from the Fredericton Daily Gleaner, our home-town paper, in which it quoted as a prelude to the editorial a statement by John F. Kennedy when he said-and I believe it pertains to this House tonight-"Our task now is not to fix the blame for the past but to fix the course for the future".
What we have on our hands in the Atlantic fishery is a serious case of unsustainable development, of fishing and processing capabilities and capacities which are now dearly beyond the tolerable yield of the ocean's fish resources. The causes are many. We have heard of scientific forecasting which has been in error and inadequate. We have seen excessive investments in boats, in plants and equipment. We see evidence of overfishing of quotas both domestically and by foreigners. There are no shortage of causes, but there are not many solutions, certainly no easy ones.
I think the first thing we must commit to do is to fix the resource itself. Our fish stocks are declining and must be rebuilt urgently. They must be built to sustainable levels so that we will not have them only for one time in a sustainable fashion, but we will have them for future generations in a sustainable fashion as well. This means that there will be dramatic cuts in quotas and there will be new disciplines in catches. It will mean fewer boats and fewer plants and fewer jobs. We may not be able to gain the levels of the past.
As I listen to my hon. colleagues from the fishing constituencies of Atlantic Canada, particularly those on the other side, criticizing the government and talking about how sinful it is to talk about training people for new kinds of work, to talk even about the horrible word of "relocation" to areas where jobs are plentiful, I cannot help but wonder if there is not just a political blind spot. They just refuse to accept the realities of the facts of the fishing industry, the fact that it is not sustainable, the fact that to make these communities and

December 18, 1989
these people slaves to an industry that is unsustainable is a crime in itself. I think that in these fishing communities the people equally with the resource are the compelling priority.
To his credit, when the hon. Elmer MacKay first addressed this crisis on behalf of the government last week his first words were clear and unequivocal. He said that the Government of Canada is fully committed to assisting individuals, families and the communities affected by the downturn in the fishery.
How is this commitment of support to be delivered? In many ways; through the industrial adjustment service for one, which I believe is a service that is going to have to be expanded and made more comprehensive in this day and age in Canada, not just with respect to the fishery. For example, it was designed, my understanding is, to support the free trade agreement in recognition that there would be dislocations, structural emergencies as a result of the transition to free trade.
We have the Summerside situation which I believe is the most compelling single area for care and compassion by this government, one that we must address through the industrial adjustment service and otherwise. I believe that we must address the fishery throughout Atlantic Canada in a very strong and profound way with this service.
As well of course we have the broad range of programs and services through the unemployment insurance administration, the Canadian Jobs Strategy, income support emergency response, job training, relocation assistance, community initiatives and special aid for older workers.
A special response for the longer term is also essential. I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Yukon tonight. This is a long-term problem we are addressing in part, and we must have long-term answers. We must, as I said earlier, face the facts of the fisheries, that there are limits to the potential of the fisheries. We must accept those limits not just for the sustainable harvest in our time, as I have said earlier, but also to serve future generations.
What does this mean? It means establishing new ways of life for many people in many communities. It means finding new economic activities, new industries and new jobs.
I believe that the greatest single challenge facing Canada today is to confront the realities of unsustainable development, to take the action that is necessary, to be sure, but even more critically to address the need for viable alternatives and to create those alternatives, to replace jobs which have become unsustainable.
This challenge is probably greater in Atlantic Canada than in any other part of the country. We do not have to apologize for that either. We are founding shareholders in the Canadian confederation. The truth is abundantly clear. There is economic disparity in the Atlantic region which must be balanced with the more economically favoured parts of our country.
Regional development action is essential to provide long-term growth in Atlantic Canada that would otherwise not occur. That special kind of assistance must be more than just a sharing with the boom areas of Canada. It must provide an advantage to Atlantic Canada that will help rationalize our disadvantages of distance, of size of our markets and of scale. It must be a unique extra that will attract new industry to our region, that will spur development by our entrepreneurs and that will relieve our overdependence on sensitive natural resources such as the fishery.
For example, while interest rates are justifiably high defending against inflation right across Canada and an adjustable or variable interest rate policy is not possible, there is a special need for regional measures to ameliorate those rates in Atlantic Canada where, frankly, the economy cannot stand the impact of those rates to the extent that it can in the overheated areas of southern Ontario.
What can be done to address the crisis in the Atlantic fisheries and what can be done for Atlantic Canada?
I mentioned special measures to ameliorate things such as interest rate policies. There are other things that can be done, that are being done, that will be done.
December 18, 1989

In terms of regional development I have said several times in this House that regional development spending in Atlantic Canada will touch $.5 billion in 1989-by far the largest in the history of the Atlantic region. It will average $425 million for the balance of the five-year fiscal plan. Perhaps, in view of the fisheries crisis, that is not enough.
The ACOA fund of $1 billion has been a major and significant initiative for Atlantic Canada. In the context of the fishery, in the context of Summerside, in the context of the structural dislocations we face in Atlantic Canada, perhaps it is time to consider increasing the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Fund for the future.
The unemployment insurance fund has a wide array of assistance both for immediate response and for longterm alternatives. The Liberal-dominated Senate of this country must pass Bill C-21 or it will penalize these very fishermen commencing January 1 of whom we speak tonight.
With respect to the free trade agreement, I would hope that the wishes of the hon. member for Yukon would never be realized. I believe that all Atlantic Canadians would hope that because one of the really bright spots in the future of Atlantic Canada is the 50 million person market that exists less than 24 hours trucking distance from our major centres. That market represents the greatest single potential for the future of the Atlantic region of any other economic factor.
We will process in the Atlantic, and the free trade agreement permits us to process it in the Atlantic region. That will help us to realize the potential of that megalopolis of the northeastern United States. I trust that the hon. member for Yukon will change her tune and come to realize that if she ever hopes to get a seat in Atlantic Canada, which I would seriously doubt, it will not be by turning off the few bright potential spots that we have.
Going beyond that, I have mentioned the industrial adjustment services. My colleagues have mentioned the community future services. There are initiatives that are required. There are major undertakings for communities such as Canso and Summerside.
In closing, I would like to remind you that in the throne speech earlier this year the government did announce a strategy for Canada. It contained several pivotal factors. One was financial stability. We are moving in those directions.
Another was economic growth. We are moving in those directions.
Another was sustainable development. We are grappling now with sustainable development in the fishery. For the first time we are confronting, as the Minister from St. John's West said tonight, the reality of people enslaved to a fishery that is inadequate to be sustainable for them.
The last thing that the throne speech stated was that we are committed to a compassionate and caring society. I call on all members of this House tonight to address the Atlantic fishery and other problems in the Atlantic region with this sense of care and compassion, with this sense of constructive, co-operative debate that will lead to solutions and not merely rhetorical problems such as we hear so often in this House.
I would like to assure Atlantic Canadians that this government is a caring and compassionate government. I would like to assure them that the Atlantic fishery has my support. Coming as I do from an area that is not directly affected, I would want them to know that I and my colleagues support the concerns and the problems. They can count on us to see that they are resolved in the future.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been a long evening and an interesting one. I have sat and listened to most of it. I have learned something, but not from all of the speakers. I can recall the Minister for International Trade speaking for example. I could not help but think of the description of a previous speech a couple of hundred years ago, "full of sound and fury signifying nothing". Add his reassurances to the people of Newfoundland that he was going to look after them to the reassurances of the previous Minister for International Trade, Pat Carney, and to those of the present Minister of Fisheries who promised also to protect the traditional jobs in the fish-processing industry in B.C.-and we know what happened there. If you put all those reassurances together in one handful it would still take 80 cents to get a cup of coffee in the government cafeteria.
The Leader of the Opposition accused the government of mismanagement. Government members have accused the Liberals of mismanagement. Madam Speaker, they are both right. But none of those accusations, right or wrong, is going to add one pound to the biomass of cod out there waiting to spawn. There is no point now in saying who did something wrong or who did not do something right. That is not the argument. The question

December 18, 1989
is, what are we going to do from here on? What is the government doing right now?
I would say if either party is more to blame than the other, it would be the Conservatives because they have been in office for over five years and they have done nothing to improve the situation in those five years. In fact, it is getting worse. There is no question about that.
In 1988, the total allowable catch of northern cod was set at 266,000 tonnes. In 1989, the federal scientists urged that the total allowable catch be reduced to
125.000	tonnes, and the Minister for International Trade proudly boasted that he would not accept that figure from the scientists. He insisted that the total allowable catch would be 235,000 tonnes. He did that to protect the jobs of the fishermen and the people in the fish-processing industry in Newfoundland-short-term gain for long-term pain.
Harvesting more than twice as much as the best scientific evidence told us should be harvested was nothing short of a disaster for the industry. For the minister to say that he is a responsible minister in this government, it would be better to say that he is an irresponsible minister when he is treating the codfish stock in that manner.
The Harris report for northern cod, released in May of 1989, talked about the codfish stocks. Bearing in mind that in 1977 the best advice available was that there should be 1.4 million tonnes in the cod biomass for spawning, the Harris report said in 1989 that the figures at that time were 725,000 to 500,000 tonnes, an average less than half of what there should be to maintain the proper spawning population. If the figure is actually
725,000,	the upper limit of what Harris said, we could rebuild the cod stocks gradually if we harvested 200,000 tonnes a year, if he was right with the 725,000 figure. If he was right at the 500,000 figure, harvesting 200,000 tonnes a year for five years would reduce the stock to the point where there would be no hope of it ever coming back. It is just that close. We have to be below the
200.000	to be able to achieve anything, to be able to guarantee the protection of that resource. Yet the Minister for International Trade proudly boasts that he insisted on it being 235,000-much higher than it should have been for any safety.
We like to blame the Europeans, and several have. Certainly, I was part of that group that went overseas. We listened and we talked. We blamed the Spanish and the Portuguese for overfishing of the nose and the tail of the Grand Banks. It was great fun. I think there is no doubt but that they are overfishing in those areas.
There is also some question as to what the Canadians are doing, and the Europeans kept throwing this at us. What about our own fishing? I talked already about us harvesting 235,000 when the scientists say it should be
125,000.	Do you think they do not know that? Do you think they do not know that we are harvesting twice as many as we should be? Of course they know it. We are pointing a finger at them and they are pointing it right back at us.
Then they say: "What other scientific evidence is there to back up your claim that it is our overfishing in the nose and the tail that are being destructive and somebody else's overfishing is not?" What about other factors? What other factors are there?
For example, what about predators? The question was raised when I think one of the government members talked about the seals and what they are doing. As far as I know, the only reports I have heard is that they have not actually found cod in the seals that have been killed. If not, perhaps the seals are eating the food of the cod. Certainly, they must be having some effect when they are increasing in the numbers that they are. Should something be done about that? I do not know. It is one of the things that has to be considered. Certainly cutting back on the harvest is also something that has to be considered pretty seriously.
What about mismanagement? Yes. What about mismanagement by both parties? Yes. Let us forget about that and let us do something about the future. That is what we have to agree to do.
Being pushed around by the Americans has been mentioned. I think again it was the Leader of the Opposition who mentioned that. Of course that is true, no question about it. Look what happened on the west coast. I spoke earlier about the promises from government members to protect jobs in the processing industry and protect the fishermen. We know that has not been done. We can blame it on GATT, but there was a solution to that which we ignored. We can blame it on the free trade panel. What is happening there? The Canadian

government said: "Yes, we accept 20 per cent." The Americans said: "No way." They are not willing to accept that, and I have not heard what has happened since. This was supposed to be decided quite some time ago.
