We gave up control of our resources when we became part of this free trade deal, not just of fish I am afraid, but other resources as well. We certainly said to the Americans: "You can have our fish." That is the way they are interpreting the agreement. They are threatening that if we do not interpret it the same way that they are going to take retaliatory action that will make us play ball the way they want us to play ball.
On the east coast there are similar problems. The same Minister for International Trade is quoted as saying as much as much as 80 million pounds of unprocessed fish could have left Nova Scotia in 1988. How many jobs is that? Those fish could have been processed in Canada, on the east coast where all these plants are shutting down. We could have kept some of those plants open had we insisted on processing all our fish in our processing plants with our workers. The Conservative member of Parliament for South Shore, Nova Scotia, said: "Nova Scotia alone is exporting 1,000 jobs a year." That would have kept some of the smaller plants open.
There has been some talk of the alternatives to cod fishing. The Minister of Fisheries, I believe, talked about some 350,000 tonnes of other species that are available for harvest. I do not think he really assigned blame, although I had the feeling when he was saying this that it was because the fishermen were not catching them, were not harvesting them. I see him shaking his head. I am glad to see that. It is not the fishermen. They would be delighted to harvest all these 350,000 tonnes of any species if there was a market for them, but we need the market. That is where the government has to come in.
I attended a meeting in Lockeport when that plant had been closed, a meeting that I think was originally organized by the United Auto Workers Union which brought together people from the community, from the council and from various organizations. They all agreed on a plan for something that might be done with Lockeport. The essence of it was: "Let's use Lockeport
as a sort of research place to find some way of using these species that are not currently being used."
I have one small example in my constituency of Nanaimo where a small processor of fish tried for years to do something with dogfish. The problem was the ammonia. What do you do with the ammonia? How do you get rid of the ammonia? He eventually produced a very tasty product, smoked, canned dogfish. The ammonia was out of it. I asked him how he did it but of course he wasn't going to tell me that. As far as I know that product is still being produced.
Through research that one person on his own was able to do something with the dogfish that was and is such a nuisance on the west coast. What about these species on the Atlantic? It would seem to me that the proposal to use the Lockeport plant or any other place as a research facility to find some way of utilizing what the minister called the under-utilized species that are there in such large quantities is a good proposal. It cannot be the fishermen who do it. Industry will not do it. Industry will go out and buy more boats. I think NatSea spent some $16 million just buying another freezer-trawler after it closed several plants in the Atlantic provinces. It has money to buy these big trawlers that put fishermen out of work, but it does not have any money for research to find what should be done with these under-utilized species.
Apart from management that has to be cleaned up, apart from using the under-utilized species to provide more economic opportunities, we also have to sustain the workforce that is being cut back now because of the closures. We hope that with proper management there will be an increase in fish stocks and we would hope to be using others. The workers are there now. It is not their fault. As I say, government members have accused the Liberals. The Liberals have accused the government members. Nobody has accused the people working in the fishing industry, whether the fishermen or the workers, of having done anything wrong. It is not their fault that the resource was mismanaged. They are there ready, willing and able to work. Hopefully, there will be job opportunities for them. In the meantime they have to be sustained.

December 18, 1989
Unemployment insurance is being cut back seriously. The government has to have the responsibility of making sure that those people, even if they are not able to work, have a decent income to keep them going until these plants reopen. If they are not going to reopen, then there has to be a period when the government will help them and help them get re-established, but not in retraining them to take jobs on VIA Rail that is going out of business or to take jobs in the tourist industry at minimum wage. They need decent jobs that will enable them to contribute to the economy in their communities.
We have to manage the stock properly. Yes, Spain and Portugal are overfishing. But one of the messages I heard in Europe time after time was that if we clean up our act in Canada and do a better job of managing the resource here, then we will be in a much better position to recommend to them that they clean up their act and we might be listened to more carefully. Let us put our own house in order. They said it is not enough just to juggle the catch. We need to have scientific analysis to find out exactly what is going wrong. Why are we so short of fish? Maybe it is the catch. They want more work done on it than to simply count the number of fish that somebody is catching.
The minister in the press release he put out talked about penalties, enforcement powers, changing the system of quotas, better systems for 1990. That is all very well, but the immediate step has to be taken to cut back on the total allowable catch. These other things make a pretty small contribution toward building up the population. It is the catch that is doing it.
The predators I have mentioned. The Minister for International Trade blamed the scientists for having gone wrong. They gave wrong information. Well, even scientists can do that. Usually the latest information is the best information. Let us go for the best we can get.
Another thing that is in some of the material I have here is that if you cannot get the truth from scientists, go to the fishermen. It was in 1988 that the fishermen said the total allowable catch of 266,000 tonnes was too much for the fish. They could not stand it. They were right. I am missing a comment from across the way. The minister said, I think, that that was why he reduced it. Remember, the scientists said reduce it to 125,000 tonnes, and I do not hear the minister saying he is going that far. It takes
drastic action. There is going to be unemployment in the meantime that the government has to look after. If we are going to build that up, we have to deal with it as a serious problem that requires drastic action. It is up to the government to accept its responsibility to save that stock.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise tonight to participate in this emergency debate because it has profound effects on the economy of Atlantic Canada and in particular it has profound negative economic effects on communities such as Canso, North Sydney and parts of Newfoundland.
Fortunately, in my constituency we were spared a closure of a National Sea Products facility. However, Madam Speaker, I want to tell you and members of this House that residents of my constituency take no great pleasure in the anguish, the uncertainty that the people in Canso, North Sydney and parts of Newfoundland are confronted with at the present time.
Some weeks ago I participated in a major rally in Louisbourg, Nova Scotia. At that time, before 700 individuals, I made a number of observations with regard to the Atlantic fisheries, particularly with respect to the solutions which were necessary to be put in place in order to resolve a very serious situation.
While the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is in the House, I would like to share with him for a moment or two the unanimous consent of those who attended that particular meeting on this cold wintry night and of individuals in communities who did not have a National Sea Products fishing plant. Nevertheless they were involved in the fisheries, whether it be the inshore or the offshore, whether it be plant workers in other plants. It was unanimous by each and every one that the first thing the Government of Canada must do and should do very quickly was ask the minister of fisheries to resign.
This minister has lost the confidence of those individuals who participate in the Atlantic fisheries. When you lose the confidence of those individuals you are supposed to represent at the cabinet table, I think it only appropriate and responsible for that individual who holds such high office as the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to exercise those responsibilities and resign forthwith as Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
December 18, 1989

That will not be the cure-all, but it will provide some segment of confidence in an industry and a region which have been bastardized by the present administration in Ottawa.
There are other solutions that could be made to address this very serious situation. The second thing that the government ought to do is to allow the Department of Fisheries and Oceans under the direction of a new minister to exercise paramount control when it comes to fisheries management of our stocks. No longer can the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the senior bureaucrats in the Prime Minister's office be giving directions to the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Fisheries and Oceans must be paramount with regard to External Affairs when it comes to fisheries related matters. No longer can we accept a secondary status.
That leads to an issue which I believe is fundamental. Even the parliamentary secretary has spoken eloquently tonight but was substantively wrong. He ought to know, not as a newcomer to the House of Commons but as an individual who has played around in the halls of power in Ottawa, that the foreign overfishing taking place on the offshore is crucial and devastating to our Canadian fishermen.
When are we as a nation going to exercise our own control? When are we as a nation going to say no to the foreign fleets whether they be Portuguese, Spanish or French, whether they be ships from the United States of America? Is it not high time that the Government of Canada stop kowtowing to foreign interests and stand up for Canadian interests first?
Recently we have seen the President of the United States confirm a law which was passed through the Congress of the United States that negatively affects lobster fishermen in Atlantic Canada. In the province of Nova Scotia it will mean a lessening of $30 million into our economy. What it means is that jobs will be lost and the domestic price for lobster will be substantially reduced not only for this fiscal year but for fiscal years in the future. What did we have? We had the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the Minister for International Trade and yes, the almighty one, the Prime Minister, sending notes to the President of the United States pleading with him not to pass this particular legislation.
Somehow those of us in Atlantic Canada are to be secure in the knowledge and in the fact that this matter now must go before a free trade panel. No one knows the sanction that it will impose. We know a bit about the time frame, but we do not know the sanction that will be imposed. Even if we knew the sanction there is no guarantee that the Americans will accept it.
I say to the parliamentary secretary who is the only one in the Government of Canada listening to the debate at this late hour that they should spend $30 million now readily available on those fishermen who are going to lose as a result of this regressive measure in the United States. If that were done, it would show a measure of good faith by the Government of Canada.
In the remaining time I want to say a few words to those people in Canso, Nova Scotia and in North Sydney in my province. I am embarrassed to stand here tonight with no federal representative from the Conservative Party of Canada in cabinet saying one word, not one sentence for those fishermen in Nova Scotia. I am sure there will be good reason for this lack of attendance tonight, but no one from cabinet has spoken out for the economic interest of Nova Scotians. We talk tonight not of statistics contained in the briefing book of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. We are talking about people, ordinary Canadians, who have mortgages, who have children, who have bills to pay and dreams yet unachieved.
Yet this government has said to those Canadians in Canso, Nova Scotia and in North Sydney: "We don't care. That is not our problem. That is National Sea's problem. Because it is their problem, we are not going to come to your assistance. We are not going to provide the kind of aid which is needed. We will dance with you for a little while, but when the song is over your future will not be in those communities; it will be elsewhere in this great country".
The situation is of a crisis nature. It requires leadership. It requires financial aid. It requires co-operation. It also requires political will by a government that has yet to show any interest or any substantive concern for those men and women in Atlantic Canada who depend so heavily on the fisheries.
I would hope that we would support both in substance and in spirit the emergency motion put forward by my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, stated by my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys and by other members from eastern Nova Scotia. We will try to resolve this particular problem, but it requires political

will by the Government of Canada which is not any being exhibited now nor has it been in the immediate past.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise tonight in support of the motion of my hon. colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, specifically that the Liberal party condemns the government's mismanagement of the Atlantic fishery.
This motion is allowing members on this side of the House to explain the real situation in Atlantic Canada, not the situation as seen from the government's point of view or expressed by Conservative members opposite.
The Government's agenda has been questioned by all Atlantic Canadians at this point in time. In fact we have been questioning it for a long time. "What does the federal government have in store for Atlantic Canada", we ask? Not much.
It has closed Canadian forces bases. It has cut back Via Rail. It has proposed major changes to the unemployment insurance system and has mismanaged the Atlantic fishery to such an extent that it is rapidly declining, causing the closure of plants throughout the maritimes and in some cases shutting down small communities. The fishery is a vital resource to all Atlantic Canadians and its preservation is integral to the survival of the Atlantic region.
It is ironic it was the Canadian government that did so much to contribute to the management of the Canadian fishery by introducing fishing quotas, fishing seasons, and minimum size for fish. Now we are seeing the government destroy the fishery by closing down fish plants in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, allowing overfishing by foreign fleets and, moreover, in the wake of the agreement signed last week, virtual inaction from either the minister of fisheries or the Prime Minister. The plant that will close in Canso causing the loss of 742 jobs, the reduction in operations at the National Sea plant in North Sydney causing the loss of 280 jobs, and the closure of the National Sea plant in St. John's, Newfoundland will add to the deplorable state of the Atlantic economy.
The Canso plant which employs over 60 per cent of the community's population of 1,200 will be closed in April 1990. This is the only industry in this small community. The government has promised to provide funding for the introduction of new industries to the area, but what good will that do for a town that knows nothing but fish? The fishery was the backbone of Canso and now it is the cause of the destruction of Canso.
Nothing has been done by this government to remedy this terrible situation. It fails to understand just how vital the fishing industry is to Atlantic Canada. It is the economic backbone for thousands of Atlantic Canadians. Prince Edward Islanders are used to hearing the horror stories attributed to the shutdown of industries and businesses. We have only to look at CFB Summerside to understand how the people of Canso are feeling right now. Prince Edward Island is reeling from a multitude of economic disasters initiated by the federal government. As well, it is reeling from the recent decision made by the United States that our own government seems powerless to fight.
I need point no further than to the signature of the President of the United States on a bill limiting the sale of Canadian lobsters. This will have serious implications for the already downtrodden economy of Prince Edward Island.
The fishery is one of the three major industries on the island, along with agriculture and tourism. The fishing industry is responsible for 30 per cent of the island's exports and contributes approximately 13 per cent to the Gross Provincial Product. The lobster fishery accounts for 70 per cent of the total value of the island fishery, a value that has been declining given the low prices during the past season resulting from a high concentration of lobster on the international market.
The major market for island lobster is the United States. Some 70 per cent of the lobsters are exported to the U.S. With the passage of the aforementioned U.S. legislation, where will the island fishermen sell their lobster? Let us think of the damage this will do to our provincial economy, an economy already suffering from massive fiscal restraint programs brought on by the federal government.
December 18, 1989

I believe that the free trade agreement is the main problem here. The import limitations brought forward by the U.S. legislation last Tuesday are a direct result of the free trade deal. Senator George Mitchell, the man behind last Tuesday's bill, attempted to have these provisions included in the FTA and now he has what he wanted all along. What has the Prime Minister done in the wake of such punitive actions? Nothing. He seems to be more concerned with building a reputation as an international statesman. Obviously he hesitates to oppose his friend, the President of the United States.
The implications for the unemployment rate in Atlantic Canada are frightening. The Prime Minister has been citing statistics for years now. Just last week he boasted about lower unemployment rates in Atlantic Canada. I would like to inform the Prime Minister that the unemployment rate in my province of Prince Edward Island has not fallen. I am also telling him that the numbers will rise drastically when the full impact of this government's assault on Atlantic Canada is realized.
With respect to fish plants, Prince Edward Island has had its share of closures. The crab plants in Tignish and Murray Harbour have shut down. These closures put 200 people out of work. That has quite an impact on P.E.I., not only on the individual workers but also on their families and the communities that depend on the spending power of these families. Another example is the Summerside Sea Products that closed its doors earlier this year with a loss of some 120 jobs.
The future of the fishing industry in Atlantic Canada is bleak, as is the future of the Atlantic economy in general. Economists are predicting that Canada is on the verge of major recession due in great part to the government's policy on high interest rates. I say that Atlantic Canada is in one now and that it will only get worse if the government does not show a firm commitment to Atlantic Canadians.
There is a growing feeling back home that this government cares very little about the four provinces on the east coast because it has done nothing to prove otherwise. In Atlantic Canada alone there are more than
100,000	fishermen and fish processors. Historically they have depended on a stable Atlantic fishery for their livelihoods. These men and women are now looking at a
bleak future square in the face. They are facing plant closures and lower imposed quotas as well as increases in quotas by the European community. EC nations continue to overfish the transboundary stocks. The European community refuses to respect and support quotas established by the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization.
Atlantic Canadians working in the fishing industry want to work, need to work, and expect nothing more or less than that, but that is not the reality they face. The reality is that more than 1,000 people lost their jobs in the crab and lobster industries in New Brunswick. The job loss in my province was 465. In Newfoundland more than 10,000 plant workers and fishermen have been affected, and in Nova Scotia at least 3,000 workers have been affected. These are ugly statistics, and the future looks even worse.
What we in Atlantic Canada face today is nothing less than a crisis, a crisis that this government could have prevented. The Prime Minister suggested today in the House that unemployment insurance was an answer to this crisis. He stated that if the UI bill were approved by the other place, it would assist fishermen who are victims of this crisis.
This is not much of a solution for fishermen facing long-term chronic unemployment. Atlantic Canadians need long-term solutions, not political rhetoric. I call on this government to put in place immediately an emergency program to financially assist these Canadians. The fishermen and plant workers of Atlantic Canada deserve nothing less.
To conclude, I support the motion put forward by my colleague and I urge this government to act immediately.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise at 10 minutes to 1 in the morning in Ottawa, a bit later in my riding, with no one on the other side of the House to hear what is going on. However, a few of my colleagues are here, those who are interested, and there is a lot of back-up support in the lobby.
This is a difficult subject to speak on in some ways, and in other ways I welcome the opportunity to get up and try to show some indication of the pain people are experiencing in my riding. I have heard a lot of statistics here tonight. I have heard a lot of excuses. I have heard a lot

December 18, 1989
of non-partisanship and a lot of partisanship, but I have not seen much concern or compassion or imagination.
I would like to start with a definition of "crisis". I thought I had better look it up before I came here tonight. It is in the Oxford Concise Dictionary, page 225, Edition 1988. It states that a crisis is a turning point derived from the Greek work "krisis". It means turning point. In order to have a turning point somebody has to decide to do something.
I have not heard much from over there tonight to tell me what that something is going to be or what is going to be done. All I have heard are excuses. "It is not our fault". I do not see how somebody can tell me that they have been running the system for five years and that it is not their fault that we are in a crisis situation.
It happens to be a crisis situation in the offshore fishery that has been brought to the attention of everybody here and has us here at one o'clock in the morning, Ottawa time. There has been a crisis in the inshore fishery for the last five to six years. It is only now that this whole thing is coming to the forefront.
There are so many issues to attack and there are so many suggestions to offer up that it is hard to know where to start. Let us not talk about the scientific gross underestimation of the stocks. I am not blaming them. I am not pointing the finger. I do find it strange that it came shortly after an election, and I do find the range strange. When one estimates something at 50 per cent or overestimates it by 100 per cent, how scientific that is is beyond me. I wonder what they knew when the election was going on, but I am not going to suggest that there are things beyond our control that we can point the finger at.
The fishermen have been telling the scientists, the politicians, and anybody who would listen that there was a problem with the estimate of the 260,000 tonnes, and they would not listen. The fishermen are saying: "If you had listened to us you would not be in this condition today".
Let us lay that aside for the time being and let us look at overfishing. They do not seem to recognize on the other side of the House that overfishing is a pretty major
part of this problem. If there had not been overfishing we may not be in this crisis.
In 1986 that crowd over there was managing this economy. It was managing the fisheries. What happened? Spain and Portugal joined the economic communities. That year 23,200 tonnes was allocated by NAFO. They took 140,000 tonnes. The next year they took
170,000	tonnes. Spain and Portugal were the ones that were really responsible.
This year the Secretary of State for External Affairs says: "It is going to be better. We are going to allocate them 13,000 tonnes, and they are only going to take 50,000". That is great. In 2J3KL, the area that we are concerned about in Newfoundland, NAFO is recommending zero and they are only going to take 27,000. That crowd over there thinks this is wonderful. I do not think that is wonderful. I think that is terrible, and my colleagues would say that that is terrible.
What are we going to do about that? We trade with Portugal and Spain. With Portugal we had around a $48 million deficit, so let us set them aside. With Spain we did almost $1 billion in trade last year, $945 million, and there was a favour to them for almost $500 million.
We are playing hard ball. Let us look at trade sanctions to Spain and Portugal. If the Europeans are to come over here and tell us when we can catch our seals, then at least we should be able to go and tell them when they cannot catch our fish.
What do we do about surveillance? We should know who is in our waters. Last year we had 165 trawlers-I am quoting the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls-in our area and we had two patrol boats in the area. We had Tracker surveillance. The Tracker surveillance gives 50 per cent of the valuable, medium range time as quoted by the hon. member for Labrador this evening. What have we done with that? We have closed down Summerside and we have taken away the Trackers.
I have evidence that DFO claimed at a committee meeting last week that they were not consulted, and my ex-military colleagues say that they were not consulted. It was a decision that was made. Summerside was closed down. It was an ill-advised decision at a time when we need increased surveillance. The surveillance capability that we had was taken away.

Last year, in our economic zone we went to bat for in 1977, we had 200,000 tonnes taken inside our area by foreign ships. One thousand tonnes equals around 30 jobs a year. It does not take a Ph.D. in mathematics to work out that is around 6,000 jobs by giving away 200,000 tonnes. In the last four years the overfishing to which I referred a few moments ago was 400,000 tonnes. We are literally giving away the shop. We are giving it away. Don't worry about the scientific advice. Don't give away the stocks.
My hon. friend from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte talked about 4,000 tonnes of fish being given to the French off his coast where the people are looking out and they cannot catch anything because of the allocation. What a way to run a country. What a way to run an economy. What a way to run a fishery.
I was surprised but it made sense when I thought about it. The first speaker up tonight was the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs. The next minister to speak was the hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is pretty obvious who is telling whom to do what. Domestic policy does not matter a darn here. We are more interested 'in kowtowing to the Europeans and making our mark in the international arena than we are concerned about protecting our fishermen at home in Newfoundland.
How interested are we in enforcing our laws? We send out a ship to patrol an American dragger that is transgressing against our laws. What do we do? We allow HMCS Saguenay to be rammed. I do not know what else happened. The dragger went off into American waters where the fine can be $10,000. In Canada, the same fine is around $750,000.
The Minister of National Defence asks: "What do you want us to do? Go and shoot them?" Our concern is for our people. You do not have to shoot them. There are all kinds of things you can do. I would remind the House that with a different minister of fisheries in 1985 HMCS Athabascan went out, followed, stopped, boarded, arrested Spanish vessels and brought them back to St. John's, Newfoundland where they were tried for overfishing, found guilty, and fined a lot of money. It would be interesting to watch the incidence of decreased Spanish fishing at that particular point in time.
I am going to make some recommendations the other side of the House might find interesting. We should
rescind the Tracker decision. We need to be more aggressive and imaginative in the enforcement of our laws. We need to consider trade sanctions. Although I did not speak of it in the body of my presentation, we have seriously to consider looking at extending our jurisdiction over the nose and the tail of the bank. I think it is about time that we started to do that seriously.
Along the backdrop of Bill C-21, 26,000 people in Newfoundland are going to have their UI reduced by $2,500 and 9,000 will be cut off. We have this thrown at us, and we have GST staring us in the face. There is an awful lot of people out there tonight who are saying: "We don't mind politicians talking about this because it is going to be a rough Christmas for us".
To think that there is not a crisis, you would have to be figuratively deaf, metaphorically dumb and literally blind. We are here tonight to say that something can be done, something should be done and, by God, as long as there is an opposition on this side of the House something will be done.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak in this emergency debate with one major concern. I have a great deal of sympathy for my friends in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, but I do want to point out the tremendous crisis we have been going through for months now in New Brunswick in the fishery, particularly in the Acadian peninsula.
Before I get into those details, I want to say that I do not often take pleasure in pointing out individuals who have suffered some misfortune. However, I can't help but say that it must be some solace to the people of Canso and Newfoundland who are anticipating further reductions in the workforce in fish plants to see that Gordon Cummings is looking for work as well.
If anybody deserved to be turfed out and to know what it is like to be looking for a job, it is the former president of National Sea, who ran a company with public funds right into the sea, if I can put it that way. I make no apologies to the House for taking some pleasure in recognizing that a person who was significant in the fight for free trade, who took the money made available to him by the Government of Canada and spent it in the United States, made a mockery of the restructuring of the fisheries, that at least that individual now shares the

December 18, 1989
fate of many of his compatriots in Nova Scotia and in Newfoundland.
I listened to my friends on both sides of the House talking about the Spanish, Portuguese and the French, when they talked of overfishing. There has even been an admission in part to the effect that some Canadians overfish. One significant omission has been made, I think, and I have tried to listen to most of what has been said here tonight. That is the question of American overfishing.
I do not think we need to be delicate when we see the problems that are occurring in Atlantic Canada as a result of mismanagement, but also as a result of our not defending our sovereignty. The American overfishing is a serious problem, not just because of the incident that my colleague referred to just moments ago, with HMCS Saguenay. The people who know the fishery off the Atlantic coast recognize just how serious American overfishing is and that it must be addressed.
I think the Europeans need to be told that we are not a bunch of wimps who will sit around and scatter when someone talks about seals. I have had some experience in the fisheries as Minister of Fisheries and Aquaculture for New Brunswick. One of the greatest threats to a new and burgeoning fishery in Atlantic Canada in my province of New Brunswick is seals. We have to defend our aquaculture industry and our salmon in cages from the attack of voracious seals. They attack the cages in the Bay of Fundy. They attack our fishery all over eastern Canada in the North Atlantic.
We worry about people who have their own problems, and this is not an opportune time to debate, but it is time we stood up and told people around the world what our fishery is about and what our communities are about.

Madam Speaker, this emergency debate on the fisheries crisis in the Atlantic provinces is an extremely important one, and I simply want to point out certain elements that are creating an enormous amount of disquiet in my province, New Brunswick, and especially in the Acadian peninsula.
Just now people are focusing their discussion mainly on the situation in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. But I want to remind the House that what is happening in Shippigan, Caraquet, Le Goulet, Tracadie and Lameque
is also very serious. Plants have been closing there for the past few months. Madam Speaker, suppose I told you that in the past two years more than 5,000 jobs in Acadia have disappeared with the collapse of the crab-fishing industry. If we put that figure in the context of central Canada, either Quebec or Ontario, it would proportionate to the larger populations there, represent the loss of
100,000	jobs. Already this fall, 1,000 other jobs disappeared when three plants in the Acadian peninsula closed-Connors and L. Gauthier in Shippigan and Baie-Chaleurs Packers in Caraquet.
Other closures are anticipated. This truly is a crisis. With respect to the value of the Canadian dollar, Madam Speaker, people don't seem to understand how disastrous the 86-cent dollar is for exports. Obviously it hurts sales, but it also hurts all the traditional arrangements between processing plants and fishermen-the pressure on prices, the uncertainty in the industry because people know the dollar isn't about to fall.
Madam Speaker, as if it weren't enough that the resource is disappearing in certain cases, the recent decision by the President of the United States, Mr. Bush, to ban part of our lobster exports is going to cost us, in the Atlantic provinces, upwards of $30 million. In my province of New Brunswick the loss will be more than seven million dollars. The government of New Brunswick has estimated that the province stands to lose up to $130 million this year because of shrinking crab stocks and the low prices offered for lobster and herring roe.
Madam Speaker, I have listened very attentively to speeches giving the impression that no one has any alternatives to offer in this debate tonight. Well, Madam Speaker, I am going to take this opportunity to suggest that the federal government must give the same priority to the New Brunswick fishing industry as it seems prepared to give to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, because as I have pointed out, the closures of the plants in Shippigan and Caraquet have the same impact as the closures in Canso and St. John's.
We must subsidize local fishermen who want to go after under-utilized species. We must provide financial and technical help to plants that want to diversify their production by processing under-utilized species. Madam Speaker, we must work with the industry to establish five-year development plans for each species of fish, and also to create, because this is very important, a seafood
December 18, 1989

marketing agency for each of the under-utilized species, such as mackerel and herring. As we know, the fishing industry did for a time profit chiefly from the price offered when crab was abundant, but we are going to have to encourage our plants to process value-added products, which they haven't traditionally done.
And because of the unpredictable character of seasonal industries like fishing, Mr. Speaker, the government must find a more flexible formula for access to unemployment insurance benefits, especially in light of the crisis that is currently shaking the fishing industry in all the Atlantic provinces.

I listened with interest to my friend, the member from Fredericton, who talked about some of the things that we need to do. He mentioned ACOA. Certainly if ACOA has done some work that has had significant positive results in Atlantic Canada, surely now the government has to look at enriching this program because when that program was put forward with its funding, no one could foresee the kind of difficulty that we would be faced within Atlantic Canada as a result of this crisis.
There are many things that must be done, but surely in these few remaining days before Christmas we do not want to hear too much more talk about relocation. Surely there is a capacity in this country to recognize that we do not want to go through "The Grapes of Wrath" in Canada. We did not do that in western Canada when we went through the drought and experienced the crisis in the agricultural community. We do not want to talk about moving people out of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or off Prince Edward Island because we have lacked the will to find ways to diversify our economic base.
It is not a question of being confrontational with the Spaniards or the Portuguese, or the French or the Americans. It is a question of putting forth our views and having people recognize our sovereignty and our commitment to our own people. It is a question of recognizing that this country cannot survive if everybody has to move to Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
If we are going to go back to a system as we had several hundred years ago when people came from Europe and
fished the banks of Atlantic Canada and returned to Europe, or what if people come down from central Canada to make sure there is enough fish caught to take care of the Canadian market, we would then be dealing with a situation that no one could ever have envisioned. Surely that is not the kind of scenario that we want to paint for the people of Atlantic Canada.
I ask the government to look at some of the suggestions we have made. There has to be a way to deal with this crisis in a meaningful way to reassure people now that something will be done in the short term, not just by throwing money at the problem in the short term, but through a medium and long term plan recognizing the reduction in the resources. But what does the government have as a plan, other than simply to react and try to play it by ear, so to speak?
I hope that all members of this House will recognize that the crisis in Atlantic Canada in the fisheries is equal if not superior to anything that has happened anywhere else in this country. We talk about the Scheffervilles, we talk about the western farmers, and we talk about the closing of mines in one-industry towns in the north. We cannot allow this to happen in Atlantic Canada.
I would suggest that all members of this House will finally come to realize that it is going to take a concerted effort. I am sure that Canadians from coast to coast in this country are prepared to share with one another and to ensure that Atlantic Canadians can feel that not only are they a part of Canada, but that people want them to survive and to have some opportunity to thrive as well.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the travesty, the tragedy that is occurring in the Atlantic provinces today. This tragedy is not merely frightening, it is eerie. This government is acting as if it were on a lifeboat, choosing who may remain and who must go. In this case, the government is telling Atlantic Canadian fishermen to jump off the boat into the cruel sea so that Americans, Spaniards and Portuguese can stay on.
Something is fundamentally warped with a government that so blatantly turns its back on the people it is

December 18, 1989
supposed to represent. Then again representation is not one of this government's strong suits. Were we in a court of law and the government an independent player, charges could be levied for the premeditated, vicious butchering of the Atlantic fishery.
The devastation of the Atlantic fishery has not been the effect of nature, it has been the effect of government. For five years, mismanagement. For five years, ignoring what was going on. The fish did not decide one day to swim away. The government has simply done everything in its power to keep Canadian fishermen, to keep Canadian fishing boats, away from the fish. Keep up away, and let others have them. This is just another example of how the government will do virtually anything to get a smile and a pat on the back from the White House. Sellout after sellout, that is what this government has been doing to the Atlantic provinces.
In the last few weeks, the Prime Minister has been responding to questions, virtually every question in this area, with predictable nonsense about how terrible things were before he came into office. He has been five years in office. Five years of mismanagement of the fishery.
No matter how bad things were, previous governments never obliterated industries. Previous governments never penalized regions and previous governments never callously undermined jobs, livelihoods and incomes. Towns like Canso and Lockeport did not look forward to becoming ghost towns under previous governments.
Well, this government can now do what it does best. It can swill its own self-adulation-another community destroyed, another Canadian industry crushed and another prize for Uncle Sam.
The sellout started with the European fisheries, the Portuguese, the Spanish and the French, all permitted to make quotas which could not be met. They could not be met because they were too high. Then came the sellout to the Prime Minister's best friend, the icon of his existence, the United States.
First, the government sold out to the Americans on the fish-processing rules for salmon and herring, then on an export tax for fish, and now, with barely less than a whimper, which is so befitting, it is making a token gesture of opposition to American legislation banning Canadian lobster imports.
What happened to the promises of free trade? The Prime Minister and every single one of the Conservatives elected to office told Canadians from coast to coast that Canada would have unrestricted access to American markets. Free trade did not open up the American market, it shut it down. We have no access and that will translate into a loss of millions for Nova Scotia and for the Atlantic provinces. It will translate into the devastation and the end, again, of towns like Canso and Lockeport, one-industry towns where the fishery has been the mainstay of existence for over 100 years and more. But, nobody cares. Nobody cares on that side of the House.
Why has this government opted to pursue a policy which devastates the Atlantic fishery? Even without the American legislation, look at the record.
Look at the record of five years. Over the past five years this government has eliminated our fish processing rules and eliminated export tax on fish. It has issued licences to foreign countries and agreed with foreign allocations to catch squid and capelin, the food stock of codfish in the Atlantic. What has been the result? Plant closures. Where? Bas Caraquet, Tignish, Canso, North Sydney, Lockeport, Woods Harbour, Port Medway and Port Mouton. There are plants in receivership in Shippi-gan and Murray Harbour. How can these events help Canada? Plant closures, plants in receivership, the slaughtering of a national industry and the devastation of communities. They certainly will not help reduce the deficit.
Perhaps, tragically, this is the new economic plan of this government. Unemployment equals debt reduction. That is how ludicrous this government's actions are. It seems to equate decimation with good government and prosperity.
When will this insanity end? Right now there are thousands of Atlantic fishermen preparing to spend the bleakest Christmas that they can remember. There are fish plant workers in exactly the same situation. Men and women. Whole communities have no idea what awaits them or their children. It is the end of a way of life in small communities all over the four Atlantic provinces. It is the end of a particular lifestyle, a particular culture and one that is endemic and dear to the Canadian fabric.
December 18, 1989

While all this is happening, while the Prime Minister plans on having a Christmas dinner of lobster and salmon from where only George Bush can tell.
But it is not too late to correct this mistake. It is not too late to stop this heinous behaviour. The government is making a mistake but it could see the light. It could, but will it? The government must reserve fish for Canso so that the plant can stay open. The government must say no to the Europeans wishing to impose a quota three times as large as the quota suggested by NAFO. The government must implement programs to keep the plants open and help the communities that so desperately depend on the fishing industry while these programs are being established.
If there is to be any hope for the Atlantic fishing industry and the survival of these communities, the survival of a way of life, the government must impose restrictions on companies wishing to process fish elsewhere than the regions which most desperately need it. This is the knife of free trade to the heart of the Atlantic fishing industry.
In closing, I would like to say that all of us here feel we do have a special calling, that every one of us here in his or her heart knows and hopes that the work we do is in the best interests of the people we represent. Those of us who are so fortunate to be here have to take with our fortune a responsibility for those we represent and a responsibility to those Canadians nationwide, whether you are an Atlantic member, a western member, a northern member, an Ontario member. We have a responsibility to help those who are less fortunate and those who are suffering because of the economic policies of this government. Prior to this government being elected to office, the Atlantic fishery was surviving. Today, we have to help it survive and go on into the future.
Intervention may be a dirty word for the government, but as much as it dislikes it the time has come to intervene. Stand up. Show some backbone and represent Canadians for a change. Say no to George Bush. Say no to the French. Say no to the Spaniards. Say no to the Portuguese. They even respect you more. It is a damn sight surer that you will begin to get the respect you don't have in Atlantic Canada if you take a stand and
stand up for the people in those small fishing communities in those four provinces clinging to the sea who have no where else but Ottawa to turn for help.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of emotion that I sat here tonight before I stood in my place to enter into this debate. I think just about everything that should be said has been said. Unfortunately, it has to be said over and over and over again. I was going to give a speech tonight that dealt with the economy of Atlantic Canada. I was going to talk about the impact of the fisheries on places like Halifax and Dartmouth. Perhaps I will slip into that at some time through my 10-minute speech, but as the night went on and I spoke and listened to some of my colleagues, I became a bit overwhelmed with the crisis that is at hand. Yes, indeed, there are 100,000 people in Atlantic Canada who depend on the fisheries for a livelihood. That is
100,000	people out of some 2.5 million people in all of Atlantic Canada.
What we have witnessed in the last year is a mismanagement of the fisheries and my colleagues have said it more eloquently than perhaps I can at this late hour, but because of mismanagement, because of a government that does not understand eastern Canada, we have seen a collapse in the fishery.
The hon. member from Cape Breton-Highlands- Canso is a good friend of mine and he had a terrible task last week when he knew that his fish plant in Canso was going to close. Not only would it throw 600 or 700 people out of work, it was going to shut down 400 years of tradition in Nova Scotia. Canso will come to symbolize the death of the maritime culture. A fishing village of perhaps 1,000 or 1,200 souls does not seem like a lot. Four hundred years of tradition is a lot.
Canso is one of dozens or perhaps over 100 small communities through Atlantic Canada that rely on the fishery, that very basic natural resource. I will not give a history lesson because I think we know it, but when this great land of ours was populated from the east coast to the west, the gateway was the east and the road to that gate was fish.
The Norse came to Newfoundland because of the fish and they settled there. The first European settlement in

North America was in the great northern peninsula, at L'Anse aux Meadows, by the Norse. It was there because of the fish.
Those who are watching this debate may be wondering what all this talk is about the fish on the east coast, that it is just another industry. It is not just another industry, it is a way of life in Atlantic Canada. It is a special way of life in Atlantic Canada that is collapsing because of this government's negligence. It is collapsing because this government does not understand the special way of life of Atlantic Canadians.
I have had an opportunity over the last few years to travel in Atlantic Canada. This is a marvellous country that we live in. It is compassionate, it is diverse. But I guess my heart will always be in Atlantic Canada.
I grew up by the sea. I grew up in a small community called New Waterford on Cape Breton Island, a rugged community where people were drawn to its harbour because of the fish and settlers came because of the coal mines. They were tough men and women who settled there. In Louisbourg there are 300 or 400 years of history where people still fish today, even though with the mismanagement they do not know if they are going to be able to fish tomorrow. Go to New Brunswick, to Shediac, that very special community, or to St. Peter's, Prince Edward Island.
We are not just debating tonight some sterile debate about a few hundred or even a few thousand jobs. We are talking about the death of a culture.
I am sure some people said my colleague from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte was exaggerating when he called it cultural genocide. It is economically based cultural genocide in Atlantic Canada. I come from a riding where we do not have a lot of fishermen but that does not mean the people who live in the riding of Dartmouth or my colleague's riding of Halifax do not have that affinity for the sea, and do not understand why the people have stayed there and why those communities in Atlantic Canada are great.
What we are witnessing, Mr. Speaker, and for all those who are still listening, is a sad, unfortunate, tragic decline, not just in the resource based industry-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: Not by accident, by design.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
My hon. friend says by design. What we are witnessing is the slow letting of the blood of people of Atlantic Canada by this government's callous approach to the problems in the Atlantic fishery.
I know that my time is limited, Mr. Speaker, but what we are seeing here is a government policy of resettlement, of taking those people from Atlantic Canada, that special and unique place with those special and unique people, and driving them into central Ontario, and into Toronto. We have seen the government try this before and it has not worked, but this time it is hell bent to make sure that this resettlement policy will be the last resettlement policy for the fishing villages on the east coast of Canada.
I started off by saying I did not want to get into a lot of the debate that we have already heard, but I know that there are probably thousands of fishermen who are still watching their televisions tonight and they are looking toward me and they are looking toward every other member in this House to give them a ray of hope. They do not want to hear more sterile debate and more talk about how members opposite are going to increase welfare payments or talk about the UIC payments that they are going to get for those men and women and for those families. What they want is real hope. They want, from the members of this place, is an understanding of what it is they are trying to say.
Fishing is a hard life. Fishermen do not make great money, although the minister of fisheries was overheard saying, "Well, you know, some of these men make over $100,000". How callous and how uncaring and how stupid can you get? Anybody who travels to the east coast of Canada, who goes into these fishing villages like Cow Head in Newfoundland and sees the difficult life that these men and women endure, the danger that they endure, would know that those statements have no place in the debate on the future of the Atlantic fisheries.
I would hope that the efforts of my colleagues, that the efforts from the members from Atlantic Canada will have some effect on the government members who like to sit down on their hands. I do not know how some of those members can ever go back to Atlantic Canada. I have listened to some of the debate tonight and most of them I am sure got up and talked the best game they could knowing that their colleagues on their side of the House were not just doing away with an industry. They
December 18, 1989

were doing away with a very special part of our Canadian culture.
I urge every Canadian who is watching tonight or who reads these debates not to allow this to be seen as just another piece of economic gibberish that goes on in this House, but that they understand it for what it is. This is an emergency debate on the very survival of our maritime culture.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing this debate to happen.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise here tonight and speak on this emergency motion put forward by my colleague for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso. I want to say that I believe the crisis that we are hearing about tonight and experiencing with the fishery in Atlantic Canada is just the tip of the iceberg.
I happen to believe this economic crisis that is happening in Atlantic Canada is about to go coast to coast and, I think, those of us in central Canada who think that we are immune are fooling ourselves because we are dealing with a government that has really passed on its responsibility to hold on to the fiscal levers of this country.
As I listened to the various speakers tonight, I reflected back to what we were doing at this time last year. We were debating the free trade bill. I pulled some notes together from the speeches of members of the government side who were trying to tell us that this free trade bill was going to be something great for the economy of this country. I pulled together some words from the various speakers on the government side and I tried to relate them to the fishery debate.
The bottom line, after going through some of the speeches, is that this government has really lost any ability to have the trust of the people of Canada. Government members told us last December that we were going to have secure access to the U.S. market. Last week, we heard about the directive from the president on lobster.
Last year in December they talked about new opportunities for Canadian exporters. For the first time in 13 years, we have month to month trade deficits. Benefits to
Canadian consumers were mentioned. Right now every region in this country is feeling higher prices. This was the appropriate time for industry readjustment, they said. We are still waiting for the package for the fishery.
They said we would have effective adjustment policies to aid sectors needing assistance. Well, we know that did not happen. They said there was no threat to our relations with other trading partners. I have to believe that the reason we are allowing the Portuguese and the French to have unfettered access to this fish is because we are concerned about other penalties that we might receive from our trading partners.
They talked about prevention of the imposition of punitive U.S. trade laws. That is what the free trade was going to do for us. That has not happened.
There would be maintenance of the ability to establish public policy in the Canadian interest, one minister said. We have never acted so wimpish in years in our relationship with the United States as the way we are acting right now.
There would be protection of our social programs, they said, of our labour laws and our health and safety programs. The Minister of Employment and Immigration would shudder if she would go back and read Hansard from a year ago.
There would be the continuation of our political independence and policy freedom, another minister said, and the provision of stability and predictability in the investment climate environment. This economic environment we are in right now, symbolized by the suffering, symbolized by what is happening in the Atlantic fishery, is going to go coast to coast, because this government has given up its responsibility to take control.
They also said that there would be a high probability of net job creation. We know that is falling apart right before our very eyes. Yet it is an incredible thing that we were sitting here on the eve of Christmas. Last year, half the seats on the government side were full because they wanted to push their free trade bill through. Yet, here we are tonight while one of the regions of our nation is going through a rough time and there is one member of the government. I find it just incredible.

December 18, 1989
Another thing they said was that the free trade bill would give us a significant improvement in national income and standard of living. How could we sell that to the people of the Atlantic provinces?
I realize I have only a short time to speak tonight. Here we are one year later and all of those things that members on the opposite side said were going to happen because of this free trade deal have fallen apart.
This government cannot be trusted. I believe we are seeing further evidence of that right now, not just for the Atlantic but for every region of this country.
We have interest rates and a dollar that are so high right now that our economy is on the verge of a total flip. This crisis in the fishery is going to go coast to coast. Those of us from central Canada, or those of us who are from the west, had better wake up and think. We had better realize that we are not exempt, that we are going to go through the same suffering that is happening in Atlantic Canada. Unless we start rallying and getting behind the people of Atlantic Canada on this problem, it soon will be on our doorsteps. I believe it is time to press this government to come to its senses.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister must give a directive to the Governor of the Bank of Canada to give us a break on interest rates so we can get this economy moving again. Madam Speaker, I see no alternative.

Madam Speaker, I have sat here this evening and I have listened to some really interesting speeches. I have learned a great deal. I can hardly believe some of the speeches that I heard in this House from the other side. I could not believe the insensitivity and the lack of realization as to the intent and the import of the decision of this government in not recognizing a crisis, a crisis that has not just happened today or yesterday, but one which my colleagues have been talking about since 1985. How this government could have allowed the situation to reach this point is beyond my ken.
I would say of my colleagues on this side of the House that as they reviewed the situation, it reminded me of my having spoken to this issue in 1985-86, talking about fishermen and women, fisher people. Some of the people in central Canada and some of the journalists in my riding of Mount Royal wanted to know what I was doing talking about fisher people. What I was talking
about was not as significant a crisis as the one I am talking about tonight.
When we listen to the concerned members of the Liberal party on this side of the House give the history and background of dramatic changes that have taken place in one of the most important basic and fundamental industries of this country, we realize that it is not something that just touches Atlantic Canada, Atlantic Canadians, it touches every Canadian.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
It is government's role to manage. This government has been absent from the field of management. I heard my colleagues talking about different kinds of fish and I do not pretend to know the industry, but they certainly talked about a variety of species that have not been caught, that are no being marketed, that are saleable in other parts of this world. Therefore, if they are saleable and edible in other parts of this world, they certainly can be marketed and sold here in Canada. Many people who live in Canada do not even know that we have these wonderful fish.
It is up to the government to have found the means to have marketed and the means to have taught or retrained fishermen if it meant fishing deeper, or using different kinds of equipment. That is what this government's role was. It was to manage. It was not to have me sit here and listen to the Minister for International Trade and the Secretary of State for External Affairs speak long before the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans spoke. Who is in charge and who is responsible? Who speaks out at the government table? It is absolutely unconscionable. He is put in third place if he is put in any place.
It really is a heartbreaking situation and I think that is what got to me the most. It is about men, women and children. There will be no Christmas for them this year, but what have we got for next year, and what have we got for the future? Some of them might even put out a Hanukkah bush if things would be different. But they can plan nothing for the future because what this government has done is literally close down cities and towns and villages.
I heard cultural genocide mentioned. That is a very harsh term, and we have seen what has happened in eastern Europe with real cultural genocide. But this is a genocide of a type. It is economic genocide, and it is cultural genocide when you have had a government that
December 18, 1989

has been so insensitive that it has not found the mechanism to enable families to stay in family homes.
Just remember what happened when there was a disaster in Baie Comeau when Iron Ore closed down. The then minister, Flora MacDonald, had a whole program to look after one little town, the Prime Minister's badly managed ex-company. When the wheat problems occurred out west, we rushed to their aid because our Deputy Prime Minister and many of our senior ministers come from the west.
What happens with the numbers which have been alluded to, and I do not pretend to have the numbers in front of me, but I heard mentioned over 10,000 jobs, and you look at the numbers of people who live in Atlantic Canada and do a percentage calculation, taking into account the fall-out that comes with that, and you know you are dealing with a serious crisis and a government which has not given a d-a-m-n! It is a sheer disgrace.
I would say, having heard my colleagues, just how much backbone this government has, whether it is going to talk to the Americans, shoot over the bow of the boat, whether it is talking to the Portuguese, to the Spanish, to the French. There has to be a way in the international market-place as well as in internal waters to find answers that will allow for a decent livelihood.
We cut VIA Rail so there is no way they can get out; we cut unemployment insurance so they cannot count on a decent way of life there. You cut out the possibility for welfare because the base of those municipalities is the fishing industry. What do you expect these people to do? Do we want everybody to come live in Montreal and Toronto? This is ridiculous. I should add Halifax to that.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it's true that it's late, it's true that just about everything there is to say on this subject has already been said in the course of the evening. I want to start by congratulating, with warm friendliness, our colleague for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. LeBlanc) who put forward this matter for debate this evening.

When I came to this House 25 years ago or more, I came as a Canadian. I came as a Canadian with a notion that wherever you come from in this country, you care for those who come from another region. I come from Montreal, from the province of Quebec. But I believe that I have a sense of solidarity. We have to have a sense of solidarity with the people who, at the moment, suffer the most in one part of our country.
If we want to define what Canada is all about to the rest of the world, I think we could say it is a different kind of country, built by different kinds of people with different kinds of problems. One of our major responsibilities as Canadians is to immediately come to the rescue of some of our Canadian compatriots who are going through a very severe crisis.
I does not matter if you come from Montreal, it does not matter if you know nothing about fisheries, it does not matter if you know nothing about agriculture. You know that these two major industries must be viable. You know that these two major industries must continue to prosper, because if they do so, all of Canada will prosper. If they are in danger of disappearing, it is a great part of our country, it is a great part of our history, it is a great part of our past that may disappear.
This sense of solidarity we have to express from time to time. I have never seen a debate with so much passion, devotion as I have seen tonight. As Winston Churchill once said, when there is a real crisis, you feel it. You feel it in the nervousness and the sensitivity. I felt that tonight. That is why I did not mind waiting to say a few words even though it is very late. I wanted to show my solidarity and to tell the Secretary of State for External Affairs that it was very strange that a debate on fisheries

December 18, 1989
was addressed first by the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I immediately caught when I saw him that he was probably ill at ease speaking before the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. That means he feels a sense of guilt for perhaps not having done more to help our compatriots in the Atlantic provinces.
It is not enough to say that I went to Europe and our trade is such that we must help them, we must not disturb our international trade, That is not the role of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He should go time after time to Europe to explain that in the long run, it is even in their own interests that the fishing industry is viable in Canada. If there is none for us today, then there will be none at all for them eventually.
In that sense you have to explain and negotiate very tightly, very intelligently with our allies and friends in Europe to convince them that it is their goddamn best interests. I do not know if that word is regular, but I get as upset as my colleagues because I feel what is going on is tremendously sad. Young families breaking-

-the discouragement, the despair, of people who are contributing to the development of this country, who are happy to belong to one of Canada's beautiful regions. I know the Maritimes. I've been there.
How can anyone remain indifferent in the face of a tragedy like this one? Do we want Canada to consist, as my colleagues often say, of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver? That's preposterous.
First of all we must show our solidarity with our colleagues from the Maritimes, with our fellow Canadians in the Atlantic provinces, because they are going through bitter days. It is the duty of everyone who is better off, of all luckier Canadians, to understand what is happening down there.
So, I have no hesitation in participating in the debate. I think the people from southern Ontario, when they lose their jobs, have multiple possibilities of finding other jobs immediately. This is not so with the people in the Atlantic provinces where whole families, villages and townships depend on this industry.
If it was an industry that should disappear, you would say, "Well, tough luck. Maybe it should disappear". But I do not believe it should disappear. I believe that if government takes its responsibility, if the government knows how to negotiate internationally first-that is the duty of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. After all, he asked for trouble, he spoke first tonight. He is taking part of the blame immediately by having offered to speak first.
I was expecting to learn more from the minister of fisheries. He does not need to tell us that we have obligations to our trading partners. I repeat, and will repeat and repeat again, his duty is to convince them that it is in their long-term interest that this industry remain viable in the Atlantic provinces.

speechtext: Hear, Hear!

speechtext:
What happens in a village when the main industry disappears? These young people represent for me, and always have, Canada's living strength, because you know, if all Canadians were city-dwellers this country would not have the same vitality, the same strength, the same renewal you have when the regions are prosperous. And God knows these people are sacrificing themselves in the Atlantic. We can't understand what it means to go out into danger, day after day! We don't have that experience in Montreal, we don't have it in Toronto. In some cities people probably have no idea what it means to be a fishermen, what risks they have to run.
And here I want to express my sympathy. There was an outpouring of sympathy in Montreal when that appalling tragedy occurred at the Universite de Montreal, but I also want to sympathize, and I think it is right and proper that during this debate we should spare a thought, as a number of my colleagues have done, for the fishermen who have had difficulties, because that too is a sign of solidarity.
I could have attacked the government myself. I listened to all my colleagues. I support what they said. I say it is the duty of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to negotiate with real feeling, because it's not enough just to say it once. Often the Europeans like to tell us how to behave here at home, on the question of seals, for example. We might also go and tell them, make them understand, invite them to come and see this tragedy. Let them come! The Secretary of


State for External Affairs has every opportunity in the world to display some imagination. Is he really so lacking in it? I wonder.
And to conclude, because you're signalling at me and you're quite right, I would like to make a special appeal to the Prime Minister of Canada. He has said to us in this House that when the people in the west experience difficulties the government knows how to shoulder its responsibilities. I recognize the importance of agriculture too. You can't talk to a Quebecker, a French Canadian, without finding, if you scratch, that he's from a farm family less than a generation or two ago, like me. I have cousins who are still farming today on the family land.
So I understand the agricultural system and I recognize its importance. And in this difficult world, we mustn't allow our agriculture to disappear, because then we would be at the mercy of others. And in international trade, we would have to pay whatever price those others felt like charging us. That's why we have to have viable agriculture in Canada, and the people in the big cities who don't understand that must be made to understand it.
But the same system applies in the case of the fisheries! If that industry disappears, we'll have to go elsewhere, when we have the fish right here. So in this holiday season I appeal directly to the Right Honourable Prime Minister, to do everything he said he would do, and more, because we cannot permit these tragedies, this despair we heard described this evening, this discouragement that must be seizing all those families. It is our duty, in the name of Canadian solidarity, to stand up, to use your patience a little, and to say that the government must intervene, and at once, not waiting for a day that may or may not dawn, but at once, as fast as it can.

Offshore is classified by vessels over 65 feet and inshore by vessels under 65 feet. It sounds oversimplistic to say, but this minister and the committee which are studying what to do with the problem were not even here tonight to hear the members from the Atlantic.
