speechtext:
Madam Speaker, not only is there an offshore and an inshore problem, it is a problem for the many hundreds of communities across the Atlantic provinces and the people who have no work and no prospect of having work. It is a problem for the spinoffs in those communities; the boat builders, the other businesses, the grocery stores. All businesses in a given community are suffering the plight that the member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso has brought to the attention of this House tonight.
We have not had one new idea from the government. Three ministers spoke but I do not want to use my time discussing what they spoke about or, more important, what they did not speak about. They wanted to blame their officials. They do not say that they have been in power for five years and they are continuing in power but incorporate no new ideas in the fishery that should be growing instead of stagnant on the east coast.
We cannot even have any assistance for these plants because of the free trade agreement. The companies would say: "No assistance because our market in the U.S. would be threatened". This government has so tied the east coast into its free trade agreement on subsidies that our whole fishery will suffer over the long term in terms of money, jobs and the lack of confidence in the fishery on the east coast which the government continues to bring about with its policies.
Canso is one town, but Lockeport, Lunenburg and Louisbourg are three major centres of fishing in Nova Scotia. We are talking offshore. I will get to my own area where it is only fishing. Those were year round operations in 1977. What is this government going to do with
its policy? What is the province of Nova Scotia going to do about allowing these towns to be totally cut off?
I know what happened in Lockeport. I have heard from the mayor and the people. I have followed it from the time it was closed. I advocated at that time that there be a community based allocation of fish, that the fish that had normally been landed there be left there and the community be allowed to handle the onshore plant and provide the work. If you do not give them fish, those communities have to die.
What do they get? What can the people in Canso and other areas where people have been laid off expect? They can expect a 10 week severance package and then unemployment. No other benefits. They are given three month's notice. It is inhuman that this government and the provincial government will allow anybody who has had a full, year-round job in those communities to be given three months' notice.
At least they have been given the notice. This Minister of Fisheries does not give three month's notice to the inshore communities that are cut off. He just tells them: "I am sorry, this week you have got your $25,000, then for the next six months there is nothing more". That is what happened at the end of June. That is what happened in all those communities in the Scotia-Fundy area south of Halifax.
The member for South Shore likes to say there are only draggers under 65 feet in South West Nova. There are some on the New Brunswick side, there are some on the South Shore. There are longliners over 45 feet and none of them have been working. They all appeared together, united, before the Hache committee to try to find a solution for the inshore. This minister tries to divide, tries to say there are only rich fishermen. He does not talk about the plant workers. He does not talk about the many people in the communities that are suffering. He just divides.
I said that there are solutions. They are pretty hard solutions perhaps, but this government has a chance to prove it. I think it should look at its groundfish management plan. In terms of the offshore, those boats that are no longer going to be fishing out of Canso and will be put aside should be allowed or encouraged to go for underutilized species and have a by-catch. They should be given a community based enterprise allocation, as Na-
December 18, 1989

tional Sea has had for the last five years. They should be encouraged to go for the under-utilized.
It is ironic to be discussing it now, but in 1977 the Government of Canada offered a subsidy to boats to go for northern cod. Imagine, northern cod, and we are all in trouble today with northern cod. The government offered a subsidy. Why can we not do that with underutilized species? We heard the minister say that there are 355,000 tonnes of under-utilized species but there is no market. Why do we not offer that same type of incentive? Why do we not allow those offshore boats that are not going to be able to fish and those onshore communities that have no hope from this government to be given some hope.
Give them some fish. That is all they need. That is all the communities in southern Nova Scotia need. They need a groundfish management plan that this minister cannot seem to adapt to the needs of the east coast.
What have we seen this government allow? We have seen it allow National Sea to put up a company in New Hampshire, to put up a company in France and to bring into its fleet two freezer factory ships that could keep two plants like Lockeport and Canso going. But no, we have to tell those communities that have been year-round communities that they cannot fish. They cannot work because there are no fish.
I think there is a solution and I just gave you one, Madam Speaker. Split the fleet from the National Sea and the offshore companies. Let the National Sea and those companies go to an exchange and let the fish be auctioned off. Allow them the incentive to bring in the under-utilized species when there are no more quotas. Unless you do that you are going to find that the inshore communities throughout the Atlantic coast are going to be shut down because of lack of incentives by this government.
We cannot compete with the foreigners unless we get out there and fish for the same thing that foreigners are fishing within our 200-mile limit and outside our 200-mile limit.
I do not know any people who do not want to work. They do not want three months' notice. They do not want 10 weeks' severance pay. They do not want one week after another and then to be shut down for six months. These are people, these are Canadians. We have a resource that is the envy of the world.
I can only say to you, Madam Speaker, that I have never seen the devastation that I have seen this year in South West Nova. This year there are 50 per cent more people claiming unemployment insurance because the groundfish management plan has not been able to accommodate, because his biologists do not have, in my view and in the view of many fishermen, reliable statistics. There are 20 per cent less people buying in the local grocery stores. If the local grocery stores are suffering like that, you can imagine what the other businesses are doing.
Yet this Minister of Fisheries can stand in the House and say that there is no hardship. The crisis is here. It has been here for a year. There are people who are suffering. It is not a very nice Christmas time. I know, Madam Speaker, that you are indicating that my time is up but I was interrupted by the member and I should have about another minute.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso for moving this motion. As the last speaker here in the House tonight, I also want to congratulate my colleagues, the members for Burin-St. George's, Bonavista-Trinity- Conception, Labrador and Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte for the very fine presentations they have given tonight.
I knew that the member for Humber-St. Barbe- Baie Verte was about to get very flamboyant and angry when I saw him repeat what an inshore fisherman had told him. I knew then his thoughts were that there were going to be in 1990 foreign ships just off his coast while the fishermen on the inshore look out and see the boat, and the fish plant worker who has been put out of work looks out and sees that 400-foot boat, and the offshore trawlerman, put ashore, looks out and sees that

December 18, 1989
enormous factory freezer trawler from St. Malo, France, catching codfish along the shores of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and the coast of Quebec in 1990. I knew, as every single fishermen knew who is watching the debate tonight, as every single fish plant worker knew who is watching the debate tonight, that they were very angry.
We have to draw a line here as to what fishing takes place. We were not even talking about foreign overfishing because in order to have overfishing you would have to be fishing over what you are licensed to fish. No, this member was talking tonight about ships that are licensed by the Government of Canada to fish within 12 miles of our coastline in Atlantic Canada.
You heard about the disaster of the longliner, 64 feet 11 inches I believe, from Shelburne County that tragically sank off the coast of Newfoundland just a couple of days ago. When you think about a boat that is 64 feet long coming from Shelburne, Nova Scotia, 100 miles, 200 miles, 300 miles, 500 miles, 600 miles to the coast of Newfoundland to fish, you realize that the fishermen in a 30-foot boat, the fishermen in a 50-foot boat, the fishermen in a 65-foot boat, and the fishermen in an 18-foot boat, all fish in the same zone 12 miles from our coast as does that factory freezer trawler from France that the hon. member was referring to.
It is not foreign overfishing, it is foreign fishing that we are talking about today, licensed by the Government of Canada. The minister said that these were under-utilized species. What are they? There is a quota of 16,000 tonnes of redfish. They might think that because it is called redfish it belongs to the Soviet Union. Well, it doesn't, it is what you would call ocean perch. We process it in our fish plants.
There are 27, 000 tonnes of Greenland halibut. Maybe the government believes that that belongs to Greenland. Well, it does not. It is what we call turbot.
There is American plaice. Now that is something. Maybe they think that belongs to the United States but then plaice really means a European flatfish, so are really confused about that one.
There are twenty-five thousand tonnes of cod. Just think about it. Just imagine if the fish plant workers in Canso, Nova Scotia, in St. John's, Newfoundland, if the inshore fishermen all along our coastline in eastern Canada who cannot get a codfish or a flatfish or a redfish because that is the fish we process. Any fish plant in eastern Canada, what do they process? They process 50 per cent cod, about 30 per cent flatfish and about 20 per cent of something else-redfish, pollock, whatever the case is. It is a mix. Add them up-16, 25 and 27. That is 68,000 tonnes. There is an average of 10,000 tonnes per fish plant average by National Sea per year. That is six fish plants. Six National Sea fish plants can be operated with just the quota given inside our 200-mile zone, licensed by the Government of Canada. That is why we are so angry.
We cannot seem to get it through their heads. They mention under-utilized species. The only under-utilized species there would perhaps be grenadier. That is a fish now that is about this long. It is a scrawny fish with a lot of needles on it. It has an enormous blown up head like some of those ministers over there.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext: It should be called the Mulroneyfish.

speechtext:
they can take legally. They have a 3 per cent by-catch of haddock. That is 3,000 tonnes. They have a 2 per cent by-catch of pollock. That is 2,000 tones.
The Soviet Union in its quota for silver hake off Nova Scotia has enough by-catch to keep Canso operating for an entire year. That is what we are talking about.
There is one thing about those foreign licences that really irks us. It is this. At this time when it is so bad, when our fish plants are closing, there is the problem of the inshore fishermen to consider. You have seen on television what is happening to the inshore fishery. The fellow in the boat goes out day after day and he gets one fish in an entire cod trap. He goes out jigging the next day and he gets one more fish. The stories are told all along the coastline. There are two rules in Canada today-one for the foreigners and the other for Canadian fishermen. The Soviet Union, Cuba, the Faro Islands, East Germany, Japan, Norway and Poland all get licences within our 200-mile zone this year for 1990. They can go out and have a by-catch of cod of 5,000 tonnes, and if they get 10,000 tonnes they can keep it. If they get 4,000 tonnes of pollock they can keep it.
When a Nova Scotian or a Newfoundlander catches one fish above his by-catch he is arrested and brought into court. In the foreigners' licence it says you can keep what you catch. The Government of Canada this year has embarked on a new program to allow our longliners, 65 feet long, to fish tuna. You can get $20,000 for an average bluefin tuna in the Japanese market. A fisherman can sometimes make $6,000 or $7,000 just selling a few bluefin tuna. It is a pretty valuable fish.
This year the Government of Canada told our fishermen that in the name of going into these areas that we are not into that it is going to give us a quota. It gave a quota to 12 boats for 175 tonnes of bluefin tuna, but it gave the Japanese fleet 180 tonnes by-catch of bluefin tuna in the same area. That is the Virgin Rocks. The Japanese get a higher quota than Canadians do on the bluefin tuna around the Virgin Rocks.
In 1990, this year, we are angry that the Government of Canada has agreed starting January 1 to increase the quotas to foreigners for what it calls the under-developed species of capelin and squid. If you were going to
go out in the ocean and catch a codfish as the Shelburne County longliners do, they go out with hook and line. What do they put on the hook? They put squid, capelin, a piece of mackerel or a piece of herring on the hook. Squid or mackerel is the main fish of the codfish. Here we are, and the Government of Canada is wondering why. It has a study on its desk that shows that the size of a codfish has gone down over 50 per cent in Nova Scotia. It has gone down 40 per cent in Newfoundland. Yet the government says that there is no proof that by giving to the foreigners 150,000 tonnes of feedstock that it is affecting us.
I will tell you how it is affecting our fishery. A man, a fisherman, whether a man or a woman today, cannot get a capelin licence unless they have a certain size of boat. They are not allowed by law past this year to move outside their own bay, while the foreigners get 38,000 tonnes in 1990. They can go wherever they want along the coastline of Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, P.E.I., New Brunswick and Quebec. How much do we get? We get 800 tonnes of that 38,000 tonnes quota for capelin off the east coast of Canada.
That is why we are so angry today. We are saying to the Government of Canada that when Canadians look at all those big trawlers they say: "How come National Sea ties up their trawlers in Canso? Why don't they go outside the 200-mile zone where the Europeans are and catch all the fish they want like the Europeans do?" That is a logical question, isn't it, Madam Speaker? What is the answer to that question? The answer is that Canada has agreed not to go outside the 200-mile zone. They cannot go out there and catch what they want. They have to abide by quotas. The United States can catch what it wants because it does not belong to NAFO. The Europeans can catch what they want because they do not agree with NAFO's quotas. We have to tie up our offshore fleet. We are boxed in and we cannot move.
The government wonders why people are so angry. We licence the Soviet Union. Why cannot the National Sea trawlers go off the Soviet Union and fish? They are not allowed. We licensed this year 15 factory-freezer trawlers for Japan. Why can't National Sea trawlers go off Japan? They are not allowed. They would be blown out of the water by that country.

December 18, 1989
We are the only country in the world today that restricts our own fishermen and allows every foreign nation that wants to come in here and get a piece of the action. In this year 1989 300,000 tonnes of fish were caught by foreign nations. Three years ago the United States threw out the Soviet Union and the Cubans from the Alaska coast. That ended it off the U.S. coast.
The EEC has a little exchange program. You will see countries going off each other's coast. Off the African coasts if you are willing to spend a lot of money in Africa in a certain country you can go there. If you want to build an institute you can go there and fish for a year.
Canada says we will give what the minister announced tonight as our underdeveloped or excess species to foreign countries. He says it is because we have to.
The writing is on the wall for this government. It must do the logical thing. First and foremost, when our inshore fishermen have no fish, when our fish plants cannot operate, the government of Canada must do one thing and one thing alone first. That is to stand up for Canadians and kick out the foreigners.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know anything I say will be a letdown after the great speakers who have spoken all evening. I watched the debate from my office. I heard every speaker from all three parties. I want to congratulate all the speakers who took part in tonight's debate.
We are not looking at just an Atlantic region problem. We are looking at a national crisis. That is why I am pleased that the hon. member moved this motion to draw the matter not only to the country's attention but also to the world's attention because this crisis is caused by countries around the world.
I will not take very much time because I know the parliamentary secretary was complaining earlier that he wants to go home. It is sad that he is not supported by any minister on his side. It is sad that one member is supporting the whole government side. It is even sadder that there is no spokesman here, no observer from the NDP, the so-called party of the disadvantaged.
In my riding and near my riding I have plants such as Stelco, Molson's, a chocolate factory, Inglis and I used to have General Electric. What I want to highlight is even if all of these factories closed tomorrow and laid off all the workers, it would not create the same crisis as the crisis which exists in the Atlantic fisheries because the workers from my riding in Toronto could drive one hour to Oshawa and be working at General Motors. They could be driving one hour in the other direction to Ford and be working there. They could drive another hour north and be working for de Havilland. Even though I could have six plant closings in one day, it would not hurt as much as this crisis is hurting the fishermen.
The reason I came here tonight is to show that two million people in Toronto are hurting today along with the fishermen in Canso by these plant closures. On behalf of my 92,000 constituents of Parkdale-High Park, we throw our support behind the people who are affected. We are hurting along with these people.
To close, I want to congratulate you, Madam Speaker, for being so patient and hearing all the speakers. I wish to thank the staff. Most of all I want to thank the mover of the motion and members of all three parties who spoke.
